The exegetes note that the address may be to the Prophet ﷺ and his community together, or to the polytheists alone, and that only a few of them remember and return to the truth. They agree that the protectors are whoever is followed apart from God: idols, soothsayers, rabbis and monks, and devils among jinn and humans who lead people to worship idols or to follow innovations and desires.

Ibn Kathir and others report that following includes the Sunnah alongside the Quran, relying on the verse "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it." Al-Hasan al-Basri said that each person is commanded to understand the meaning of every verse in order to act on it. Al-Tabari and those who follow him hold that the command is addressed to all people rather than to the Prophet alone, and that the verse implies leaving aside personal opinion when a clear text exists. Others consider the Prophet the primary addressee and the community included by extension.

The commentators differ over the pronoun in "besides Him". Most refer it to God, while others link it to "what was sent down" or to the Book itself. As for "little", al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan treat it as describing an implied noun, meaning rare remembrance, whereas others read it as a plain negation. Ibn Kathir compares this passage to the verse "Most people will not believe, however much you desire it."

This verse tells us that Allah destroyed many towns because their people rejected His messengers, and that His punishment came upon them suddenly, by night while they slept or at midday while they rested. The commentators agree that the word 'town' refers to its people, and that the purpose is to warn the listeners against a similar fate. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that night and the midday rest were singled out because they are times of ease and heedlessness, so punishment then is more severe; al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi agree. The problem of the destruction being mentioned before the coming of punishment, though punishment caused it, has several answers. Al-Farra' holds that the fa' here means waw and implies no order, others read it as 'we intended to destroy', and al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy take the second clause as an explanation of the first. As for the people's claim, al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy take it as a plea or supplication, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi take it as a claim; most explain that they ended by admitting their wrongdoing. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith from Ibn Mas'ud stating that no people perish until they are made to face their own fault. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also note that Allah will question the nations about how they answered their prophets, and the prophets about how they delivered the message. The commentators do not decide between these readings.

This verse tells us that God destroyed many cities when His punishment reached them, either by night while they slept or by day during their midday rest, a time of ease and heedlessness. The commentators largely agree on the meaning: what those people said when the punishment came was neither a useful supplication nor a useful claim, but only an admission that they had been wrongdoers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this confession came when it could no longer help them, and al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi read it similarly, though al-Tabari takes the word da'wa here to mean supplication.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan prefer the sense of claim: what they had been asserting about their religion, which dwindled into an admission that it was false. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that this does not exclude the meaning of supplication. On the grammar of the verse, al-Farra' reads the particle fa (then) as wa (and), since the punishment seems to arrive before the destruction; al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur take the punishment as an explanation of the destruction, and others say the verse means that God intended to destroy them.

Scholars also differ on whether the destruction targets the city itself or its people. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur add that the warning is directed at the people of Mecca, who are reminded that they too could be struck in the same way.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection God will question the nations to whom messengers were sent about how they answered their messengers, and will question the messengers about whether they delivered the message and how their peoples responded. The commentators agree that this questioning is one of rebuke and reproach for the disbelievers, not a question asked to gain knowledge, since nothing is hidden from God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi report that the nations are asked what they answered their messengers and the messengers are asked whether they conveyed the message. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi explain that the purpose is to establish proof and to rebuke the unbelievers, while al-Zamakhshari adds that God, who knows everything, asks in order to draw out confession.

The scholars differ on the question denied in another verse, which says that the guilty will not be questioned about their sins. Al-Razi and al-Alusi understand the denied questioning as a request for information, or as questioning about the motives behind deeds, while others hold that the Day of Judgment has several stages, with questioning at some and not at others. Al-Shinqiti distinguishes the denied questioning about sins from the affirmed questioning of rebuke and testimony.

Some commentators also discuss the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgment. Ibn 'Abbas reports that the scales may weigh the records, the persons, or the deeds themselves shown in visible form, and that a believer's deed comes in its best form. Mujahid takes the weighing to mean the perfect justice of the judgment. Al-Razi notes the questions of how a deed can be weighed, and the wisdom behind such a weighing, namely to test believers and to establish the proof against the unbelievers.

This verse says that God will question the nations to whom messengers were sent about how they responded, and will also question the messengers about their delivery, and then will recount to them their deeds with full knowledge, nothing escaping Him. The commentators generally agree that this questioning is meant as rebuke, reproach and establishing proof, not as a request for information, since God knows everything. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya understand the questioning of the peoples as concerning their response to their messengers, and that of the messengers as concerning their delivery, citing other verses such as God asking the messengers what answer they received. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it as reproach after the people have confessed their wrongdoing, and Al-Razi adds that what is asked is the motives and the obstacles rather than the deeds themselves. Ibn Abbas explains the phrase "with knowledge" as the book of their deeds speaking against them, a view al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, though they judge the divine knowledge reading closer to the truth. Ibn Atiyya suggests the expression may be figurative. As for "We were not absent", most read it as God's complete knowledge and encompassing awareness of their acts. Al-Razi draws from it the argument that God is not in a place or direction, and the Sunni scholars reply that absence here means knowledge and encompassment. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that the interrogation serves reproach, and that a question seeking information is excluded for God. Several exegetes reconcile this with verses denying that the sinners are questioned about their sins, by distinguishing different stations of the Day of Judgment or different kinds of questioning.

This verse states that the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgment is true and free of any wrong. Those whose scales are heavy with good deeds are the successful and the saved. Most commentators understand the weighing to be that of deeds or their records, which displays perfect justice and removes any excuse. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi describe a balance with a tongue and two pans, and cite the hadith of the card bearing the testimony of faith as well as the hadith of the stout man who will not weigh the wing of a gnat. Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-A'mash understand the word as a figure for justice and judgment, a view later adopted by some scholars and by the Mu'tazilites, who hold that deeds, being accidents, cannot be weighed. Al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi list several views on what is weighed: the deeds themselves, their records, or the persons. Al-Hasan al-Basri held that each person has his own balance, while the majority hold that there is a single balance and that the plural refers to the many things weighed. Success is generally explained as salvation, achieving the good, and entering Paradise, while losing oneself means ruin and eternal abode in the Fire. Ibn al-Qayyim discusses those whose good deeds outweigh their bad, and whether the lighter deeds are cancelled out. Al-Alusi and others note that the concrete nature of the balance remains a matter of debate. All agree that the word translated as wronging in the verse means denying and rejecting the signs of God.

This verse describes the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgment: the one whose good deeds outweigh his bad ones is among the successful, while the one whose scales are light has lost himself by denying and rejecting the signs of God. The commentators agree on this general meaning, with the loss understood as the loss of the soul, meaning the forfeiting of reward and the entry into punishment. They differ, however, on what the weighing is. The majority, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, hold that there is a real balance with two pans and a tongue, on which the records of deeds, the deeds themselves, or their doers are weighed, relying on the hadith of the card of testimony and the hadith of the heavy man who weighs no more than a gnat's wing. Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-A'mash understood the weighing as a figure of speech for just judgment, while the Mu'tazila denied a literal scale because accidents cannot be weighed. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the literal reading stronger, whereas al-Zamakhshari reports both views without choosing. Scholars also differ on the plural 'mawazin': some take it as the plural of 'mawzun', meaning the weighed deeds, others as one scale expressed in the plural, and al-Hasan holds that each person has his own balance, a view most reject. Al-Razi and others understand the verse as referring to disbelievers, while Ibn al-Qayyim discusses mixed cases where good deeds outweigh bad ones. The second verse, on God's establishing people on earth and providing livelihood, is noted by al-Tabari, who prefers the reading without a hamza in 'ma'ayish', a hamza being judged unusual in Arabic.

This verse reminds people that God established them on the earth and gave them the means to live in it, then notes how little they give thanks. The commentators explain the word tamkin in two ways: God gave them a place and a dwelling on the earth, or He gave them dominion over it and power to act within it. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi mention both senses, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi favour the first. As for ma'ayish, most take it to mean what people live on, such as food and drink, while others understand the means of obtaining them, such as farming, trade and crafts. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi give both, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di include plants, minerals and trades. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan add that some provisions come directly from God, like fruits, and others through human effort, and that all of them are blessings.

On the closing phrase, qalilan ma tashkurun, there is broad agreement that gratitude is scarce. Al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi, citing Ibn Abbas, take it to mean that they are not thankful at all, whereas Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn say that most are only slightly grateful. Al-Razi notes that people do sometimes give thanks, but unevenly. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the address is to the polytheists, and that their worship of others is why their gratitude is so small.

On recitation, the majority read ma'ayish without a hamza, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya consider correct because the yā' is original. Al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-A'mash and Ibn 'Amir, and Nafi' through Kharija, are reported to read it with a hamza. The Basran grammarians called this an error, but Abu Hayyan defends it, citing the reliability of its transmitters and similar forms in Arabic.

God reminds humankind of a favour rooted in their origin: He created their father Adam from clay, gave him a fine form, and then commanded the angels to prostrate before him in honour. They all prostrated except Iblis, who refused out of pride. The commentators differ on the meaning of the creation and the shaping mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak understood creation as referring to Adam himself and shaping as referring to his descendants in the wombs. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, followed by Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud, held that the whole passage concerns Adam alone, the plural being a mark of honour for the father of mankind. Mujahid held that both took place in Adam's back when the covenant was taken, while 'Ikrima and al-A'mash placed creation in the loins of fathers and shaping in the mothers' wombs, and Ma'mar said all of it occurs in the womb.

The particle "thumma" raised a difficulty, since the command to the angels seems to come after the creation of the descendants though it actually preceded it. Al-Tabari explained that it marks a break rather than immediate succession, others accepted a reversed order, and al-Akhfash read it as "wa". Al-Razi took creation and shaping to mean divine decree and the recording of forms in the Preserved Tablet, which he found the most convincing reading. Opinions also differ on the prostration itself: most treat it as a respectful salute, while others see Adam as a direction of prayer like the Ka'ba.

All agree on Iblis's argument that he is better because he was made of fire and Adam of clay, and on his punishment of being cast out of Paradise. Ibn 'Abbas considered him the first to reason by flawed analogy, and Ibn Sirin noted that sun worship arose from analogy. On Iblis's nature, al-Hasan held that he was not among the angels, while most scholars regard him as an exception among them or as belonging to the jinn, a kindred order.

This verse recounts God's rebuke of Iblis for refusing to bow to Adam when commanded, and his reply that he is better than Adam because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay. The commentators agree that the question is one of reproach rather than a request for information, and that the refusal was a plain act of disobedience. On the particle "lā" in "allā tasjud", al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, followed by most, treat it as an emphatic addition, while others hold it meaningful; al-Tabari proposes an implied phrase meaning "what compelled you not to prostrate", which Ibn Kathir calls strong and sound. As for Iblis's answer, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya say it is not a direct reply but a statement that contains the answer and an argument. Al-Tabari holds that Iblis erred in preferring fire to clay, since clay has steadiness, patience and humility while fire has lightness and haste. Several scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, call Iblis the first to use analogy, and some cite the passage against restricting a general text by analogy. Al-Razi argues at length for the superiority of fire's substance, whereas Ibn Sa'di and al-Biqa'i reject this ranking, holding that worth lies in purpose rather than origin. Most conclude that the command implies obligation and that Iblis's disobedience, rooted in contempt for Adam, brought his expulsion and punishment.

God tells Iblis to go down from the garden, since it is not fitting for him to be arrogant there, and to leave because he has become one of the humbled and debased. The commentators agree that arrogance is a disobedience unfitting for the place of the obedient, and that sagharr is the humiliation that befalls the proud, reversing his aim. They differ on the meaning and place of the descent. Al-Tabari, al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi take it as a descent from the Garden, and Ibn Kathir notes it could also refer to the lofty station he held. Al-Hasan and others place it in the heavens, a view favoured by al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi. Abu Rawq reads it as a change of his fiery form, while al-Samani reports it as a descent to the islands of the sea. On arrogance, some take it as defiance of God, others as refusing to prostrate before Adam. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the phrase 'it is not for you' as a denial of propriety rather than a permission for pride elsewhere. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya examine Iblis's argument from the superiority of fire over clay; most judge it a flawed analogy, and al-Razi uses it against analogy overriding a text. Al-Shinqiti stresses that God treats him in the opposite way to his intent, and Ibn Kathir notes that the humiliation fits the arrogance.

This verse reports Iblis asking God to grant him respite until the day when mankind is resurrected, meaning that he should be given time and not be made to die. The commentators agree that he sought this so as never to taste death, since there is no death after resurrection, and so that he could mislead the descendants of Adam and take revenge for his expulsion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, along with Ibn 'Atiyya, explain that the respite God granted ends at the first blast of the trumpet, when all creatures die, as the verse in Surat al-Hijr about the 'known time' makes clear. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that others hold that this known time is a secret in God's knowledge that Iblis does not know, and he mentions a weak report about his death at Badr. Al-Razi sets out the arguments of both sides on whether knowing the time of one's death encourages disobedience. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan observe that this respite is a trial for the servants, who are thereby tested through obedience and disobedience. Ibn 'Ashur holds that God's reply announces something already decreed rather than granting a request. Opinions differ on the scope of the respite: al-Tabari holds that it also covers all who will remain until the Hour, while others see it as specific to Iblis. Sayyid Qutb emphasises that the permission is part of the testing of mankind.

This passage recounts Iblis asking God to delay his fate until the day of resurrection, and God replying, "You are among those given respite." The commentators agree that this respite is not a granting of his request as he intended, since he wanted to avoid death, whereas God specifies elsewhere that it lasts until "the appointed time." Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that this is the first blast of the trumpet, when all creatures die. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that another view holds that this appointed time is known to God alone, and that Iblis will die at a moment only God knows. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi add that those still alive at the Hour are also given respite, and that Iblis is among them.

The commentators also differ on the meaning of the word "misled" which Iblis attributes to God. Most, such as al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, understand it as leading astray, while al-Hasan takes it to mean cursing and Ibn al-Anbari destruction. Al-Razi notes that the verse reveals Iblis's uncertainty on the question of predestination. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the respite serves to test God's servants. Al-Alusi records a debate on whether an unbeliever's supplication may be answered, some seeing it as a form of gradual testing.

As for his claim "I am better than him," Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Atiyya describe it as a flawed analogy. Finally, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand the "straight path" as the way of Islam, while others such as Mujahid take it as the truth, and Ibn Mas'ud and 'Awn as the road to Mecca.

The Qur'an here gives Iblis's words after he has been granted respite until the Day of Resurrection: because You have led me astray, I will lie in wait for humankind on Your straight path, that is, the way of Islam, to turn them from it. Most commentators understand the verb 'to lead astray' as causing a person to lose the way: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and the majority take it as misguidance, al-Hasan as cursing, and others as destruction or being cut off from mercy. Al-Tabari notes that 'ghayy' in Arabic means corruption and ruin. As for the straight path, Mujahid explains it as the truth, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah as the road to Mecca, Jabir as Islam, while Ibn al-Qayyim argues that all these phrases describe one route leading to God. Grammarians differ on the structure: many take the particle 'bi' as an oath or a causal marker, others read it as 'li', and most supply the omitted word 'on' before the path. Al-Zamakhshari presents the verb as a constant ambush. Several scholars cite the hadith of Sabra ibn Abi al-Fakih, in which Satan sits on the paths of Islam, emigration and jihad; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir use it to extend the path to every way of good. Ibn Kathir regards Iblis's words as a guess that came true. The Mu'tazilites read the misguidance as a command to prostrate, which Sunni scholars reject, attributing misguidance to God; al-Razi treats this as a theological dispute.

The commentators explain that Iblis, after being granted respite until the appointed day, declared that he would sit in ambush on the straight path of the children of Adam and come at them from every direction. The early scholars gave related meanings to the four directions. According to Ibn Abbas, what is before them is the Hereafter, which he casts doubt upon; what is behind them is this world, which he makes attractive; the right side stands for good deeds, from which he discourages them; and the left side stands for evil deeds, which he makes appealing. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and others gave closely related explanations, such as that the directions express temptation from every possible side. The top is omitted, they say, because mercy descends from above, and the bottom because approaching from below would be alienating. Al-Tabari considers the most sound view to be that Satan comes to a person through all the paths of truth and falsehood, turning him from the truth and adorning falsehood for him. Ibn Abbas and others take shukr to mean faith in God's oneness, Muqatil takes it as thankfulness for blessings, and al-Hasan as steadfastness in obedience. Scholars differ over how Iblis knew this: some say it was a guess that happened to be correct, others that he read it in the Preserved Tablet or learned it from the angels. Al-Razi offers further readings that link the directions to the faculties of the soul, doubts and desires, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi present the verse as a picture of persistent temptation. Several commentators conclude that the verse establishes Satan's enmity toward the children of Adam, and that protection from him lies in remembering God and being grateful for His favours.

This verse reports that God commanded Iblis to leave the Garden, described as blameworthy and cast out, and swore that He would fill Hell with him and with every one of Adam's descendants who follow him. The commentators agree that "madhu'um" means blamed or despised, and that "madhur" means expelled and removed from God's mercy. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the first term as disgraced or repudiated, al-Suddi and Mujahid as banished and driven away, and Ibn 'Abbas as hated. Scholars of language differ on the exact sense of the root: al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as simple reproach, Ibn Qutayba as blame in the strongest terms, and al-Akhfash as a more severe fault than ordinary censure. As for the lam in "liman tabi'aka", most exegetes, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, treat it as the introductory lam of an oath, while a reading transmitted from 'Asim with a kasra ties it to the threatened punishment. Most commentators hold that the pronoun "minkum" includes Iblis, his offspring and the humans who follow him, the masculine plural taking precedence over the absent party. Ibn Kathir links the passage to several other verses that express the same meaning.

The verse reports God's words to Adam and his wife: dwell in the Garden, eat from it freely wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers. The commentators agree that the command addresses Adam and his wife together, that they were allowed the Garden's fruits in general, and that one tree was excluded. Most also see the prohibition as a test of obedience. They differ on the Garden itself: al-Mawardi reports two views, the eternal Garden of paradise or a worldly garden without religious obligation, while al-Shawkani and al-Sha'rawi describe it as a place of training for the earthly vicegerency rather than the garden of reward. On the identity of the tree, Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said wheat, al-Suddi a vine, Ibn Jurayj a fig tree, 'Ali a camphor tree, and others the tree of immortality; al-Mawardi lists six opinions, and Ibn Sa'di judges its identity unknown and of no practical benefit. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur examine the particle fa, which signals eating after dwelling, in contrast with the waw of al-Baqara. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that most exegetes hold Adam deliberately committed the forbidden act, while others hold he erred by thinking the prohibition applied only to one specific tree. Some jurists drew on the verse in the debate over whether things are presumed forbidden, permitted, or left in suspense, and Ibn 'Atiyya sets out these divided positions. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that exposing nakedness is a grave matter, and notes that forbidding approach is a stronger warning than forbidding eating, since it closes the path to sin.

God tells us that Satan whispered to Adam and his wife Eve in order to expose to them what had been hidden of their private parts. He told them that their Lord had forbidden them this tree only so that they would not become two angels or be among the immortals, and he swore that he was a sincere adviser to them. The commentators explain that waswasa means a quiet, repeated murmur, and that the lam in liyubdiya may indicate result rather than purpose, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold, while others take it as a deliberate intention to harm. They differ on how their nakedness was covered before the sin: Wahb ibn Munabbih and Mujahid speak of a light that shielded them, others of a covering like a fingernail, and Ibn Abbas thinks the cover was removed only after eating. On the word malakayn, the reading with a fatha is the common one, while Ibn Abbas and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir read it with a kasra, meaning two kings, supported by the verse about a kingdom that does not decay. Scholars debated what this passage implies about whether angels surpass prophets; some accept that reading, while others reply that the desire was for angelic qualities rather than their rank. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the oath was a deception, and Qatada remarks that a believer may be deceived by someone swearing by God. Adam, who did not imagine anyone would swear falsely by God, was taken in, and repentance followed.

In this verse, God reports that after whispering to Adam and his wife, Satan swore to them by God that he was one of their sincere advisers in urging them to eat from the tree. Most commentators understand the word 'qasamahuma' as 'he swore to them'. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir state that he swore by God until he deceived them, citing verses by the poet Khalid ibn Zuhayr al-Hudhali and by al-A'sha. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, on the authority of Qatada and Ibn Abbas, that Adam thought no one would swear by God falsely and was thus deceived, and some scholars said: whoever deceives us by God, we are deceived by him. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that the reciprocal form may mean that he swore to his sincerity and they swore to accept it, or that he divided the oath by assigning good to them and harm to himself, a reading also given by al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya remark that the form can have a single agent, as in 'afahu Allah'. Al-Razi also gives the explanation that Satan claimed to have been created before them and to know realities they did not. Ibn al-Qayyim sees this oath as the first of Satan's tricks, as he took on the appearance of sincerity to win their trust. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the connective phrasing suggests that Adam and his wife hesitated, which led Satan to press them with the oath. The commentators do not settle between these readings; they agree that a false oath by God is Satan's sin and that a believer can be deceived by such an oath.

The commentators explain that Satan deceived Adam and Eve with false oaths until they ate from the tree, thereby moving from obedience to disobedience. When they tasted the tree, their private parts, previously hidden, became visible to them, and they began to stick leaves of the Garden over themselves to cover up. Their Lord then called out to them with a rebuke, reminding them of His prohibition and of Satan's manifest enmity. The exegetes agree that ghurur means showing sincere advice while concealing deceit, and that covering nakedness is a natural instinct whose exposure is reprehensible. The address is read as a reproach for transgressing the prohibition and for trusting the enemy's words. They differ on the tree, which was said to be the ear of grain, the vine, or something else, and on the leaves, with Ibn 'Abbas and most commentators naming fig leaves while others name banana leaves. They also differ on the garment worn before the sin, Wahb ibn Munabbih describing light, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas a nail-like covering, and others a ruby. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b about Adam fleeing and a tree catching his hair, with Ibn Kathir noting the stopped version is sounder than the version traced to the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi discuss whether the call was direct or through an intermediary. Al-Razi notes that the interrogative form serves as reproach, and Ibn al-Qayyim sees Satan's trick as a promise of immortality. Some hold the prohibition to be absolute, while most read it as a recommendation.

This verse records the confession of Adam and Eve after they tasted the tree and their nakedness became visible: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers." The commentators agree that this confession and plea is itself repentance, in contrast to Iblis, who did not admit his fault. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that Adam asked for repentance and was granted it, while Iblis asked for respite. Al-Dahhak identifies these words with the words Adam received from his Lord, as mentioned in Surat al-Baqara.

The verse is also used in debates about minor sins. Al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and Al-Alusi take it as evidence that minor sins can be punished if not forgiven, while Al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites explain that the prophets and righteous magnify small faults out of humility, and that avoiding major sins expiates minor ones. Al-Razi holds that the act occurred before prophethood, and Ibn al-Qayyim connects it to a state of weakness. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that they called their fault wrongdoing even though it was minor.

Several exegetical details are discussed. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi mention various identifications of the tree and of the leaves of Paradise (fig, banana), and the garment of light or of nail that covered them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw from the verse the duty to cover the nakedness. Al-Jaza'iri stresses that repentance requires acknowledgement and a plea for forgiveness.

This verse reports that God commanded Adam, Eve and Iblis, and according to some commentators also the serpent, to descend from the Garden to the earth. He states that some of them will be enemies to one another, and that they will have a place of settlement and enjoyment for a set term. The commentators agree that the address includes Adam, Eve and Iblis, but differ on whether the serpent is included. Ibn Kathir holds that the core enmity is between Adam and Iblis, with Eve following Adam and the serpent following Iblis if its mention is sound. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan take the phrase about being enemies to one another as a circumstantial clause, meaning that they will be hostile. On the place of settlement, al-Tabari understands a resting place and a dwelling for life, while Ibn Abbas relates it to the graves, and Ibn Atiyya holds that the word covers both life and residence in the graves. For the term, al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas understand the end of the worldly life, while Ibn Atiyya takes it as the appointed time of each person's death. The next sentence, 'therein you will live, therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth', is generally read as explaining this settlement, leading to resurrection.

This verse records God's words to Adam, Eve and Satan, according to most commentators, that they will live on the earth, die there, and be brought out from it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that all the pronouns refer to the earth: it is where life is lived, where death occurs, and from it people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Baghawi, al-Jalalayn and Abu al-Su'ud likewise understand the bringing out as the resurrection from the graves. Ibn Kathir presents this as an irrevocable decree from God, whose purpose is reward and punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya link the verse to the preceding statement that the earth is a dwelling and a provision for a time, and note that a person lives and is buried only on the earth. The main difference concerns the reading of the verb "tukhrajun": Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the ta, while the others read it with a damma. On who is addressed by the command to descend, al-Razi limits it to Adam, Eve and Iblis, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir add the serpent. Several commentators, such as Ibn Sa'di and al-Qasimi, relate the passage to the reminder of God's favours, especially the clothing that covers nakedness.

In this verse God reminds the children of Adam of a favour: He sent down clothing to cover their private parts, and finery, the word rish, meaning what one adorns oneself with in clothes and wealth. The commentators report that some Arabs in the pre-Islamic period circled the Kaaba naked, and the verse rejects that practice. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that rish mainly means wealth or adornment, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean beauty, and Mujahid and Ibn Abbas take it to mean property. As for the word sent down, most read it figuratively: God created these garments or sent down their causes, such as the rain that makes cotton and wool grow, whereas al-Zamakhshari holds that whatever is on earth is treated as sent from heaven because it was decreed and recorded there. On the garment of piety, opinions vary: Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj say it is faith, Ibn Abbas says good deeds and a good bearing, Mu'adh... Mu'bad al-Juhani says modesty, Urwa ibn al-Zubayr says fear of God, and Ibn Zayd says covering the nakedness. Al-Tabari adopts a comprehensive reading that includes faith, good works, modesty and fear of God. Ibn Amir and al-Kisa'i read the word in the accusative, linking it to the earlier garment, while the others read it in the nominative, which changes the grammatical structure. The verse closes by describing all this as one of God's signs, so that people may take heed.

This verse warns the children of Adam not to be led astray by Satan as he led their parents Adam and Eve out of Paradise, stripping them of their garment so that their private parts were exposed. It notes that Satan and his offspring see humans while humans cannot see them. The commentators agree that the prohibition, though addressed to Satan, is in essence a warning to people not to follow him, and that attributing the expulsion and the stripping to Satan reflects his role as the cause. The word fitna is explained as trial or seduction. They differ over the garment that was removed. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima say it was the fingernails, left as an adornment; Wahb ibn Munabbih says it was light; Mujahid says it was piety. Ibn al-Jawzi also cites garments of Paradise, and al-Razi prefers this view because the unqualified word libas suggests it. al-Tabari declines to choose and holds that each explanation is possible since no conclusive report settles the matter. On the word qabil, meaning Satan's kin or host, Mujahid and most scholars take it to mean jinn and devils, Ibn Zayd takes it to mean his descendants, and al-Suddi his generation. The question of whether jinn can be seen has been much debated. al-Zamakhshari, followed by the Mu'tazilites, concludes that they cannot be seen by humans, whereas Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi reply that the verse denies only ordinary sight and that authentic hadiths report exceptional appearances. Finally, the statement that God made the devils allies of those who do not believe is read by some as leaving them free to act, by others as granting them power over unbelievers, and by others as a matter of shared nature.

This verse reports that when the idolaters committed a gross indecency, they justified it by saying they had found their fathers doing it and that God had commanded it. God replies that He does not command indecency and rebukes them for speaking about Him without knowledge. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, take the indecency to be circumambulating the Kaaba naked. Al-Tabari notes that men circled by day and women by night, and that the Quraysh, called the Hums, circled in their clothes while other Arabs went naked. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir add that the rest of the Arabs did so out of a belief that they should not circle in garments they had sinned in, and Mujahid and Ibn Zayd speak of uncovering the private parts. Al-Hasan and 'Ata' understand it as shirk, al-Kalbi as the practice of the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and ham, and al-Razi extends it to every major sin.

The commentators agree that the argument from imitation of the fathers is no path to knowledge, and that the claim that God commanded it is a fabrication. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi observe that God leaves the first argument unanswered because its invalidity is obvious. Al-Zamakhshari, following Mu'tazili doctrine, holds that God does not will evil, whereas al-Alusi and al-Qasimi report the Sunni reply that command and will are distinct. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the verse does not invalidate taqlid in all matters, only in those whose wrongness is manifest.

The following verse, saying that God commands justice and that people should direct their faces toward every mosque, is explained by al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir as referring to facing the Kaaba in prayer. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith that each person is resurrected in the state in which he died, and mentions the various views on the meaning of 'as He originated you, so you will return.'

This verse reports that God commanded His Messenger to tell the pagans that his Lord orders justice, not the indecencies they claimed their fathers practised and that God had commanded. Commentators differ on the phrase "set your faces upright at every place of prostration." Mujahid, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean facing the Kaaba in prayer wherever one is. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas understands it as sincerity in prostrating to God alone, without idols, and al-Tabari prefers this reading because the audience was pagan Arabs who had no churches. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak read it as praying in whichever mosque prayer time finds you, without postponing it. "Call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him" is generally understood as pure worship free of association. On "as He began you, so you will return," the views vary. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others say people will be raised in the state in which they died, happy or wretched, believer or disbeliever, citing a hadith narrated by Jabir. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand a return after annihilation, as in the first creation, which al-Tabari adopts. Sa'id ibn Jubayr sees it as meaning that you will become what was decreed for you. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim note that these views can be combined: God guided one group and left another in error, and those who went astray took the devils as allies while thinking they were rightly guided.

This verse states that people divide into two groups by God's will and decree: one group that God guided and enabled to believe, and another upon whom misguidance was made binding, so that they remained in it. The reason the commentators give is that this second group took the devils as allies besides God and obeyed them, while still thinking they were rightly guided. Most exegetes take this plain meaning, and several, including al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, conclude that the mistaken disbeliever and the stubborn one deserve the same blame. Al-Tabari also draws from the verse that God does not punish a sin or error unless it was committed with knowledge of the right path, but this point is disputed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qadi read the verse in line with Mu'tazili principles, taking guidance as reward and misguidance as punishment, while al-Razi uses it to argue that guidance and misguidance come from God and answers the Mu'tazila. Ibn al-Qayyim cites Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said a person may act like the people of guidance and yet return to what he was created for, and links this to a hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, though he admits this is contested as the verse's meaning. Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Abbas and Mujahid understood "as He began you, so you will return" to mean that people will be resurrected in the state in which they were created, believer or disbeliever. The reading attributed to Ubayy, "you will return in two groups", supports this sense, according to Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari.

This verse tells the children of Adam to take their adornment, meaning what covers their nakedness and beautifies them, at every place of prostration, that is at prayer and at circumambulation, and to eat and drink without excess. The commentators relate that the occasion of revelation was the custom of some Arabs in the pre-Islamic period of circling the Ka'ba naked. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite, through Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others, that women would circle the House with only a cloth over their private parts, and that the verse abolished this practice. They largely agree that the adornment means the garment that covers the nakedness. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir derive from it the obligation to cover the body during prayer, while al-Alusi considers wearing one's finest clothes to be a recommendation. Other views, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Zamakhshari, take adornment to mean the comb, perfume or sandals, but these remain minority opinions.

As for food and drink, according to al-Kalbi, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, the verse responded to those who, out of devotion during the pilgrimage, forbade themselves meat and fat. The commentators agree that extravagance means going beyond the proper limit. Ibn 'Abbas said there is no excess in what is lawful, excess lying in disobedience. Ibn Zayd understood it as eating what is forbidden, al-Zajjaj as eating beyond need, and al-Suddi as forbidding what is lawful. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also read a warning against gluttony and its harm to the body. Some scholars claim the verse gathers the principles of medicine, and the story of the Christian physician is cited, though Ibn Kathir and others do not rely on that anecdote.

This verse rebukes those who forbid for people the adornment God created for His servants and the good sustenance He provided. The commentators agree that the question is rhetorical and denies any such prohibition, so that clothing and food are permitted in principle. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link the revelation to Arabs who went naked around the Kaaba and forbade themselves some good things. Al-Tabari reports that the good things may mean meat and fat forbidden during the pilgrimage, while Qatada and Ibn Abbas understand the bahira and sa'iba animals the pagans had prohibited. On the meaning of adornment, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi take it to be the clothing that covers the body, whereas al-Razi and al-Qurtubi extend it to anything that beautifies. Regarding the phrase saying these gifts are for believers in this life and exclusively on the Day of Resurrection, Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that unbelievers share them in this world but they are reserved for believers in the hereafter, while Ibn Jarir and al-Hasan take the exclusivity to mean freedom from grief and distress. Nafi' reads the last word in the nominative, while the other readers use the accusative, a choice al-Tabari prefers. The verse ends by stating that God thus explains His signs for people who know.

This verse lists the prohibitions that God has established: gross sins, whether open or hidden, sin in general, wrongful oppression of others, associating partners with God without evidence, and speaking about God without knowledge. The commentators agree on the main lines: the verse answers pagans who had forbidden lawful things on their own authority, such as adornment and good food. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di explain the gross sins as serious wrongs, chiefly sexual, and al-Sa'di adds inner faults such as pride and showing off. Mujahid links them to circling the Kaaba naked and to fornication, while Ibn 'Abbas speaks of public and secret fornication. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the gross sins to be major offences and sin in general to be broader. Most exegetes hold that sin means any wrongdoing. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and one report from Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean wine, but Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nahhas and Abu Hayyan reject this, noting the sura is Meccan. On oppression, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir describe it as tyranny and arrogance, while Tha'labi understands it as slandering others without right. Associating partners with God is condemned as lacking any proof, and al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim draw from this an argument against blind imitation in religion.

The verse states that every community has a fixed term, and when it arrives, its people cannot delay it by a single moment or bring it forward. Al-Tabari reads it as a threat to the polytheists of Makkah, who falsely attributed their practices to God, and as a reminder of what befell earlier nations. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Muqatil, understand the term as the time set for the punishment that destroys a rebellious people, and al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi follow this reading, while Ibn Kathir takes a community to mean a generation. Al-Razi reports this view and prefers it, while mentioning a second view that the term is each person's lifespan. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also speak of an individual term, and al-Qurtubi uses the verse to argue that a person who is killed dies at his appointed time, rejecting the view of many Mu'tazilites. Al-Mawardi lists three meanings: a written decree of happiness or misery, given by Juwaybir; a prophet sent to each nation, given by Mu'adh ibn Jabal; and the lifespan. Ibn Ashur explains that the term applies to the whole group that rejected its messengers, and that the verse warns the Arabs by the precedent of earlier peoples. Ibn al-Jawzi, citing Muqatil, reports that the verse was revealed when the disbelievers asked for the punishment to be hastened. Abu Hayyan notes the grammatical difficulty of the second negation, which the commentators resolve in different ways.

God addresses all the children of Adam: if messengers from among them come to recite His signs and explain His commands, then whoever fears Him, abstains from polytheism and sin, and sets his deeds right will have no fear and no grief. The commentators largely agree that piety and righteousness mean believing in the messengers and following them, and that the absence of fear and grief means safety from God's punishment and no regret over what has been lost in this world, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di explain. Al-Tabari supplies an implied command to obey the messengers, while others take 'whoever fears God' as the direct answer to the condition. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the address as covering all nations, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi also mention, without deciding, the view that 'messengers' refers to the Prophet Muhammad alone. On whether believers will feel fear and grief on the Day of Resurrection, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi record differing views: some hold that no fear reaches them, others that the terrors of that day will touch them but that their final state is security. Al-Razi adds that the grief denied is grief over worldly losses. The verse contrasts this with those who deny Our signs and turn away from them in arrogance: they are the companions of the Fire, where they will abide forever.

This verse states that those who denied Allah's signs and rejected them out of arrogance are the companions of the Fire, where they will remain forever. It is set against the fate of those who are mindful of Allah and do good, who will have no fear and no grief. The commentators agree that denial means rejecting what the messengers brought, and that arrogance means refusing to submit to the truth.

Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi explain that God mentions arrogance because every disbeliever is arrogant: he denies and disbelieves out of pride. They cite the verse about those who, when told there is no god but Allah, grew arrogant. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn describe a denial of the heart and a refusal to act on the truth, a point also noted by al-Nasafi and al-Alusi.

Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud observe that the particle fa is placed before the first clause, the reward of the God-fearing, and not before the second, in order to stress the promise and soften the threat. Ibn Sa'di and al-Razi draw from the word hum, meaning "they," a restriction: only those who combine denial and arrogance will remain forever in the Fire, which al-Razi presents as a Sunni argument. The other commentators do not take up this question.

Al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur link the verse to the warning against Satan and to the sending of messengers. The general meaning on which all agree is that following the messengers leads to salvation, while rejecting them with arrogance leads to endless ruin.

This verse states that no one is more unjust than one who fabricates lies against God, attributing to Him a son, a partner, or rulings He never decreed, or who denies His revealed signs. The commentators agree that "their share of the Book" means what has been decreed for them, but they differ on what that share is. Al-Hasan, as-Suddi and Abu Salih take it to be the punishment destined for them; Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to be what was written for them of misery or happiness; Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to be their deeds, good or bad, for which they will be recompensed; al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Ibn Zayd and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi take it to be their provision, lifespan and works. Al-Tabari prefers the last view, since the verse continues with "until Our messengers come to take them," suggesting a share enjoyed until death; Ibn Kathir finds this view strong and supported by the context. Ibn al-Jawzi lists several meanings of "the Book", including the Preserved Tablet, the Qur'an and the records of deeds. Most commentators identify the messengers as the Angel of Death and his helpers, and the taking as the seizing of souls, though al-Hasan holds that it refers to angels of punishment on the Day of Resurrection. The scene shows these people at death, asked where the deities they worshipped are, and answering that they have vanished from them, while they bear witness against themselves to their disbelief. Al-Razi notes that such a dreadful depiction moves the reasonable person to reflect and to examine carefully.

God says that on the Day of Resurrection He will tell those who invented lies against Him and denied His signs to enter the Fire among earlier communities of jinn and humans. Each community that enters curses its sister, meaning the one it followed into error, a sisterhood of creed rather than of blood. When they have all gathered there, the later ones, the followers, say to their earlier leaders: Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire. God replies that each has a double punishment, but you do not know it. The commentators agree that these communities are the disbelievers of past nations and that both followers and leaders deserve punishment. They differ on the meaning of ḍi‘f. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take it as a doubling or a multiplied punishment, while Mujahid also explains it as a multiplied punishment and, as reported from Ibn Mas‘ud, some say it refers to serpents and vipers. Al-Razi and Ibn ‘Atiyya argue that the word in Arabic means any increase beyond an equal, not only a double, and Ibn Ashur reads it as a strong augmentation. Al-Razi reports that the followers complain to God, while Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi hold that the leaders receive an increased punishment for having established misguidance. Readers differ: Abu Bakr and ‘Asim read ya‘lamun, the majority read ta‘lamun. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that each group does not know the other's punishment. The leaders then tell the followers they have no advantage over them and should taste the punishment they earned.

This verse reports what the leaders and their followers say to one another in the Fire. Most commentators understand that the first group, the leaders who set the path of error, tell the later group, the followers and the common people, that they have no advantage over them: both sides shared in disbelief and error, so both deserve the same punishment, and all are told to taste the torment for what they earned. Al-Tabari, Abu Mijlaz and al-Sudi take these words as the leaders' speech, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi allow that God may be the speaker, addressing all of them. Ibn Kathir reads it as a rebuke that follows what came before. On the meaning of 'fadl', al-Tabari and others take it as a lightening of the punishment, and he reports that Mujahid read it this way, though he finds that reading inconsistent with the context of reproach. Al-Sudi glosses it as being misled just as they were. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the followers chose to follow, so they cannot ask for relief. The scholars agree on the substance, namely equality in fault and in punishment, but differ on who speaks and on the exact sense of 'fadl'. The 'kasb' is understood by most as polytheism, denial of the signs and sins.

The commentators explain that this verse warns those who denied God's signs and refused to submit to them that the gates of heaven will not be opened for them: no righteous deed or supplication will rise for them, and their souls will not be received at death as those of believers are. It adds that they will never enter Paradise, since this is tied to an impossibility, a camel passing through the eye of a needle. Most agree on this general sense of deprivation but differ on its nature. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report, citing Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others, that it is the souls that are not admitted, supported by a hadith of the Prophet transmitted through al-Bara'. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibrahim and al-Nakha'i understood deeds and supplications, a view Ibn Kathir considers compatible with the former. Al-Razi and others add that heaven is where Paradise lies. On the word jamal, the common reading means the camel, which Ibn Mas'ud identified as the male of the she-camel, while Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrima read jummal, a thick ship's cable. Al-Zamakhshari judged the common reading more striking for expressing the narrowness of the eye of the needle. Commentators also note that the Arabs use such examples of impossibility to express permanence, as in saying 'I will not do it until the crow turns white.' Regarding the following lines, Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn read the beds and coverings as fire surrounding them from below and above.

This passage describes the fate of those who denied Allah's signs and were arrogant towards them. The commentators explain that they will have in Hell a bed beneath them and coverings above them, meaning that the fire surrounds them on every side. Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi take the mihad to be a bed and the ghawashi to be quilts, al-Hasan understands them as shades and garments, and 'Ikrima mentions smoke covering them from above. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and al-Baydawi agree that the image conveys total encirclement by punishment, and that the closing phrase refers to the requital of wrongdoers, which Ibn 'Abbas explains as the polytheists. The meaning of the preceding phrase, that the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, is debated: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi take it to mean that their deeds and supplications do not rise and are not accepted, while others hold that their souls are not admitted at death as the souls of believers are, or that Paradise, being in heaven, is closed to them. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib on the death of the disbeliever. Al-Razi stresses the severity of the warning. Commentators also note the variant readings of 'al-jamal': Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read it as a ship's cable, while most read it as the camel, and the comparison means that their entry into Paradise is as impossible as a camel passing through the eye of a needle. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi point out that the terms 'criminals' and 'wrongdoers' refer to the same people, while emphasising the gravity of their crime.

This verse states that those who believe and do righteous deeds are the companions of the Garden, abiding in it forever, and that God burdens no soul beyond its capacity, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain. The commentators agree that the clause "We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity" is a parenthetical remark placed between the subject and the predicate, meant to encourage good deeds that are within reach and not burdensome. Al-Razi quotes Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said the capacity is "its ease, not its hardship", and al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan note that the clause could alternatively serve as the predicate with an implied pronoun, though the parenthetical reading is the more common one.

On the phrase "We will remove what is in their breasts of rancour", al-Tabari, al-Samarqandi and Ibn Kathir understand it as the removal of the enmities and grudges that existed between them in this world, and al-Tabari cites Dahhak and Qatada who define the ghill as hostility and resentment. Al-Mawardi lists four meanings, including passions and innovations according to Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah, envy, hatred, and wishing for what others have. He also gives al-Hasan's view that it refers to the rancour of the pre-Islamic era. Several reports attribute to 'Ali the hope that he, 'Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr are among those meant, and some say the verse was revealed about the people of Badr.

Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Razi, considers the meaning of differing ranks more fitting, so that someone of a lower rank does not envy someone of a higher rank. Al-Razi also records the theologians' debate over why God removes hatred but not the need for food and drink. Regarding entry into Paradise through deeds, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir link it to works, while al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir cite the authentic hadith that no one enters Paradise by his deeds alone but by God's mercy.

This verse says that God removes from the hearts of the people of Paradise any rancour they held against one another in the world, while rivers flow beneath them. They then praise God for guiding them to this state, acknowledging that they could never have been guided without His guidance, and affirm that the messengers brought the truth. They are finally told that this Paradise has been given to them as an inheritance because of their deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi explain that the removal (naza') means the erasing of hatred and envy, and that ghill means hidden hatred. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite a report from Ali that the verse refers to the people of Badr, and Ali hopes to be among them together with Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi instead prefer the view that the ranks of the blessed differ, so that someone in a lower rank does not envy someone in a higher one. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list several meanings of ghill, including the rancour of the pre-Islamic age or of desires and innovations. On guidance, al-Tabari takes it to mean being enabled to do good deeds, Ibn 'Atiyya to mean being directed to the causes of Paradise, while al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim see in it proof that guidance comes wholly from God. As for 'you have inherited it', al-Tabari understands it as the Paradise that the disbelievers would have had had they believed, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi take it as a gift of divine grace rather than a reward owed. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir read the particle bi-ma as indicating causation, Ibn Kathir citing the hadith that no one enters Paradise by his deeds alone, and Ibn al-Qayyim reconciling the two.

The people of Paradise, once settled in their abodes, call out to the people of the Fire: they say they have found true what their Lord promised them, and ask whether the people of the Fire have found true what they were threatened with; the latter confirm it. A crier then proclaims among them that God's curse is upon the wrongdoers. The commentators see this exchange as a rebuke, a taunt and a humiliation of the damned. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir specify that the promise concerns reward and punishment, and that the object is dropped in the second question either for brevity or to deny the unbelievers the honour of direct address. Al-Zamakhshari holds instead that the omission widens the meaning to everything promised, including resurrection and judgement. Readings of the word for 'yes' differ: the fatha form is the most widely transmitted according to al-Tabari, while al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash read it with kasra, and al-Akhfash considered both to be dialect variants. Grammarians debate the particle 'an', generally taken as a lightened form of 'anna' or as an explanatory particle, and some read 'anna' with 'la'nata' in the accusative. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take 'the wrongdoers' to mean the disbelievers, while al-Qadi, as al-Razi reports, extends it to any wrongdoer. As for the people of the A'raf, opinions diverge: Ibn 'Abbas, Hudhayfa and Ibn Mas'ud say they are those whose good and bad deeds balance, who wait before entering Paradise; al-Hasan and Mujahid identify them as eminent believers and scholars; Abu Mijlaz says they are angels.

This verse describes those who bar people from the path of God and seek to make it crooked, while disbelieving in the Hereafter. The commentators place it within the scene where the people of Paradise address those of the Fire, and a crier then proclaims God's curse on the wrongdoers, so the verse specifies their traits. Commentators agree that sadd means obstructing or turning people away from God's way, meaning His religion and obedience, and that 'iwaj means deviation and departure from straightness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that this obstruction can take the form of barring people from Islam or of turning away oneself, and that those who seek to make the path crooked try to distort the religion. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Baghawi, understands it as praying to other than God and venerating what God has not venerated, whereas al-Razi takes it as sowing doubts and objections against the proofs of the religion. Al-Nasafi and al-Razi take sadd as preventing others from accepting the religion, while al-Alusi and al-Qasimi also allow the sense of turning away oneself. All agree that denial of the Hereafter is the cause of this conduct, since one who fears neither reckoning nor punishment does not care what he does. Ibn Sa'di emphasizes that this denial and the lack of fear of punishment push them toward deviation, while God's mercy embraces the believers. Ibn 'Ashur notes that 'the wrongdoers' refers here to polytheists, and that the present tense conveys a lasting habit. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi remind us that the proclamation expresses disgrace and curse upon those who combine these traits.

This verse describes the barrier between Paradise and Hell, which is the wall mentioned in Surah al-Hadid, and al-A'raf, its heights. On these heights stand men who recognise the people of Paradise and the people of Hell by their marks: white faces for the first, black faces for the second. These men greet the people of Paradise although they have not yet entered it, yet they hope to enter. When they turn their gaze toward the people of the Fire, they ask God not to place them among them.

The commentators agree that the barrier is the wall itself, that al-A'raf are its upper parts, and that the marks are the whiteness or blackness of the faces, a view transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi among others. The identity of these men, however, is widely debated. Ibn Mas'ud, Hudhayfa, Ibn 'Abbas and others say they are people whose good and bad deeds were equal: their good deeds did not raise them to Paradise and their bad deeds did not send them to Hell. They remain on the heights until God decides their fate, then admits them to Paradise by His mercy. Others, such as Shurahbil ibn Sa'd, say they are martyrs who went out to fight without their parents' permission, a report traced to the Prophet through chains that many scholars consider weak. Mujahid describes them as righteous scholars, Abu Mijlaz as angels, and al-Hasan as meritorious believers.

The meaning of the word translated as hope is also disputed. Some read it as expectation, others as certainty, and some take it to refer to the people of Paradise. Al-Tabari prefers the view that the men had equal deeds, which he regards as the best known among the Companions, and Ibn Kathir follows him, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi set out several opinions without fully settling the question.

This verse describes the people of al-A'raf, who stand between Paradise and Hell. When their eyes turn toward the people of the Fire, they ask God not to place them among the wrongdoers. The commentators agree that al-A'raf is a raised barrier separating the two groups, and that the damned are recognised by blackened faces and blue-tinged eyes, while the blessed have bright white faces. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, citing Hudhayfa, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, that these are people whose good and bad deeds were equal; they wait there until God decides their fate and then admits them to Paradise. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi record other views: they are martyrs, prophets, eminent believers and scholars, or angels appearing in human form, as Abu Mijlaz held. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani also transmit the view that they are fighters who were killed without their parents' permission. Scholars also differ on the word for hope in the verse: Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan take it as certainty and a favour from God, while Ibn Kathir understands it as genuine hope of entering Paradise. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the passage may indicate that entry into Paradise follows different ranks according to merit, without deciding between these readings.

This verse describes the people of the A'raf, who stand on the barrier between Paradise and Hell. They call out to men among the leaders of the disbelievers, whom they recognise by their marks, and tell them that neither their numbers nor their arrogance have been of any use to them. The commentators agree that those addressed are the great polytheist notables and that the aim is to rebuke and shame them. On the identity of the people of the A'raf, however, opinions differ. Ibn Mas'ud, Hudhayfa, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi say they are people whose good and bad deeds balanced, so they remain between the two groups until God grants them entry to Paradise; Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim regard this as the best-attested view from the Companions. Abu Mijlaz holds that they are angels, Mujahid that they are righteous scholars, and Shurahbil ibn Sa'd that they are martyrs who went out without their parents' permission. Al-Zajjaj describes them as the witnesses of the Day of Resurrection.

The commentators identify those referred to as "these whom you swore" as the poor believers in Paradise, such as Bilal, Salman, Khabbab and Suhayb, whom the disbelievers mocked and swore God would never show mercy to. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi attribute these words to the people of the A'raf, while others take them to be spoken by the angels or even by God. The readings differ in the verb form, "enter" or "cause them to enter", but the meaning remains close.

This verse describes the people of al-A'raf, who stand between Paradise and Hell, addressing men of the disbelieving leaders in the Fire. They remind them that their numbers and arrogance did not avail them. They then point to the weak believers whom the disbelievers scorned in this world and swore that God would never show mercy to, and who are now in Paradise. The people of al-A'raf are then told to enter Paradise, where no fear or grief will touch them. The commentators agree that the scene belongs to the Hereafter and that reward follows deeds. They differ over who is speaking and who is addressed. Ibn 'Abbas, Hudhayfa and Ibn Mas'ud, as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, hold that the people of al-A'raf are those whose good and bad deeds were equal, who enter neither Paradise nor Hell until God admits them by His mercy. Abu Majlaz holds that they are angels, al-Tabari takes the words to be God's address to the people of Hell, and others say the angels are speaking. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that entry into Paradise follows the period of waiting on al-A'raf, so that the difference in rank is shown by deeds. Abu Hayyan notes several readings of the verb, which do not change the general sense. Ibn al-Qayyim mentions other views, such as martyrs or children of unbelievers, and prefers the view of the Companions. Ibn 'Atiyya considers that the people of al-A'raf may be prophets, martyrs or sinful humans, without deciding.

This verse describes the cry of the people of the Fire to the people of Paradise, begging them to pour water on them or to give them some of what God has provided, since thirst and hunger have overwhelmed them. The people of Paradise reply that God has forbidden both to the disbelievers. The commentators agree that the verb to pour out means to pour or to extend abundantly, and that water refers to drink. On the phrase what God has provided, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, following al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, take it to mean food, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan extend it to all drinks and fruits.

Most exegetes read the prohibition as a prohibition of withholding rather than a ritual prohibition, as al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain. Al-Zamakhshari draws the lesson that those who were showered with blessings in this world and gave no thanks are deprived of them in the next.

Opinions differ on the state of mind behind the appeal. Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the people of the Fire, seeing the people of the Heights enter Paradise, regained hope. Al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan hold instead that they were despairing, much like a drowning man clutching at foam. Al-Mawardi understands the water either as the water of mercy or as the water of life.

Al-Qurtubi notes that this verse shows the great merit of giving water to drink, and that some jurists deduce from it that the owner of a well or a waterskin has a prior right to his water. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi also observe that the exchange presupposes that each group can hear the other, which is possible through a special perception, sight, or across the barrier between them.

This verse describes those who took their religion as amusement and play, and whom the life of this world deceived. God says that today He will forget them just as they forgot the meeting of this day, meaning He will leave them in punishment and treat them as the forgotten, because they denied His signs. Most commentators understand these words as spoken by the people of Paradise in reply to the people of the Fire, who begged them for water and food, and that God has forbidden these to the disbelievers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that forgetting here means abandoning them and withholding mercy, while Qatada and al-Suddi specify that they are deprived of good but not of evil. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read it as a comparison with how one treats someone one has forgotten, and Ibn 'Ashur sees a corresponding equivalence between the punishment and the deed, the particle kama expressing cause as much as likeness. As for what is meant by making their religion a game, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi identify it with the mockers, al-Tabari and al-Razi with the practices of the pre-Islamic age such as forbidding the bahira and clapping and whistling around the Ka'ba, and Abu Rawq with their festival. All agree on the core meaning: whoever treats religion as a game and is seduced by this world deserves deprivation and punishment.

This verse states that God sent down to people a Book that He had explained in detail, clarifying what is lawful and unlawful, its promises and threats, its stories and admonitions, and that He revealed it with knowledge of what is good for them, so that it would be guidance and mercy for those who believe. The commentators agree that the pronoun 'We brought them' refers to the polytheists and that the Book is the Quran. They differ on the meaning of 'We detailed it': al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as distinguishing truth from falsehood, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as setting out the lawful and unlawful, the promises and warnings, and the histories of earlier nations. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read it as detailed with full knowledge of how to detail it, so that it came wise and free of crookedness. They agree that 'guidance and mercy' are circumstantial qualifiers, guidance meaning proof and direction, and mercy meaning kindness. Al-Qurtubi notes that some said it was revealed in parts, and that Ibn Muhaysin's reading 'fadalnahu' means it was preferred over other scriptures. All agree that mentioning believers is specific, since they are the ones who benefit from it. Al-Tabari links this verse to the opening of the sura, while Ibn Kathir finds that link unconvincing given the long gap, and connects it instead to the announcement of loss in the hereafter: God had already removed the excuses of the people in this world by sending messengers and Books. The verse thus exalts the Quran and presents it as God's proof against those who reject it.

This verse says that the disbelievers are only waiting for the outcome of their affair, that is, the punishment the Qur'an has promised them. The word ta'wil means the final result or consequence. The commentators give closely related meanings: Qatada and Mujahid take it as the reward or consequence, while as-Suddi includes both events in this world, such as the battle of Badr, and events of the Hereafter. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas says it unfolds gradually until it is complete on the Day of Judgment. Most read 'the day its fulfilment comes' as the Day of Resurrection, while al-Hasan reads it as the day of judgment. Then those who had forgotten the message will say that the messengers of their Lord came with the truth. They will then ask for intercessors, or to be sent back to the world to act differently. At-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take this request as a lie meant to escape punishment, and hold that intercession will not benefit them. Ar-Razi and an-Nasafi say these words are spoken in despair, while al-Jubba'i argues from them that these people could have believed had they been returned. Ibn Abi Ishaq's reading 'aw nuradda' with a subjunctive and al-Hasan's reading with a nominative lead to grammatical discussion. The verse concludes that they have lost themselves, and that what they used to invent, such as the claim that their idols would intercede, has vanished.

This verse states that God, the true Lord, created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself on the Throne in a manner befitting His majesty. Commentators differ on the length of these days. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, relates that each day is like a thousand years, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand them as days like ours or as a measure of time. Several scholars, among them al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, explain that God, who could create everything in an instant, chose a gradual creation to teach people patience and deliberation in their affairs. On the istiwa' upon the Throne, Malik, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, following the Salaf, affirm it as a divine attribute to be accepted without asking how, whereas the Mu'tazila and some Ash'aris interpret it as domination or sovereignty. Al-Razi reports several readings and leans toward the sense of governing and arranging the kingdom. The verse then describes the swift succession of night and day and the subjection of the sun, moon and stars to God's command. Finally, creation and command belong to God alone: Ibn Uyayna draws from this a distinction between creation and command, while Ibn Kathir sees in it God's absolute sovereignty.

In this verse God commands believers to call upon Him with humility and in a low voice, and states that He does not love transgressors. The commentators broadly agree that the supplication here includes both asking from God and worship. Tadarru' means humbling oneself and submission, while khufya means secrecy, which reflects sincerity. Al-Hasan al-Basri says the secret supplication is seventy times better than the public one, and he cites Zechariah's quiet call to his Lord. Several commentators also cite the report of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, in which the Prophet told people to lower their voices because the One they call upon is near and hears them. The meaning of transgression is disputed. Abu Mijlaz says it means asking for the ranks of the prophets; Muqatil says it means invoking curses and destruction upon those who do not deserve them; Ibn Jurayj and others say it means raising the voice and shouting in prayer; Ibn Abbas takes it broadly as going beyond what one was commanded in any matter.
