Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Qayyim cite the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas about those who overstep in supplication. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that supplication should combine fear and hope. There is agreement that God's mercy is near to the good-doers, but scholars differ on why the adjective 'near' is masculine although 'mercy' is feminine: al-Zajjaj explains it by reading mercy as reward or favour, al-Farra' by the rule that 'near' used of distance may take either gender, and an-Nadr ibn Shumayl by treating mercy as a verbal noun. Finally, the commentators agree in forbidding corruption on earth after it has been set right, reform being the sending of prophets and the revelation of law, and corruption being disbelief and disobedience.

This verse tells believers to call upon God humbly and in private, not to spread corruption on earth after it has been set right through the prophets and divine law, and to call upon Him in fear and hope, for God's mercy is near to those who do good. The commentators agree on several points. Tadarru' means humility and submission, and khufya means praying quietly and sincerely; al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith in which the Prophet told people to lower their voices, as well as the verse about Zakariya who called upon his Lord in a hidden voice. According to al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, transgression in prayer includes asking for the rank of the prophets, as Abu Mijlaz said; Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari also report Ibn Jurayj's view that shouting during prayer is disliked. On corruption after reform, al-Kalbi and al-Hasan take it to mean polytheism, disobedience and killing, Ata links it to disobedience that brings drought, and al-Dahhak to the spoiling of springs and fruit trees; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi read it as a general prohibition. The masculine form qarib with the feminine noun rahma prompted many explanations from al-Zajjaj, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash, who understood mercy as forgiveness, reward or rain. The commentators conclude that prayer combines fear and hope, and that doing good brings one close to God's mercy.

This verse shows that God sends the winds as bearers of good news before His mercy, meaning the rain. When the winds lift a heavy cloud, God drives it to a dead land with no vegetation, sends down water upon it and brings forth fruits of every kind. The commentators see in this an image of the resurrection of the dead: the One who revives the earth after its death can revive bodies after their decay, so that people may remember. The readers differed on the wording. Some read 'al-riyah' in the plural and others 'al-rih' in the singular; some read 'nushran' as winds that spread the clouds, and Asim reads 'bushran' meaning bearers of good news of rain. The exegetes agree that the mercy here is the rain. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that wherever winds are mentioned in the Qur'an together with mercy the plural form is more fitting, while the singular usually accompanies punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir present the verse as an illustration of resurrection, and some reports, notably one from Abu Hurayra about a rain between the two blasts of the trumpet, are cited, though not all commentators treat them as firm proof. As for the sentence 'the good land brings forth its plant by the permission of its Lord', most commentators read it as a parable of the believer and the disbeliever: the good soil is like the heart that receives revelation, and the salty land like the heart that benefits from nothing. Others take it as a plain description of the land itself. Al-Razi concludes that souls differ in their readiness to receive good.

This verse offers an image drawn from the earth: fertile land, watered by rain, brings forth abundant and good vegetation by the permission of its Lord, while poor land, such as salty soil, yields only meagre growth with no benefit. Most commentators read this as an example of the believer and the disbeliever. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid explain that the believer hears the Qur'an and benefits from it, showing its effect, whereas the disbeliever is not affected. Al-Tabari also reports from Mujahid that the image concerns all the children of Adam, among whom are both good and bad, and from al-Suddi that it concerns hearts receiving the Qur'an. Al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir follow this reading, while al-Razi sees in it a lasting difference between human natures in their readiness for knowledge and goodness. The word nakid is explained by Abu 'Ubayda and the exegetes as meagre, hard and useless. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the phrase about the bad land as a description of the land, with an ellipsis of the word for growth. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse elaborates on the revival of the earth and shows that people differ in accepting guidance. The readings of nakid vary, and al-Tabari prefers the most widespread one. The verse concludes that the signs are thus clarified for a grateful people, meaning those who benefit from them, which Ibn 'Ashur identifies as the believers.

In this verse God relates that He sent Noah to his people, and that he called them to worship God alone, declaring that there is no deity worthy of worship besides Him, and warned them of the punishment of a great day. Most commentators understand this as the Day of Resurrection, while some understand it as the day of the flood. The commentators agree that this call is the essence of the mission of all the prophets, and that Noah addressed his people with gentleness, sincere counsel and compassion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note that Noah was the first messenger sent to the inhabitants of the earth after Adam, and that his people worshipped idols named after righteous men of the past: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr. Several of them hold that the announcement of punishment was not a mere threat but a revelation Noah had received. On recitation, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read 'ghayrihi' in the genitive as a modifier of 'ilah', while the others read 'ghayruhu' in the nominative, based on the position of 'min ilah'. Some grammarians permitted the accusative as an exception, though Abu 'Amr and others considered it weak. Scholars also differ on the meaning of 'akhaf': some take it as certainty, others as genuine fear, since Noah allowed that they might believe or persist in disbelief. His people called him manifestly misguided; he replied that he was not astray at all, but a messenger from the Lord of the worlds who conveys his Lord's message and advises them sincerely, knowing from God what they do not know.

This verse reports the reply of the notables of Noah's people when he called them to worship God alone: they say they see him in clear error. The commentators agree that al-Mala' means the notables and leaders, those whose presence fills the eyes and the gatherings, and al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya add that it refers to men only, excluding women. Most take the verb 'see' as meaning to believe or judge rather than seeing with the eyes, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain, and Ibn Atiyya considers this the more likely reading. Error here means departing from the path of truth. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that Noah says 'there is no error in me' in the indefinite singular, which denies any kind of error more forcefully; al-Zamakhshari adds that the word for error is more specific and less general than the word for going astray, so denying it is more emphatic. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di see this as the usual habit of the wicked, who accuse the righteous of error, and Ibn Sa'di stresses the harshness of this charge set against Noah's gentleness. On the readings, the commentators note that 'ghayrihi' is read with a kasra or a damma, and 'uballighukum' with shadda or without, without much change in meaning. Al-Sha'rawi reads the reaction as the fear of the notables of losing their power before a call to one God.

The commentators explain that when the chiefs of Noah's people accused him of manifest error for calling to the worship of the one God and to abandoning the idols, he replied that there was not the least misguidance in him, but that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, delivering His messages, giving sincere counsel, and knowing from God what they do not know. All agree that negating "ḍalāla" is stronger than negating "ḍalāl", since it is the narrower word: denying one instance denies all lesser ones. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see in this a way of denying the greater by denying the lesser. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read the clause introduced by "but" as a correction: being a messenger means being at the furthest degree of guidance. Al-Alusi adds that it removes any suspicion that he had abandoned his forefathers' religion. For the word "mala'", al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand the notables and chiefs. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the alternation between "ḍalāl" and "ḍalāla" serves stylistic variety rather than a difference in meaning. The commentators agree on the sincerity of Noah's mission and on his people's rejection, which led to their drowning as described in the verses that follow.

This passage records Noah's reply to his people, who had accused him of error. He first denies any error in himself, then states that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. The commentators explain that he conveys to them the messages of his Lord and gives them sincere counsel, wishing for them what he wishes for himself. He also says that he knows from God what they do not know, namely that God's punishment will not be turned away from the wrongdoers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi focus mainly on this last point, and Ibn Kathir stresses that the messenger must be eloquent, sincere and knowledgeable of God. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur read the knowledge more broadly, as possibly covering future events or the divine attributes. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as God's overwhelming power and the severity of His punishment. Several scholars, among them al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi, note that the messages may include the scrolls of Idris and Shith, while Ibn Ashur links the plural to the varied times and themes of revelation. On the reading, Abu Amr recites the verb without doubling the letter, and the others with doubling, with the same meaning according to Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi. Al-Zamakhshari also explains why the word for error is changed in the reply, since the form used is more emphatic in denying it.

This passage from Surat al-A'raf reports Noah's reply to his people, who were astonished that a human being should be sent to them. He tells them that the reminder and admonition from their Lord has come through a man of their own, whose lineage they know, so that he may warn them of God's punishment, that they may guard themselves against it by faith and obedience, and that they may perhaps receive mercy. The commentators agree that the hamza in "awa'ajibtum" is an interrogation of reproach and rebuke, and that the waw is a conjunction linking to an implied clause, roughly "you denied and you wondered". They also agree that "dhikr" means admonition, clarification or message, and that the sequence from warning to piety to mercy is intended. Al-Baydawi, Ibn 'Ashur and Abu al-Su'ud note that "la'alla" expresses hope, since mercy depends on God's grace rather than being owed to piety.

Opinions differ on the preposition "'ala". Al-Farra', followed by al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, takes it to mean "with", whereas Ibn Qutayba, al-Zamakhshari and most exegetes read it as "through the tongue of" a man. Al-Zamakhshari explains their wonder by their preference for an angelic messenger over a human one, while al-Razi holds that they rejected the very principle of a prophetic mission. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that "jā'a" carries the sense of "descend", which justifies the use of "'ala".

On the meaning of "dhikr", al-Hasan takes it as revelation, others as a miracle, and some as the Book revealed to Noah. On "'amin", Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir understand blindness of the heart to the truth, al-Dahhak sees disbelievers, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl understands blindness of insight rather than of the eyes.

This verse reports that Noah's people denied him after he had called them to worship God alone and abandon their associates. God saved Noah and those with him in the ark, and drowned those who denied His signs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy agree that the ark (al-fulk) is the ship, and that those drowned were the stubborn deniers. They explain their destruction by saying that they were a blind people, blind of heart to the truth and to the knowledge of God. As to the number of the saved, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud report forty men and forty women according to one view, and nine according to another, namely Noah's three sons and six believers. Ibn Ishaq, cited by al-Tabari, counts Noah, his three sons, their wives and six people. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi attach "with him in the ark" to the sense of companionship, while others attach it to the verb "saved". Al-Zamakhshari notes that the pattern "'amin" expresses established blindness, and that the reading "'amin" is less forceful. Al-Alusi relates the distinction between blindness of insight and blindness of sight, presented as one opinion among others, since some consider the two terms equivalent. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di draw from the story the lesson of a constant divine law: final victory belongs to the messengers and the pious believers, and ruin to the obstinate.

The commentators explain that Allah sent to the people of 'Ad their brother Hud, meaning one of them by lineage rather than by religion. He called them to worship Allah alone, since they have no deity but Him, and to fear His punishment through piety. The impious chiefs of his people replied that they saw him as foolish and considered him a liar, and he answered that there was no foolishness in him, but that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, delivering His messages faithfully and sincerely advising them. The scholars note that the verse begins « Qala » without a conjunction, unlike the account of Noah. Ibn 'Ashur and others explain this by the fact that the people of Hud already knew what had happened to the people of Noah, so a simple reminder of piety sufficed. On the meaning of « brother », Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari take it as kinship, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi understand it as one of their own kind or compatriot. Genealogists differ on Hud's ancestry: Ibn Ishaq and al-Baydawi trace him to Sam, son of Noah, while others place him among the descendants of 'Ad himself. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the people of 'Ad were of great stature and that Hud was buried in Hadramawt, a claim Ibn Kathir transmits from 'Ali without every commentator endorsing it. Al-Zamakhshari observes that the description of the chiefs as those who disbelieved distinguishes them, since some notables believed, unlike the case of Noah's people. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya also differ on the sense of « zann » in their claim that they take him for a liar: some read it as certainty, others as mere supposition.

This verse records the scornful reply of the disbelieving notables of Hud's people: they say they see him in foolishness, meaning weakness of judgment and error in abandoning their people's religion and their idols, and they consider him among the liars in claiming to be a messenger. The commentators agree that the term al-mala' refers to the leaders and notables of the people, and that the description of them as disbelievers distinguishes them, since among the notables of Hud's people was a believer, Marthad ibn Sa'd, who concealed his faith, whereas Noah's people had no believer among their notables. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain that foolishness means feebleness of mind and lightness of reason, and that the phrase 'in foolishness' is figurative, meaning he is firmly fixed in it. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the root refers to the thinness of a woven cloth. As for the word zann, al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj take it in its literal sense, an accusation based on supposition rather than certainty, while Ibn Juzayy, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur sometimes take it to mean certainty. Ibn 'Ashur also notes the similarity between the words of Noah's and Hud's peoples. Hud's reply, which denies the foolishness plainly and affirms that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds and a trustworthy counsellor, is praised by al-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i as a lesson in good manners toward the foolish. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di note that Hud was of noble lineage among his people, and that this people, known for their strength, hardened themselves in denial.

This part of the verse records Hud's reply to his idolatrous people, who had called him foolish and considered him a liar. He states that there is no folly in him and that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. The commentators treat this reply as a lesson in courteous speech: he rejects the accusation by simply denying it, without answering insult with insult, and God recounts the exchange so that believers learn how to address the foolish and turn away from them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that sufaha here means error, folly and lightness of judgment, the people meaning that he had abandoned their fathers' religion and the worship of their idols. As for the charge of lying, al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj take it to mean that they denied him on supposition rather than certainty, so they rejected the message while doubting without being sure. Others, such as Abu Hayyan, understand the verb to mean certainty or the stronger of two possibilities. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the reply mirrors their charge: Hud presents himself as a sincere and trustworthy adviser. Al-Razi adds that the difference from the people of Nuh lies in the nature of the accusations made against each prophet.

This verse recounts Hud's words to his people 'Ad: he conveys the messages of his Lord and is a sincere and trustworthy counsellor to them. The commentators explain that his counsel was his call to repent and to abandon the worship of anything besides God, and that his trustworthiness means he is faithful in conveying the revelation, adding nothing and omitting nothing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report, together with Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak, that his integrity was known among them before his mission, so they had no grounds to doubt him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the verse as a reply to their charges of foolishness and lying, and as a model of patient restraint toward the foolish. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur observe that Hud's phrasing differs from Noah's: the verbal form in Noah's words signals repeated, renewed counsel, while the noun form here signals a settled quality, since Hud did not repeat his warning day and night as Noah did. On details the reports differ: al-Kalbi and al-Suddi give heights from sixty to a hundred cubits, Muqatil gives twelve cubits, and a report from 'Ali places Hud's grave in Hadramawt. All agree that the verse leads into the call to give thanks for God's favours.

In this verse Hud speaks to his people, the 'Ad, reminding them of God's favours: He made them successors to the people of Noah on earth and gave them greater stature and strength. He also tells them not to be astonished that a message from their Lord has come through a man from among them, sent to warn them. The commentators agree on the general sense: remembering blessings leads to gratitude, and gratitude leads to success. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain the 'basta' as great height and exceptional strength, and report that the tallest among them was a hundred cubits and the shortest sixty. Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi cite other estimates, while al-Qasimi considers these figures unreliable and sees them as the exaggeration of historians. For al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, 'basta' also refers to vigour. On the word 'ala', all see it as bounties. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that 'idh' is a direct object rather than a time adverb. Al-Razi notes that the command to remember implies acting upon the remembrance, while Ibn 'Ashur explains that recalling blessings prompts gratitude. Several commentators praise Hud's forbearance towards the insults of his people, which al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi present as a lesson in manners for preachers. The account of the 'Ad's destruction by wind, reported by al-Tabari, is judged by Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi to be doubtful in many of its details.

This verse records the reply of the people of 'Ad to their prophet Hud when he called them to worship God alone and abandon what their fathers had worshipped. They found it strange that worship should be reserved for God alone, refused to give up the gods of their ancestors out of attachment to what they had grown up with and to imitation of their forefathers, and then challenged him to bring about the punishment he had threatened, if he was truthful. The commentators explain that the word 'come' may be taken literally, Hud having withdrawn from his people to worship in seclusion, or in the sense of a descent from heaven used ironically, or figuratively as intention, as in the expression 'he went to insult me'. Hud replied that the rijs and the wrath of their Lord had already fallen upon them, meaning that punishment was decreed, the expected being treated as accomplished. Concerning the meaning of rijs, Zayd ibn Aslam and most scholars take it as punishment, Ibn 'Abbas as anger, and al-Qaffal as a stain on the hearts that increases disbelief, while al-Razi rejects the idea that the punishment had already occurred. As for the 'names' they dispute, most commentators see them as idols given the title of gods though they have no divinity, and all agree that no divine authority supports them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others relate at length the drought, the delegation sent to Mecca and the storm that destroyed this people, while Hud and the believers were saved.

This verse records Hud's reply to his people, who had asked him to bring the punishment he threatened: punishment and wrath from your Lord have already fallen upon you. He then rebukes them for disputing with him over names that they and their fathers gave to idols, names with no true divinity behind them and for which God has sent down no authority. Finally he tells them to wait, adding that he too is waiting with them. The commentators agree that « rijs » means punishment and « ghadab » means anger or the will to punish, though Ibn Abbas takes rijs as wrath, and az-Zamakhshari also notes the sense of uncleanness or a seal over the heart. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala holds that rijs and rijz have the same meaning, the sin being a substitution for zay. All agree that the « names » are the idols that have no divine reality. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain that the idolaters called them gods without any proof, whereas al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that they attributed specific powers to them, such as sending rain or healing. Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya place the dispute in the names rather than the objects, while others place it in the idols themselves. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the past tense expresses a certainty regarded as already accomplished. Many exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, recount the destruction of 'Ad by a violent wind. The commentators present these views without judging between them.

According to the commentators, God saved Hud and those who believed with him by His mercy, and He uprooted those who denied His signs so completely that none of them remained. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani agree that cutting off the 'dabir' means total annihilation, the 'dabir' being the last of a people, whose destruction entails that of all. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di report that the destruction came by a barren wind, and Ibn Kathir supports this with the surahs al-Haqqa and adh-Dhariyat, as do Ibn Ashur and al-Shinqiti. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the denial of faith to them is an allusion to the believers among their people, such as Marthad ibn Sa'd, so that it is understood that perdition struck only the deniers; al-Tayyibi and al-Alusi follow him. Al-Razi understands that God knew they would never believe even had they been left alive. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate the story of 'Ad at length, including the delegation sent to Mecca, Mu'awiya ibn Bakr and the two singing girls, but Ibn Ashur judges that not all of these accounts are established, and Ibn Atiyya keeps only what bears on the wording of the verse. Modern works such as Fi Zilal al-Quran and Taysir al-Karim limit themselves to the general notion of destruction without further detail.

This verse records the mission of the prophet Salih to his people, Thamud. He calls them to worship Allah alone, with no partner, and states that the she-camel brought forth from the rock is a clear sign from their Lord. He commands them to leave her to graze on Allah's earth and not to harm her, lest a painful punishment seize them. The commentators agree on the central meaning: a call to monotheism supported by a miracle that the people themselves had requested. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi report that the Thamud asked for a sign; Salih prayed, and a rock in al-Hijr split to release a pregnant she-camel who then bore a young one. These same authors report that she drank from the water in her turn and gave them milk in return, and that two women urged her slaughter, which Qudar ibn Salif carried out. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the camel was a miracle because she came forth without ordinary begetting, and they discuss several aspects of this wonder. Ibn 'Ashur stresses the respite Salih gave the people before any confrontation, which he sees as a sign of divine patience. Ibn Sa'di judges that many popular details of the story derive from Israelite narratives that cannot be affirmed as certain, and al-Alusi shows similar caution. All agree that the camel is a sign to be respected, whose violation brings ruin. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith in which the Prophet told his companions not to enter the dwellings of the punished peoples except weeping.

Salih, peace be upon him, reminds his people of the Thamud of God's favour in making them successors to 'Ad and settling them in the land: they built palaces on its plains and carved homes out of the mountains. He tells them to remember God's blessings and not to spread corruption on earth. The commentators broadly agree on this plain meaning: recalling blessings leads to gratitude and away from corruption, and Ibn Kathir and al-Samani take 'ath as the gravest kind of corruption. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain that the carving of mountains was due to the long lives of this people, since buildings wore out before their builders died; Ibn al-Jawzi cites Wahb ibn Munabbih, who says men rebuilt repeatedly until they turned to the mountains. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take the verse as permitting lofty construction, while Hasan al-Basri disliked it. Ibn Sa'di regards the detailed account of the she-camel as one of the Israelite narrations that should not be placed in the tafsir, and the Jalalayn do not mention it. Some readings are noted: Hasan reads tanhatun with a fatha, and al-A'mash reads ti'thaw with a kasra. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat buyutan as a future-sense state, since the mountain is not yet a house while it is being carved.

The verse reports the words of the arrogant chiefs of Salih's people to the weak who had believed in him: "Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" The commentators agree that this question was asked mockingly rather than as a real inquiry. The believers answer that they believe in what he was sent with, and their reply avoids a plain "yes" in order to affirm their faith firmly. All read the weak as the common people and followers whom the nobles had belittled, and they note that few of them believed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that the arrogant replied, "We disbelieve in what you believed," and that the believers avoided saying "what he was sent with" so as not to acknowledge his mission. On the scope of the humiliation, opinions differ. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi take the pronoun "among them" to refer to the people, so that the humiliation concerned only the believers; others, as Zamakhshari also notes, take it to include both believers and unbelievers. Al-Razi draws from the passage that poverty is better than wealth, since arrogance grows from money and rank while faith came from their lack of both. Ibn Sa'di warns that the Israelite narratives told around this story must not be used in Quranic exegesis.

This passage of the Thamud story records the reply of the arrogant notables to the weak believers among Salih's people. The notables mockingly asked the weak whether they knew that Salih was sent by his Lord; the believers answered firmly that they believed in what he had been sent with. The arrogant ones retorted that they disbelieved in what the believers had believed. Commentators note that the reply says 'what you believed in' rather than 'what he was sent with', so as not to acknowledge the mission; Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur see this as a feature of the Qur'anic narration rather than the speakers' own words. Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi read the question as mockery or denial, while Ibn Ashur sees an attempt to cast doubt on the believers' knowledge. All agree that the slaughter of the she-camel is attributed to the whole people, though one man did it, because they consented; Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan report that Qudar acted after consultation. Tabari and Baghawi understand the arrogance as refusal to obey God's command, conveyed by Salih, to leave the camel to graze, while Zamakhshari also allows that the defiance arose from that command. On the quake, Mujahid and Suddi call it a cry, Ibn Abbas an earthquake, and Farra and Zajjaj a violent tremor; Razi holds that the terms refer to one catastrophe. On 'he turned away from them', Razi, Baydawi and Qurtubi place it after their death, others before the punishment, and Ibn Kathir and Zamakhshari compare it to the Prophet addressing the dead of Badr.

This verse describes the people of Thamud who slaughtered the she-camel that God had given them as a sign, defied their Lord's command, and challenged Salih, saying: bring us the punishment you threaten us with, if you are truly among the messengers. The commentators agree that the killing was a collective decision, even though one man struck the blow: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi attribute it to their shared complicity, and Ibn Kathir cites Qatada saying all consented, including women and children, while Ibn Juzayy, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan name Qudar ibn Salif as the one who did it. All explain 'ataw' as overstepping in wrongdoing and refusing to obey; 'the command of their Lord' is, for most, the prohibition to harm the camel, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also suggest their defiance itself arose from that command. On the 'rajfa', al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir take it as an earthquake, whereas al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani also mention a cry or a thunderbolt, and Abu Hayyan links the quake to the cry. The scholars differ on when Salih said 'I delivered my Lord's message to you': before the punishment according to al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, after their death according to al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, who compare it to the Prophet addressing the dead of Badr. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi judge that many narrative details come from Israelite sources and should not be included in Qur'anic exegesis.

The commentators explain that God seized the people of Thamud after they hamstrung the she-camel and rebelled against their Lord's command. They were struck by al-Rajfa, which most identify with a terrifying cry, as al-Tabari, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi do, while al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi understand it as a violent earthquake. Al-Alusi reconciles the two views by suggesting the quake came from below and the cry from above. In the morning they were found in their homes, lifeless and motionless. The meaning of jathimin is discussed: al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as fallen or crouched on their knees, some report they were burned by lightning until they lay like ash, and Ibn 'Atiyya sees it as the posture of the bodies at death. The word dar is read by al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Alusi as the town or the category in the singular, whereas the plural used elsewhere refers to individual dwellings. As for Salih's words after their destruction, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take them as a lament over the dead, like the Prophet addressing the dead of Badr, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy also allow that he spoke before their fall. Ibn Sa'di, al-Qasimi and Sayyid Qutb warn that many of the detailed narratives about these events come from Israelite traditions and should not be taken as Qur'anic exegesis.

This verse tells that Salih turned away from his people of Thamud after they slaughtered the she-camel and hastened their punishment, saying that he had delivered his Lord's message and given them sincere counsel, but that they did not love those who counsel. The commentators agree on the main meaning: Salih fulfilled his mission, and the people persisted in denial. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan explain that the slaughter is attributed to the whole people, although one man carried it out, because it was done by common agreement. The main debate concerns when these words were spoken. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani hold that they were spoken after the people had died, in the manner of the Prophet's address to the dead of Badr, expressing grief and reproach. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy allow that they were spoken before the punishment, while al-Baydawi and al-Alusi prefer the first view but accept the second. To the objection of addressing the dead, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi answer that a man may speak thus to a deceased friend, either to clear himself or to instruct the living. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb relate the story of Thamud at length, though Ibn Sa'di warns against Israelite narratives that have no basis in the Qur'an. Al-Jaza'iri and the Tafsir al-Muyassar keep to the plain sense of the verse.

This verse recounts the story of Lot, who rebuked his people for committing an indecency, which most commentators understand as sodomy, and asked them whether they did something no one among the worlds had done before them. The commentators agree that Lot was sent to the people of Sodom and the nearby towns, that he was Abraham's nephew, and that the verse stresses the grave ugliness of this act and that they were its first practitioners. Several scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, cite the saying of Amr ibn Dinar that no male mounted another male until the people of Lot did so. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi also report al-Hasan's view that they only approached strangers, and al-Kalbi's account that Iblis first led them into the practice.

The readings differ: some read "innakum" as a statement and others as a question with a double hamza, a point noted by al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya. Many treat "shahwatan" as an accusative of purpose, meaning that they had no motive beyond bare desire. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain "musrifun" as going beyond the limits.

Al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn 'Ashur also discuss the legal ruling. Malik holds that both partners are stoned, al-Shafi'i gives a punishment similar to that for adultery, and Abu Hanifa prescribes discretionary punishment. Ibn al-Qayyim reports that Abu Bakr had a man called al-Fujaa'a burned on the advice of 'Ali. The scholars do not agree on these points, and Ibn al-Qayyim presents a view he favours.

Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi mention the people's reply: "Expel them from your town, for they are people who keep themselves pure." They read this as mockery or as a boast of their own corruption, while some take it as a reference to the abstainers' disdain for these acts.

This verse records Lot's rebuke of his people for approaching men in lust rather than their wives, which God had made lawful for them, and calls them a people who exceed the bounds. The commentators agree that the abomination meant is intercourse with males, and that israf means going beyond what is lawful into what is forbidden, as al-Tabari and al-Baghawi explain. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the word shahwa to mean that nothing drove them except bare desire, with no reasonable motive such as seeking offspring, and al-Zamakhshari adds that their habit of excess in everything led them beyond the usual into the unusual. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that the claim about their 'purity' was mocking, and they differ on its sense: abstaining from anal intercourse with men and women according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, or washing from impurity according to others. On the punishment, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur set out the views of Malik, who prescribes stoning, and of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Ahmad, without the commentators settling the matter. Ibn Kathir reports that the act was unknown among mankind before this people, while al-Razi lists rational reasons for its ugliness, such as the cutting off of offspring.

This verse reports that the people of Lot did not answer his admonition with an argument; instead they said to one another: expel them from your town, for they are people who keep themselves pure. Commentators agree that the pronoun refers to Lot and his believing household, and that this reply was beside the point of his words. On the meaning of the verb, al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas explain it as abstaining from anal intercourse with men and women alike. Al-Mawardi offers another reading: purifying oneself by approaching wives during their times of purity. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the people spoke mockingly, in the manner of dissolute men ridiculing a pious man. Qatada says they blamed him without any genuine fault, and Ibn 'Abbas says they disparaged him with what is normally praised. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi take the expulsion as their real intention, which God frustrated by saving Lot. Ibn 'Ashur observes that purity is a moral virtue which such a people, accustomed to depravity, regarded as a burden. Several scholars note that the verb's form suggests a repeated and continuous habit.

The commentators explain that God saved Lot and those of his household who believed, but excepted his wife, because she did not believe and kept close to her people while concealing her disbelief. She is therefore counted among those who remained in the punishment or who perished with them. On the meaning of 'al-ghabirin', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as those left behind, that is, those destroyed, while Abu Ubayda and al-Tabari also mention the sense of the long-lived elderly who grew old before the destruction, and al-Zajjaj understands it as those who missed salvation. Abu Ubayda and al-Tabari note that the verb 'ghabara' means both to remain and to pass, and they support this with poetry. Al-Razi observes that the masculine plural is used to include the women. Regarding 'his household', Ibn Abbas and al-Tha'alibi take it to mean his two daughters, while others include the believers who followed him, and al-Razi leaves both readings open. As for the wife, Ibn Kathir judges it more likely that she stayed with the people without Lot knowing she had remained, whereas others report that she followed them, looked back and was struck by a stone. Ibn 'Ashur adds that she was a disbeliever who hid her unbelief.

This verse describes the rain that God sent down on the people of Lot, an extraordinary punishment. The commentators identify it as stones of hardened clay, as the Qur'an states elsewhere, and see it as the total destruction of their cities. The command to look is addressed to the Prophet or to anyone able to reflect on the fate of the wicked. All agree that this rain was a punishment, but they differ on how it happened. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that stones fell upon the people. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi report that Gabriel uprooted the cities, lifted them and overturned them, and that stones pursued those who were travelling or outside the towns. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi explain the linguistic difference between matara and amtara, the first used for mercy and the second for punishment, and note that the expression here means an unusual kind of rain. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take the rain to be stones, while Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi also mention the sinking of the inhabitants into the earth. Al-Razi draws from the verse an argument for the legal punishment of sodomy, a view defended by al-Shafi'i, whereas Abu Hanifa disagrees. Ibn Kathir records the differences on the penalty, between stoning and throwing from a height. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also note that Lot's wife, who stayed with the wrongdoers, perished with them. For the commentators as a whole, the central message is that God severely punishes wrongdoers and that their fate should serve as a lesson.

This verse tells us that Shu'ayb was sent to the people of Madyan, his kinsmen, and told them to worship God alone, since they have no other god, and that a clear proof had come to them from their Lord. He commands them to give full measure and weight, not to cheat people of their goods, and not to spread corruption on earth after it has been set in order. The commentators agree on the core: monotheism comes first, then honesty in trade and refusal of corruption, and this is better for them if they are believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that Madyan names both the tribe and a town near Ma'an, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note it may be a personal name or a land, and that Madyan was a son of Abraham according to Ibn Ishaq. On the "proof", al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi take it to be a miracle the Quran does not describe, and they list miracles attributed to him; Ibn 'Ashur instead reads it as the argument he had made against their idolatry, and others understand it as his mere coming. On the prohibition of sitting on every road, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain that they threatened anyone who wished to reach Shu'ayb, while Abu Hurayra and al-Suddi take it as highway robbery or tax collecting. The commentators present these views without deciding between them.

This verse forbids the people of Madyan from sitting on every road to threaten those who pass and to turn them away from God's path, which is faith in Shu'ayb, while seeking to make that path crooked. The commentators broadly agree on the basic meaning: these people sat on the roads leading to Shu'ayb, threatened anyone who wished to meet him, called him a liar, and threatened believers with death. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and as-Suddi, and it is followed by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi.

Al-Tabari takes a wider view: the verse covers any obstruction of the truth. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read the 'roads' as the many paths of religion, since the path of truth is one but branches into doctrines, limits and rulings, and they hold that the people blocked anyone who began on any of these branches. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that these people were tax collectors, and both extend the warning to unlawful exactions.

Other readings are also recorded. Abu Hurayra, followed by al-Wahidi, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi, understood it as a prohibition of highway robbery, and al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi cite the report of the Night Journey in which the Prophet saw a plank on the road that tore every garment passing it. Al-Alusi notes that this sense may be figurative. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse instead to cheating in measure and weight.

On the wording, the commentators differ over 'tabghunaha 'iwajan': some take it as seeking to sow doubt, others as describing the road as crooked. 'Kathrakum' is explained as an increase in numbers after a small population, or as wealth after poverty, and they recall Madyan's marriage to Lot's daughter. The verse ends by calling the listeners to consider the fate of the corrupters of earlier peoples.

Shu'ayb tells his people that if one group among them has believed in the message he was sent with while another has refused, they should wait patiently until God judges between the two sides, for He is the best of judges. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: the people had split into believers and deniers, and the awaited judgment is a decisive act of God that will give victory to those in the right and humble those in the wrong. Al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi explain that this means God will punish the deniers and save the believers, and al-Tabari adds that God's judgment is perfectly fair, with no favouritism toward anyone. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the words are at once a consolation for the believers and a warning to the deniers. The main disagreement concerns who is addressed by the command to be patient. Ibn Abbas, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and, according to Munthir ibn Sa'id, take it as a promise to the believers, while Muqatil ibn Sulayman, al-Zamakhshari and al-Naqqash take it as a threat to the deniers, a reading Ibn Atiyya presents as the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan also allow that it may address both groups together, each having to bear what troubles it. Al-Alusi considers the threat reading the most apparent. Ibn Sa'di notes that those who refused were in fact the majority. Al-Qurtubi points out that the verb is masculine because the sense is of a group, even though the word ta'ifa is feminine. Al-Sha'rawi sees both meanings intended at once.

This passage reports the threat of the proud chiefs of Chou'ayb's people, who warn him and the believers with him that they will be expelled from the town or forced to return to their religion. Chou'ayb answers with astonishment: would we return even if we were unwilling? The commentators agree that the word millah means the false religion and that Chou'ayb never followed it; the speech therefore includes the believers in the 'we' by a rule that the group is given precedence over the individual. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain this, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that the verb 'ada can mean 'to become', which removes the need to suppose an earlier state of unbelief. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi add that returning to idolatry would be a lie against God. On the clause 'unless God wills', the Sunni scholars, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, take it as proof that disbelief occurs by God's will, whereas the Mu'tazilites, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report, read it as divine abandonment or as a formula of submission and humility. Finally Chou'ayb puts his trust in God and asks Him to judge between him and his people with truth; Ibn 'Abbas explains that 'fatah' means to judge in the dialect of Yemen.

This passage records Shu'ayb's reply to the arrogant chiefs of his people, who threatened to expel him and those who believed with him unless they returned to their religion. The commentators explain that he answers that if they returned to disbelief after God had saved them from it, they would be inventing a lie against God, and that such a return is not possible for them. His qualification "unless our Lord wills" is read in different ways: at-Tabari and as-Suddi take it to mean unless God has already decreed in His knowledge that they would return, while az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see it as an expression of courtesy toward God and an acknowledgement of His power. al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir hold that the divine will extends over all things. ar-Razi and al-Qurtubi report these views and note that Ash'arites and Mu'tazilites each cite the verse to support their doctrine of divine will. On the meaning of "return", many, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and an-Nasafi, consider it a rhetorical device in which Shu'ayb includes himself among his people, while others, such as ar-Razi and Abu Hayyan, take it to mean "become". Several commentators, including at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, explain that "open" means "judge" or "decide", a term they attribute to the Yemeni or Murad dialect, and report that Ibn 'Abbas did not understand the word until he heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say "come, let me judge you". Shu'ayb ends with "You are the best of judges", which some read as a prayer offered after he had despaired of his people's faith.

The disbelieving chiefs of Shu'ayb's people said to those around them, warning them against following him: if you follow Shu'ayb, you will surely be losers. The commentators give several meanings to the word loss. Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean being cheated, 'Ata' took it to mean being ignorant, and al-Dahhak took it to mean being weak or wicked. Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him understood that they would lose guidance by exchanging it for error. Others, such as al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, read it as a worldly loss, since Shu'ayb forbade them to cheat in weights and measures and ordered them to give full measure, so they would lose the gains they made from such practices. The scholars note that the clause introduced by the emphatic oath and the conditional clause share a single answer, the oath's answer standing in for the missing answer of the condition, and that Abu Hayyan and others raised grammatical objections to this analysis. The commentators present the speech as a sign of the chiefs' stubbornness: having grown proud and fixed in disbelief, they feared that Shu'ayb's words and sound arguments would win over the ordinary people.

This verse says that the violent earthquake seized the disbelievers of Shu'ayb's people, so that by morning they lay dead, fallen on their knees in their homes, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy explain. The commentators agree that the rajfa is a destructive quake, and that the people were destroyed after they threatened Shu'ayb with expulsion from their town or with forcing him back into their religion. Most link the event to a wider punishment: a scorching heat, then a cloud from which fire rained down, which corresponds to the punishment of the Day of the Canopy mentioned in Surat al-Shu'ara. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur suggest that the cry mentioned in Surat Hud may refer to part of the same event. Qatada holds that the people of Madyan were struck by the cry and those of al-Ayka by the cloud, while Ibn 'Atiyya allows that the two groups may have been destroyed separately or together. On the phrase as if they had never dwelt there, three readings are reported: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Akhfash take it as not having lived, Qatada as not having enjoyed life, and Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj as not having stayed. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, note that repeating the phrase those who denied Shu'ayb serves to magnify their shame, and that the true loss falls on the deniers rather than on the believers who followed him. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi also relate accounts about the kings of Madyan and some elegiac verses, though Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi treat these as uncertain.

This verse states that those who denied Shu'ayb were utterly destroyed, so that it is as if they had never dwelt in their homes, and that the real loss was theirs and not that of those who followed him. On the phrase « as if they had never dwelt there », the commentators give close meanings. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd that it means they never lived there, never enjoyed prosperity, or never existed there. Ibn Qutayba, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean they did not remain or settle there, while al-Zajjaj explains it as living without wealth or with ease. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the verb is generally used for a stay accompanied by comfort. All agree that the loss meant is that of both this world and the next. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur explain that repeating the relative pronoun and the clause adds emphasis, rebuts the notables' claim and mocks their reasoning. On the nature of the punishment, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir link the quake and the fire to the Day of the Shade, Ibn 'Atiyya allows that two groups may have perished in different ways, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that a single event combining thunderbolts and an earthquake struck them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mention Shu'ayb's grief, and al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi offer two readings of his words « how could I grieve »: a rebuke directed at himself or an excuse for not grieving more.

The commentators explain that Shu'ayb turned away from his people once the punishment had come upon them, and then addressed them in a tone of lament: I conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and gave you sincere counsel, so how should I grieve over a disbelieving people? The majority of exegetes read the question as a denial: he should not grieve over people who deserved what befell them because of their disbelief and stubbornness. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Sudi take the word asa to mean grief, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir follow this reading; Ibn Ishaq reports that Shu'ayb was overcome by intense sorrow and then consoled himself. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi offer another sense, namely that he is making an excuse: he gave them every warning and they did not listen, so there is no cause for him to grieve over them. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the statement as an expression of regret and a confession that the people did not accept him. Ibn Ashur sees in the address «O my people» a cry of lament and a disavowal of their conduct, and in the interrogative form a turning of the thought back upon the speaker himself. Al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi note a reading attributed to Yahya ibn Waththab, «fa-kayfa iysa», with a vowel change, which belongs to a known dialectal form.

This verse states that God never sent a prophet to a town without first afflicting its people, who rejected him, with hardship and adversity, so that they might humble themselves and turn back to Him. The commentators agree on this general sense but differ on the precise meaning of the terms. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Samani, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan take al-ba'sa'' as poverty in wealth and al-darra'' as bodily illness, while Ibn 'Abbas understands hunger and poverty, and al-Hasan drought and calamities; al-Baghawi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi also mention war. As for the phrase that they 'increased' (hatta 'afaw), most, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir, read it as growing in wealth and children, whereas Qatada reads it as rejoicing and al-Hasan as becoming plump. Nearly all agree that the ease following hardship is a further test, and that the disbelievers' claim that such is the custom of time reflected heedlessness and arrogance, so they were seized suddenly while unaware. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur present the passage as both consolation for the Prophet and a warning to Quraysh, while al-Sha'rawi sees hardship as a means of awakening man to his Lord.

This verse describes God's pattern with peoples who rejected their messengers. When a prophet was sent to a town and its people denied him, God struck them with hardship and adversity so that they might humble themselves before Him. When this failed, God replaced their hardship with ease, so that they multiplied in person and wealth. The commentators agree that the word 'afaw' means to increase and flourish. Al-Tabari also reports Qatada's reading as 'they rejoiced', which he considers hard to justify in Arabic, and al-Hasan's reading as 'they grew fat'. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take the bad to mean hardship and the good to mean ease, while Mujahid reads them as evil and good in general. All agree on their words, 'Our fathers too were touched by hardship and ease', which they took as the ordinary course of time rather than a punishment, and so they persisted in disbelief. Ibn Kathir, al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di hold that God tested them with both states so that they would give thanks and humble themselves, which they did not do; Ibn Kathir adds that the believer gives thanks in ease and is patient in hardship. All conclude that God seized them suddenly, while they were unaware, which made their punishment more bitter and served as a warning to the Quraysh.

This verse says that if the people of the towns had believed and feared God, He would have opened to them blessings from heaven and earth; but they denied, and God seized them for what they had earned. The commentators generally understand the blessings of heaven as rain and those of earth as plants and fruit, and the opening as an abundant facilitation of good. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the definite article in 'the towns' refers back to the destroyed towns mentioned before, while al-Zamakhshari also allows that it may denote the category as a whole. Ibn Kathir and others see in the verse a statement about the weak faith of the peoples to whom messengers were sent. Ibn Abbas and al-Sam'ani explain the heavenly blessings as the answering of prayers and the earthly ones as the easing of needs, whereas al-Sudi takes them more broadly as provision. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi add that blessing means continuity and increase. In the following verses on feeling secure against God's punishment and plan, most scholars treat such security as a sign of loss, and Ibn Kathir explains God's plan as a gradual leading on through favours. Ibn al-Qayyim links the loss of blessing to sins, Sayyid Qutb sees in the verse a link between faith and prosperity, and Ibn Ashur reads an allusion to the pagans of Mecca while avoiding a general rule.

The verse questions the people of the towns who rejected their messengers: do they feel safe from God's punishment coming upon them at night while they sleep, or during the day while they are busy with their amusements? Most commentators take 'the towns' to mean Mecca and its surroundings, since the Prophet ﷺ was rejected there, while az-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur take it as any town that rejected its messenger. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the punishment comes at a moment of heedlessness, and al-Razi notes that night sleep and midmorning are times when a person is absorbed in pleasures, which makes the blow harder.

The commentators agree on the main message: a warning against heedlessness of God's way, and that feeling safe from God's scheme leads to ruin. Ibn Kathir reports al-Hasan al-Basri's words that the believer acts in fear while the wrongdoer sins feeling secure. They also discuss the particle: the reading of Ibn Amir and the people of the Hijaz with a silent waw presents an alternative, while the majority reading with an interrogative hamza after the conjunction is a sequence of questions.

As for the 'scheme of God', Qatada and al-Baghawi explain it as gradual drawing-in through blessings, while al-Baghawi (citing 'Atiyya) and others understand it as punishment, and al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur describe it as a figure of speech where the punishment takes the name of the sin. On the next phrase, 'awa lam yahdi', Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read it as 'has it not become clear', while Ibn Atiyya explains that the sealing of hearts is presented as a continuing consequence.

In this verse, God rebukes the people of the towns who feel safe from His punishment, whether it comes by night while they sleep or by day at mid-morning, while they are busy with their diversions. The commentators explain 'ba's' as punishment, 'duha' as the forenoon when the sun has risen, and 'yal'abun' as heedlessness and occupation with what brings no benefit. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir tie the verse to God's way with earlier nations, who were tested first by hardship and then by ease, before being seized suddenly. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read it as a question of rebuke, and they explain how it connects to the preceding verses through the particles fa and waw. The readers differ on 'aw amina': Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read the waw as sukun, which gives an alternative or a division, while 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and the others read it with fatha and an interrogative hamza. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the two readings do not carry exactly the same meaning. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the choice of night and day, sleep and play, a sign that these are the times when people are most unguarded, so the punishment would be the more severe. For Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, God's 'makr' is istidraj, a gradual leading on that ends in loss, and the verse warns the disbelievers of Mecca, or all people according to Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur. The commentators agree that feeling safe from God's plan is a sign of ruin.

God rebukes the people of the towns who deny Him for feeling safe from His stratagem, that is, His gradual testing through blessings in this world until He seizes them when they least expect it. Only the losers feel secure against it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that these losers are those who perish, and al-Nasafi says they are the disbelievers who ruined their own souls. Ibn Kathir quotes al-Hasan al-Basri: the believer does good deeds while fearful and anxious, while the wicked commits sins while feeling secure. Al-Zamakhshari compares the wise person's watchfulness to a warrior fearing an ambush, citing Rabi' ibn Khuthaym's answer to his daughter. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that early scholars disagreed about praying not to be made secure from God's stratagem, and that Mutarrif ibn Abd Allah disliked the phrasing. Al-Alusi reports the legal dispute: the Hanafis consider such security a form of disbelief, like despair of God's mercy, while the Shafi'is consider it a major sin, and some scholars tie the ruling to inner conviction. For the next verse, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take the word yahdi to mean 'make clear', so the question is whether it has not become clear to the heirs of those peoples that We could strike them for their sins, and that We seal their hearts so they no longer hear.

The verse addresses the contemporaries of the Prophet, the people of Mecca and its surroundings, in the form of a rebuke: have they not understood that if God willed He could seize them for their sins as He seized those before them, and that He seals their hearts so that they no longer hear admonition? The commentators agree that the verb yahdi here means to make clear or to show, as Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy explain, and the verse is generally read as a warning. Some readers used the first-person plural nahdi, which makes the clause about God's will its object, while the third-person reading makes it the subject; al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the particle an is a lightened form. The most debated point concerns wa-natba'u: most scholars link it to an implied idea, namely that they neglect guidance while We seal their hearts, or treat it as an independent sentence. Al-Zamakhshari rejects coordinating it with asabnahum because sealing presupposes that the people are already sealed, an objection Ibn al-Munir finds insufficient. Al-Razi holds that destruction and sealing cannot coexist. Al-Jubba'i understands the seal as a mark, al-Asamm as persistence in error until death, and Abu Muslim as divine abandonment. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi take yasma'un to mean accepting, a well-attested sense in Arabic. The shared lesson is that one who hears the accounts of the destroyed peoples without taking heed deserves to have his heart sealed.

This verse speaks of the towns that God destroyed, those of the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot and Shu'ayb. God tells the Prophet some of their stories so that they serve as a lesson. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, yet they did not believe in what they had already rejected. The commentators understand this persistent refusal as the sealing that God sets on the hearts of the disbelievers, meaning the hardening that results from their obstinacy. The verse consoles the Prophet and gives a warning to those who come after him. The meaning of the phrase 'they would not have believed in what they had denied before' is, however, disputed. Al-Tabari, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Rabi' ibn Anas take it to mean God's eternal knowledge, who knew from the primordial covenant that they would deny. As-Suddi says they believed under compulsion at that covenant. Mujahid holds that they would deny again if they were returned to this world. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir favour a causal reading: their early denial prevented later faith, which Ibn Kathir considers a sound interpretation. Al-Zamakhshari explains that their refusal persisted until their death. On 'they kept no covenant', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir refer it to the covenant taken from the loins of Adam, while others see it as fidelity to the prophets' messages. Ibn Kathir adds that the 'wicked' are those who depart from obedience. Several commentators also discuss the grammar of 'in' and 'lam' without firmly deciding between readings.

This verse states that most of the peoples whom God destroyed, such as the people of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb, did not keep the covenant that bound them. The commentators differ on what this covenant was. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, relying on Ibn Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, identify it with the pledge taken from the descendants of Adam while they were in his loins, when they acknowledged God as their Lord. Al-Hasan al-Basri understands it as the commandment, conveyed through the prophets, to worship God alone and to associate nothing with Him, and Ibn Mas'ud relates it to faith. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the pronoun may refer to people in general, so that the meaning is that most of them broke God's covenant of faith and piety, and they also mention peoples who swore to believe when in distress and then broke their word once saved. Al-Razi lists several possible senses, including faith and the establishment of proofs of God's oneness. Ibn Ashur explains that the verb 'to find' here means 'to know', and that the denial of a covenant expresses the absence of fidelity to it. On the meaning of fisq, the exegetes agree that it denotes going out of obedience and breaking the pledge. Some, such as the Kufan grammarians cited by Abu Hayyan, read the particle 'in' as a negation, while most take it as a lightened form of the emphatic particle.

The commentators explain that this verse speaks of Moses, sent after the prophets mentioned before him, with God's signs as proof of his truth, to Pharaoh and the chiefs of his people. They rejected those signs out of injustice and obstinacy, and the verse invites the reader to consider the end of these corrupters. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that injustice (zulm) here means disbelief, since rejecting clear signs places denial where faith was due. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi add that the injustice may also fall on people, as Pharaoh's court turned them away from faith and harmed the believers, and that the particle bi may then indicate cause.

They also agree on the outcome: Pharaoh and his people were drowned in the sea. Al-Tabari sees the addressee of 'look' as the Prophet ﷺ, while Ibn Ashur addresses any listener able to reflect. Ibn Ashur also explains that Pharaoh was a title for the kings of Egypt, and that 'thumma' signals a long interval between Moses and the earlier prophets. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di note that the verse is a summary whose detailed narrative follows in the surah, with the signs, the magicians and the Children of Israel.

Al-Razi notes that Moses was given many signs and reports Ibn Abbas's list of the uses of the staff. The disagreements therefore concern mainly the nature of the injustice and the meaning of the preposition, not the substance of the account.

This verse records Moses saying to Pharaoh that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, the Creator who governs all creation. The commentators agree that Moses addresses Pharaoh by the title used for the rulers of Egypt, and that the main purpose of his opening is to establish the divine source of his mission against Pharaoh's claim to lordship. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read it as a direct statement, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya link what follows to Pharaoh's reply that he was a liar. On the phrase 'it is incumbent upon me to say nothing about God but the truth', the scholars differ. Nafi' reads 'haqiqun 'alayya', meaning 'binding upon me', while the other readers read 'ala', understood as 'worthy of' or 'eager to'. Al-Farra' and al-Farisi take 'ala' to mean 'bi', as in the expression 'I came in a good state'. Abu 'Ubayda gives the sense of 'eager to'. Az-Zamakhshari offers several explanations, including inversion, mutual obligation, and an exaggeration of Moses' own sincerity, and he considers the last the most fitting. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the emphasis answers the likely disbelief of the listener. All agree that the purpose of the mission is to release the children of Israel. The traditions about Pharaoh's name vary, and the exegetes do not base the meaning on it.

Moses tells Pharaoh that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, that it is his duty to say nothing about God but the truth, and that he brings a clear sign from his Lord. He then asks Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel so they may go with him. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the messenger does not lie about God, and he has proof to back his claim. The meaning of the word 'haqiq' is debated. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi take it to mean 'worthy of' or 'bound to', while al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda explain that 'ala' stands in for 'bi' ('I am worthy to say only the truth'), and Abu 'Ubayda also renders the word as 'eager'. Nafi's reading 'haqiqun 'alayya' (with a doubled yā') means 'it is incumbent upon me to say only the truth'. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi set out several other possible readings, including a reversal of wording and an emphasis on Moses' own truthfulness. As for the 'sign', al-Tabari understands it as an argument and a proof, while Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes identify it as the staff; al-Baydawi notes that the context points to the staff and the white hand. According to Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, after Joseph's death Pharaoh reduced the Children of Israel to hard labour, and Moses asks for their release so they can return to the Holy Land.

This verse records that Pharaoh, after Moses presented his message from the Lord of the worlds, asked him for a sign to prove his truthfulness: if he has brought a sign, let him produce it, if he is among the truthful. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: Pharaoh demands a miracle, and Moses throws down his staff, which becomes a manifest serpent, then draws out his hand, which appears white to onlookers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan stress that the mission rests on a proof from God and that Moses' words are an invitation to faith. The main disagreement concerns the reading of the word haqiq. Nafi' reads 'haqiqun 'alayya', meaning 'it is incumbent upon me', while the others read 'haqiqun 'ala', meaning 'worthy of', with 'ala' standing for 'bi' according to al-Farra', al-Farisi and Abu Hayyan. Abu 'Ubayda takes it to mean 'eager', and al-Zamakhshari suggests Moses is affirming his own truthfulness. Ibn 'Ashur notes that 'bayyina' may mean a rational proof as well as a miracle. Some reports describe the miracle in detail, including the huge serpent, Pharaoh's terror and the number of dead, while summaries such as the Jalalayn and al-Muyassar limit themselves to the demand for a sign.

This verse describes Moses throwing his staff before Pharaoh, and it becomes a plainly visible serpent. Most commentators understand thu'ban as a large male serpent, as Ibn 'Abbas, as-Suddi and ad-Dahhak state. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that mubin means it is clearly a real snake and there is no illusion about it. Al-Razi notes that this clarity distinguishes the miracle from the sorcerers' tricks. The white hand in the next verse is described by the commentators as an extraordinary whiteness that was not a disease, since Moses had a dark complexion, and it returned to its normal colour when he put it back in his garment. The accounts of the serpent's details differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate that Pharaoh was terrified, defecated, and that many people died in the stampede, while Ibn 'Atiyya and an-Nasafi mention only the flight. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi consider these details not to be found in reliable reports. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur explain that haqiq means worthy or bound, and the grammarians debated the sense of 'ala after it, some taking it to mean bi and others implying eagerness. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also suggest that Moses is describing his own truthfulness in that setting. Overall, the commentators agree that this passage presents a clear sign of Moses' truthfulness before Pharaoh.

This verse describes the miracle of the white hand that Moses showed Pharaoh after the staff. The commentators explain that Moses put his hand into his garment or under his armpit, then drew it out and it appeared white and radiant, with a light that outshone the sun according to Ibn Abbas and others. This whiteness was not a disease, since Moses had a dark complexion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the whiteness was extraordinary and that people gathered to look at it, while Mujahid compares it to milk or something even whiter. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that the phrase 'for the onlookers' means the whiteness was so striking that it drew their gaze. The commentators differ on where Moses placed his hand: some say the collar of his garment, others under his armpit. Al-Razi notes that multiple signs increase certainty, and mentions an allegorical reading of the two miracles, which he rejects. Ibn Ashur stresses that the white hand was a clear proof of Moses' mission. The commentators agree that the white hand was a sign of his mission, a luminous whiteness and not a sickness, and that it returned to its former colour when he put it back.

The chieftains of Pharaoh's people said that Moses is a skilled and knowing sorcerer who wants to drive them out of their land, and they asked what should be done. The commentators agree that they called Moses a sorcerer because the staff turning into a serpent and the hand shining white without blemish went beyond anything familiar to them, and that their aim was to discredit his sign and turn people away from it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that sorcery makes a thing appear other than it is, and Al-Tabari compares this to the mirage. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur note that the same words are attributed to Pharaon in Surat al-Shu'ara, and that either Pharaoh said them first and the chiefs repeated them, or the chiefs relayed them to the people as kings do with their counsel. On the phrase "what do you advise", Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as Pharaoh's question to his counsellors, while al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it as the chiefs speaking to Pharaoh alone out of respect. On "arjih", Ibn Abbas says delay him, Qatada says detain him, and Ibn Kathir finds detention the sounder meaning. The readings differ on this word and on "sahhar". The reports about how many magicians were gathered vary widely, from seventy to hundreds of thousands.

This verse reports the words of the chiefs of Pharaoh's people after they witnessed Moses' two signs, the staff turned into a serpent and the white hand. They call him a knowing sorcerer and say he wants to drive them out of their land, Egypt. The commentators differ on who speaks these words. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take them as the chiefs speaking among themselves, or as Pharaoh consulting his council, so that the phrase means: what do you advise? Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi suggest that Pharaoh said it first and the chiefs then repeated it to the people. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir describe the words as fear-driven. Al-Razi, Ibn Ashur and Ibn Kathir explain that the expulsion may mean driving them out by force or by trickery, or the departure of the Children of Israel, who served the Copts, which would ruin the land. Al-Nakkash, cited by Ibn Atiyya, says the Israelites paid a tribute and the chiefs feared the end of their rule. Al-Tabari defines sihr as an illusion that makes a thing appear other than it is, and Ibn Atiyya cites a line of Dhu al-Rumma to illustrate the image. All agree that the chiefs then advise delaying Moses and his brother and gathering the sorcerers from the cities. They differ on the meaning of arjih: Ibn Abbas and Ata say postpone, while Qatada and al-Kalbi say imprison.

The Qur'an recounts that the chiefs of Pharaoh's people, after seeing the staff turn into a serpent and the hand come out white, accused Moses of sorcery and feared he would drive the Egyptians from their land. They advised Pharaoh to delay the matter of Moses and his brother Aaron, and to send men into the cities to gather the magicians so they could confront what Moses had brought. The commentators agree that 'arjih' means to postpone, though Qatada and 'Ata' take it to mean to detain. Al-Razi considers the detention reading weak, since Pharaoh could no longer hold Moses after the signs he had witnessed. Regarding the 'gatherers', Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars identify them as police officers charged with assembling the magicians, and al-Mawardi reports that there were seventy-two of them. Readers differ on the pronunciation of the verb, on the hamza, and on the vowel of the final heh, and al-Farra' considers the sukun a genuine Arabic usage that the Basrans rejected. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and others locate these cities in Upper Egypt. Zamakhshari suggests that Pharaoh first uttered the words 'this is a knowledgeable sorcerer' and the chiefs then repeated them to the public, a view Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi discuss further.

The verse relates the counsel given to Pharaoh by the chiefs of his people after they witnessed the staff turning into a serpent and the hand shining white. They advise him to delay the matter of Moses and his brother, and to send agents into the cities to gather every skilled magician. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the intensive form « sahhar », which the readers agree on in the Surah of the Poets. Ibn Abbas and most commentators understand the summoners to be police officers, while al-Zamakhshari suggests the words may have come from Pharaoh himself, passed on to the people in the manner of kings. The commentators agree that « irjih » means to delay, though Qatada and al-Kalbi take it to mean to imprison. Ibn Kathir notes that magic was widespread in that era and that the chiefs feared Moses would be confused with a sorcerer.
