The reports on the number of magicians vary widely, from twelve thousand according to Ka'b to seventy thousand according to Ikrima, eighty thousand according to Ibn al-Munkadir, and seventy-two according to Muqatil. Ibn al-Jawzi lists more than a dozen opinions. Regarding the magicians' question about whether they will receive a reward, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it as a statement, while others read it as a question, and al-Razi prefers the interrogative reading.

The verse reports that the magicians came to Pharaoh, after he had sent agents to gather the sorcerers from the cities, and asked for a substantial reward if they prevailed over Moses. Pharaoh agreed and added that they would be among his closest courtiers. The commentators broadly agree on this meaning. The readings differ between a declarative and an interrogative form of the request: some prefer the question, since the magicians were not certain of the payment, while others take the affirmation as fixing the reward. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the indefinite "ajran" magnifies the reward, as in the Arab saying that someone surely has camels, meaning he has many. The number of magicians is widely disputed: Ibn 'Abbas gives seventy-two, Ka'b al-Ahbar twelve thousand, Ibn al-Munkadir eighty thousand, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy judge these figures to lack a reliable basis. Several authors, including al-Baydawi, note that the reward sought was wages, a gift and a high rank. Sayyid Qutb sees in the scene the link between tyranny and religious professionals who serve for pay, whereas Ibn 'Ashur reads the phrase "qalu" as an explanatory resumption that establishes the demand rather than expressing doubt about it.

This passage recounts how the magicians came to Pharaoh asking for a reward if they defeated Moses. Pharaoh agreed and added that they would also be among those brought near to him. The commentators agree that the promise combined material payment with high rank, meant to spur their effort. Al-Kalbi, as cited by al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, explained that nearness meant they would be the first to enter his presence and the last to leave it. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Hafs read the opening words as a statement, while the others read them as a question. Abu 'Ali found the interrogative more suitable, since the magicians were not certain of the reward. The reported number of magicians varies widely, from seventy to around eighty thousand. Ibn al-Jawzi notes that none of these figures has a reliable chain of transmission, and al-Qurtubi leaves the matter to God's knowledge. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the magicians let Moses choose whether to throw first, out of courtesy and confidence. Ibn 'Ashur sees this offer as a way of testing Moses' assurance, while al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan read it as an expression of their self-assurance. Several detailed accounts of their ropes and staffs, transmitted by Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti, appear in the traditional tafsir works.

This verse reports that after Pharaoh's magicians were promised a reward and a place among his closest courtiers, they gave Moses the choice of going first: either he throws his staff, or they throw theirs. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir read this as a courteous gesture towards Moses. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan also see confidence and pride in it, noting that the magicians stressed the pronoun 'we' and made the predicate definite, which shows their wish to act first. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i allow the particle 'an' in the accusative with the sense of 'choose'. Al-Razi argues that Moses' command to throw was conditional on the magicians' act being genuine, and that the permission was given so that the miracle would be clearer, a view that Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also link to God's purpose of strengthening Moses. The commentators agree that when the magicians threw their objects they deceived the onlookers' eyes and struck them with fear. They differ on how this was done: al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir mention cords and staffs filled with mercury, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur stress illusion and staging. For most, the central point is that the truth ultimately became manifest against the deception, and that the question of who went first was not significant in itself.

The passage describes Moses telling the magicians to throw down what they have. When they threw their ropes and staffs, they deceived the people's eyes so that the objects seemed to be moving snakes, which frightened the onlookers, and they produced a great magic. The commentators agree that the magic here is deception and illusion that diverts the eye from what is really there, and that the effect lies in the spectators' sight rather than in the objects themselves. Al-Tabari and al-Suddi report that the ropes and staffs were very numerous, each magician bringing his own. Ibn Abbas describes thick ropes and long wooden poles that filled the valley. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi explain that istarhabuhum means they terrified them greatly, while al-Mubarrad held that the sin is merely an added letter. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan report that the magicians had dyed the ropes and placed mercury inside, a detail al-Qurtubi also mentions. The reports on the number of magicians differ widely, and Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan regard these figures as lacking reliable support. Al-Razi argues that the command to throw did not endorse disbelief but was meant to show the miracle clearly, a view supported by Ibn 'Ashur. Al-Alusi notes that most Sunni scholars accept that magic is real, while the Mu'tazilites deny it, as al-Zamakhshari points out. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that magic does not change the nature of things but the perception of those who watch.

The commentators explain that God inspired Moses to throw down his staff; when he did, it became a great serpent that swallowed everything the magicians had thrown, ropes and rods which their trickery had made appear to move. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that after it had swallowed them Moses took the staff back and it returned to its former shape, and the magicians, recognising that this was a sign from heaven and not sorcery, fell down in prostration. All agree on the meaning of the key words: talqafu means to seize or swallow quickly, and ya'fikun means to lie or to turn the truth into falsehood, as Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas explain. The phrase fa-waqa'a al-haqq means that the truth became manifest and established, and falsehood was annulled. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the truth as the appearance of Moses' sign over the magicians' ropes, while al-Razi sees in it the demonstration of Moses' prophethood against Pharaoh's claim to lordship. On the prostration, al-Mawardi records two views: that they bowed to Moses in submission, or to God in acknowledgement of His lordship, the latter being the more widely held. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya discuss why Moses told the magicians to throw first, offering reasons such as a condition that they be sincere, or a wish to make his own miracle more striking. The number of magicians varies widely across the reports, from several dozen to tens of thousands, and no commentator settles on a single figure.

This verse from Surat al-A'raf describes the triumph of truth: Moses' staff, cast at God's command, became a serpent that swallowed what the magicians had thrown, so the truth was established and their magic was annulled. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, and Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan and al-Baghawi all explain that 'the truth was established' means it became manifest and prevailed. Al-Mawardi gives two possible meanings of this truth: the staff's dominance over the magicians' cords, or the prophethood of Moses overcoming Pharaoh's claim to lordship.

The commentators agree that when the magicians' cords and staffs vanished, they realised the event was not sorcery, as al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that the magicians' work was illusion and deception, and Ibn 'Atiyya reports that the staff swallowed everything that had been thrown. Al-Razi observes that mentioning the annulment after the establishment of truth emphasises that the objects were truly gone. Opinions differ on what 'what they were doing' refers to: Abu Hayyan and al-Wahidi take it as the magic itself, while Ibn 'Ashur sees it as the effect of magic that was exposed as hollow.

All agree that the verse states Pharaoh and his people were overcome and returned humiliated, while the magicians fell prostrate in faith.

This verse describes the outcome of the contest between Moses and Pharaoh's magicians. After the magicians threw down their ropes and staves, which seemed to the onlookers to be moving serpents, Moses was commanded to throw his staff. It swallowed what they had falsely contrived, the truth was established, and their work came to nothing. The commentators explain that "they were overcome there" means that Pharaoh, his people and the magicians were defeated in that place, and that "they returned humiliated" means that they went back, or became abased, confounded and subdued. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir give this same general sense. Ibn Sa'di and al-Shawkani note that the defeat applies to Pharaoh and his people, while al-Sha'rawi extends the humiliation to everyone who opposed Moses. Opinions differ on who is included in the subject of "they returned." Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that if the return happened before the magicians believed, they are included, but if belief came first, they are not subject to this humiliation. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verb as meaning "became," which takes in everyone. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the word "inqalaba" is more eloquent than "raja'a" or "sara," since it suggests a change to a lower state. The commentators present these readings side by side without judging between them.

This verse describes the moment when, after Moses' staff had swallowed everything the magicians had made of ropes and staffs, the magicians fell down in prostration as though they had been thrown down, saying: we believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron. The commentators explain this prostration in different ways. Al-Hasan and Mujahid say the truth became manifest, while al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the magicians, seeing what lay beyond all magic, understood it came from heaven. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi say God inspired them to prostrate, or cast them down; al-Akhfash explains they prostrated so quickly it was as if they had been thrown. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan note that they could not restrain themselves before what they saw. Some, including al-Mawardi, al-Samani, al-Baghawi and al-Alusi, report that Moses and Aaron prostrated in thanks to God and the magicians followed them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur observe that naming the Lord through Moses and Aaron ruled out any idea that they bowed to Pharaoh. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir record widely differing figures for the number of magicians. Al-Razi cites the theologians who hold that their complete knowledge of magic let them recognise a miracle. Al-Razi and al-Alusi hold that their prostration was directed to God. Qatada and al-Hasan say they were unbelievers at the start of the day and faithful martyrs by its end.

This verse describes how the magicians, after seeing Moses' staff swallow their ropes and staves, recognised that what they had witnessed was not sorcery but a sign from God. They fell down in prostration and declared their faith in the Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree that the faith preceded the confession, and that the prostration expressed submission. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the words 'the Lord of Moses and Aaron' were added to distinguish the true Lord from Pharaoh, who claimed divinity; al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud say the appositive was meant to prevent the same misunderstanding. On the cause of the prostration opinions differ. Al-Mawardi reports that it was an act of homage either to Moses or to God, while al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that God inspired it in them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as a fall so sudden that they seemed to be thrown down. Al-Razi draws from the passage the lesson that their deep knowledge of magic let them recognise the miracle, and Abu Hayyan sees the prostration as gratitude for knowledge and faith. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that they were magicians at dawn and martyrs by evening. The number of magicians is given in many differing figures, and the commentators do not settle it. Ibn 'Ashur notes that Pharaoh's threat that follows was an accusation, and the verse does not state that it was carried out.

According to the commentators, when the magicians saw the miracle of Moses, namely his staff swallowing their ropes and staves, they understood that it was not of the kind of sorcery. They fell down prostrate and said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds," then clarified, "the Lord of Moses and Aaron," so that no one would think they meant Pharaoh, who claimed lordship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the magicians recognised that the matter came from heaven, while al-Razi holds that their deep mastery of magic is what allowed them to distinguish the miracle from it, and he draws from this a proof of the value of knowledge. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain the prostration as submission and faith, whereas Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi see it as a grateful acknowledgement of God after knowledge was gained.

The reports about the number of magicians differ widely: Ibn al-Jawzi records several versions, ranging from seventy to over nine hundred thousand, and no single figure is preferred. As for Pharaoh's reply, "You believed in him before I gave you leave," most commentators read it as a threat and an attempt to weaken Moses' authority, and Ibn 'Atiyya reports that Pharaoh accused Moses of collusion with the magicians. Al-Jaza'iri draws the lesson that truth always prevails over falsehood, and Al-Sha'rawi notes that the phrase "Lord of Moses and Aaron" was meant to remove any ambiguity about the divinity Pharaoh claimed.

This verse records Pharaoh's words to the magicians after they believed in Moses. He rebukes them for believing before he gave permission, claims their conversion is a plot hatched with Moses in the city to drive out its people, and then threatens them. The commentators generally read this as a rebuke and a threat, whether the opening phrase is taken as a statement or a question. Al-Tabari, al-Samani and Ibn Kathir relay, from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, that Moses had agreed with the chief magician that he would believe if defeated, and that Pharaoh overheard this. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take the 'plot' as a deliberate stratagem, while al-Razi sees Pharaoh as trying to turn the common people away from faith with two claims. The threatened punishment, cutting off hands and feet on opposite sides and then crucifying, is described by most, including al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, who report Ibn Abbas's view that Pharaoh was the first to inflict it; al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note, however, that the Qur'an does not state that he carried it out. The magicians' reply, 'to our Lord we shall return', is read by al-Qurtubi as a defiant answer, and by Ibn 'Ashur as a longing to meet God. All agree that their prayer for patience and for death as Muslims shows firmness in faith.

This passage records Pharaoh's threat against the magicians who had just believed in Moses: he says he will cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides, and then crucify them all. The commentators read this as a threat, and most note that the Qur'an does not explicitly state that he carried it out. Nevertheless, al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas as reported by al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say that Pharaoh was the first to practise cutting from opposite sides and crucifixion, and al-Nasafi repeats this. Ibn Juzayy points out that the threat alone does not prove it was executed. Al-Razi sets out both possibilities: some think Pharaoh did carry it out, while others hold that God granted the magicians' request to die as Muslims. All agree that 'from opposite sides' means a hand and a foot from different sides. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di take the threat mainly as a means of striking fear into the public. The magicians reply that they are returning to their Lord, that they resent nothing from Pharaoh except that they believed in the signs of their Lord, and they ask for patience and to die in submission. The commentators agree that these words express firmness in the face of the threat.

This verse records the reply of the believing magicians to Pharaoh's threat to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them: 'Indeed, we are returning to our Lord.' The commentators offer two closely related readings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as a return to God on the Day of Resurrection, and as a belief that His punishment is more severe than Pharaoh's. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it to mean that they do not fear death, since it leads them to their Lord's meeting and mercy; al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan also mention the possibility, which Abu Hayyan considers weaker, that Pharaoh and they will all return to God to be judged. Al-Wahidi and al-Sam'ani see mainly a comfort to their hearts. All agree that the sin Pharaoh finds in them is only their belief in the signs of their Lord, which al-Zamakhshari presents as the root of all virtues. They then turn to God and ask for an abundant patience, which al-Tabari explains as restraint from disbelief and al-Zamakhshari links to the purification of sins. They also ask to die as Muslims, which al-Tabari understands as steadfastness in the religion of Abraham. Scholars differ on whether the threat was carried out: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Kalbi report that Pharaoh did carry it out, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the verse does not confirm it. The verse contains no legal ruling, though several commentators clarify the meaning of cutting limbs on opposite sides.

The Quran recounts that when Pharaoh threatened the magicians with having their hands and feet cut off on alternate sides and then crucified, they replied that they were returning to their Lord and so did not fear his threats. They added that what he held against them was not a fault: they had believed in their Lord's signs when these came to them. They then turned to God, asking Him to pour out abundant patience upon them and to take them back as Muslims. The commentators agree that 'tanqimu' means to dislike and to find fault with, and that 'afrigh' is a metaphor for pouring patience until it fills the heart, the patience meant being steadfastness under cutting and crucifixion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Pharaoh did carry out the threat by killing and crucifying them. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say the magicians were magicians at the start of the day and martyrs by its end. Al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold instead that God answered their prayer and kept them firm in faith. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan argue that the verse does not by itself prove the threat was carried out, since it speaks of asking for patience in the face of trial. Al-Zamakhshari gives several readings of 'returning to our Lord', including indifference to death because they are going back to meet God, or hope for reward for their sufferings. Al-Razi notes that the exception in this verse carries praise in the form of blame. On readings: most read 'tanqim' with a kasra on the qaf, al-Hasan with a fatha, both being attested. Some read 'wa-ilahataka' meaning your worship, while the majority take it as your gods, and some identify these with the sun or a sacred animal.

The verse reports that the leading men of Pharaoh's people urged him to act against Moses and his people, fearing that they would spread corruption in the land by turning people away from Pharaoh's rule and worship, and by abandoning his gods. Pharaoh replied that he would again kill the sons of the Israelites and spare their women, declaring that his power over them was secure. The commentators broadly agree that "corruption" means calling people to defy Pharaoh and withdraw from his authority, and that the speech of the notables is an incitement full of indignation, while Pharaoh's threat was meant to reassert his strength after Moses' signs. The phrase "and abandon you and your gods" is explained differently. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that Pharaon had made small idols that his people were to worship, while Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi mention a cow, al-Hasan an object hung on his neck, and al-Razi argues that he worshipped the stars. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read "wa ilahatak" meaning your worship, which leads Ibn Kathir to note the saying that Pharaoh was worshipped but did not worship. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the grammar of "wa yadharaka" as coordination with "to corrupt" or as an answer to the question. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari add that Pharaoh's renewed killing was meant to show his continued dominance and to prevent the common people from thinking that Moses was the child the astrologers had foretold would end his rule.

Moses tells his people, the Children of Israel, who are frightened by Pharaoh's threat to kill their sons and spare their women, to seek help from God and to be patient. He reminds them that the earth belongs to God, who gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills among His servants, and that the final outcome belongs to the righteous. The commentators agree that the words are meant to comfort and to promise victory. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani take the final outcome to mean triumph in this world, while al-Mawardi also mentions the reward in the Hereafter, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi mention Paradise as one meaning, and al-Razi combines both. On the word 'earth', al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as Egypt, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur read it as the earth in general. The exegetes report that the people complained of the suffering they endured before and after Moses came, and that he answered that God might destroy their enemy and make them his successors, which Ibn Kathir reads as a test of their gratitude. Commentators also differ on what Pharaoh worshipped: al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas and others describe it in different ways, and some, such as Ibn Juzayy, note the reading 'his worship' instead of 'your gods'. These points remain differences of interpretation rather than settled matters.

This verse records the complaint of the Children of Israel to Moses: they say they were harmed before his coming and after it. Moses replies that their Lord may destroy their enemy and make them successors on the earth, so that He may see how they act. The commentators agree that the harm refers to what Pharaoh inflicted on them, namely the killing of the sons and the sparing of the women for servitude. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that the first harm was the slaughter of the newborn boys and the second was the renewed threat and punishment, while al-Hasan al-Basri held that both refer to one and the same harm, the poll tax. Juwaybir and al-Kalbi mention other forms of forced labour, such as work until midday then all day without food, or making bricks with straw supplied or not. Ibn 'Atiyya considers that the speech fits the known character of the Children of Israel, marked by restlessness and weak patience. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that they were not rejecting Moses' mission but pressing for the promise to be fulfilled. On the word "perhaps", al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj took it as a certainty from God, whereas Sibawayh read it as hope mixed with apprehension. Al-Tabari explains that God observes their conduct after the enemy's fall, whether they are eager or slack in obedience. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi relate that the promise was fulfilled through Pharaoh's drowning and the settling of the Israelites in his land, while others place the conquest of Egypt in the time of David and Solomon, or the conquest of Syria under Joshua.

God says that He tested the family of Pharaoh with years of drought and famine and with a loss of fruits, so that they might remember and turn back from their error to their Lord. The commentators agree that the word "years" means drought and dearth, and that hardship softens hearts and leads a person to humble supplication. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that this was a trial of hunger and scarcity, year after year, and they report from Mujahid and Qatada that the years struck the desert dwellers and their herds, while the loss of fruit affected the towns and villages; Ibn Kathir also cites Raja' ibn Haywa that a palm tree bore only a single fruit. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada, according to al-Mawardi, took the years to mean hunger, whereas al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj took them to mean drought. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi stress that the purpose was to make them realise that their disbelief was the cause, and that people in distress become more humble and tender-hearted. Al-Razi holds that these calamities were meant to bring them back, and al-Wahidi answers the objection that God only wanted them to remember rather than to persist in unbelief. Ibn 'Ashur reads "perhaps" as expressing hope in its ordinary sense, while noting that God knew they would not remember but wished to remove their excuse. The passage continues with their reaction: in good times they said "this is ours by right", and in bad times they blamed Moses and his people. God replies that their fate is with Him, that is, by His decree, though most of them do not know it.

The verse describes the people of Pharaoh: when prosperity and plenty come to them, they claim it as their due and do not see it as a blessing that calls for gratitude; when misfortune strikes, they blame Moses and those with him. Commentators explain that the original sense of tatayyur is the observation of birds in pre-Islamic Arab omen-taking, later extended to any belief in ill omen. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid understand the good as health and ease and the evil as drought and affliction, while al-Hasan takes the evil to mean fear. On the phrase 'their omen is with God', Ibn 'Abbas and, through him, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as saying that misfortunes come from God's decree, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean that their own deeds, recorded with God, are the cause of what befalls them. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud affirm that all good and evil come from God, while most people attribute events to visible causes. All agree that most of them do not know that what afflicts them comes from God. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur note the Prophet's prohibition of tiyara, and Ibn 'Ashur observes that the definite article on the good and the indefinite on the evil reflect their frequency and rarity. Variant readings such as al-Hasan's tayruhum and Talha's tatayyaru are also mentioned.

The verse reports that Pharaoh's people told Moses that whatever sign he brought to bewitch them, they would not believe him. Commentators agree that this stubbornness came after they had been struck by drought and loss of crops without turning back, and that mahma means roughly whatever thing. They called what Moses brought a sign only in mockery, since they regarded it as magic. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari then describe the plagues that followed: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood. On the flood, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it as heavy rain or water, others as death or plague, and Abu Ubayda as a torrent. On the lice, Ibn Abbas takes it as the weevil of grain, Mujahid and Qatada as young locusts, Ibn Zayd as fleas, and Abu Ubayda as a large kind of tick. Most scholars take the blood to be the Nile or drinking water turned to blood, while Zayd ibn Aslam takes it to be nosebleeds. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi add that the plagues came one after another with intervals, a week of affliction followed by a month of respite, so that the proof would be established against them. The scholars agree that they grew arrogant and were a criminal people.

This verse tells of the people of Pharaoh who, after defying Moses and swearing they would not believe whatever sign he brought, were struck by a series of afflictions: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and blood. These signs are called clear and distinct, yet instead of leading them to faith they only increased their arrogance, for they were a people of criminals. The commentators agree that these plagues did not come together but one after another, with an interval between each during which the people were tested. The length of that interval varies between them: some say a week, others a month. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also report that Moses remained among them for years after the defeat of the magicians, with reports ranging from twenty to forty years. The children of Israel were spared.

The meaning of the word tufan is debated. Ibn Abbas, in one report, together with Qatada and al-Dahhak, takes it as a violent rain that floods the fields; Mujahid and Ata take it as death or plague. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith from Aisha that defines it as death but judges it rare; al-Tabari considers all these readings possible without choosing one. On the lice, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid speak of young locusts without wings, others of grain weevils, fleas, bedbugs or ticks, and Abu Ubayda of a kind of tick. For the blood, most exegetes, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, hold that the water turned into blood, while Zayd ibn Aslam sees it as a nosebleed.

Al-Razi notes that the Egyptians mistook these wonders for magic, unable to distinguish a miracle from sorcery.

When the scourge, the « rijz », fell upon Pharaoh's people, they came to Moses and asked him to call upon his Lord by the covenant He had made with him, promising to believe and to release the Children of Israel if the plague were lifted. The commentators agree that « rijz » means a punishment, but differ on which one is meant. Al-Tabari links it to the plagues already listed (the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood), while noting that it could also be a plague, and he holds that no authentic report settles the matter. Al-Razi likewise prefers the plagues already mentioned, since the definite article points back to them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, followed by Ibn al-Jawzi, identifies it as a pestilence that killed seventy thousand Copts in a single day.

Opinions also vary on the phrase « by what He has covenanted with you ». Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan take it to mean the prophethood Moses held, or the answered prayer Moses had been taught to make, or else as an oath by God's covenant. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list several readings. Ibn 'Ashur observes that these polytheists saw the God of Moses as a god particular to his people, which explains the wording of their request and their promise to believe in Moses himself.

Most commentators agree on the core point: the people of Pharaoh made promises under distress and broke them once the punishment was lifted, which the following verse makes explicit.

This verse describes Pharaoh's people: when the plagues struck them, they asked Moses to pray to his Lord to lift them, promising to believe and to release the Children of Israel. Once God removed the punishment for a set term, they broke their word at once and persisted in disbelief. The commentators broadly agree on this basic meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy list the plagues (flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood) and read 'rijz' as punishment, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies it as a plague that killed seventy thousand Copts in one day. Al-Razi holds that it refers to the five plagues already mentioned, since the definite reference points back to them. On the meaning of 'ajal' the views differ: Ibn Abbas and others take it as the moment of drowning, al-Hasan as death, Ibn Atiyya as each person's own appointed end, and al-Mawardi and others as the period set for their faith. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan debate the grammar, most treating the clause introduced by 'idha' as the answer to 'lamma', meaning that they broke their promise immediately. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di stress the repeated pattern in which Pharaoh asked for relief and then reneged. Ibn Ashur adds that their request did not stem from true faith in God, since they still held polytheistic views. All agree on the outcome: they were drowned in the sea because they had denied God's signs and turned away from them.

The commentators explain that God took vengeance on Pharaoh and his people after they broke their pledges once the punishment had been lifted, drowning them in the sea (al-yamm). For some, this is the sea whose bottom cannot be reached; for others, it is its deep current and the bulk of its water. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the cause of their drowning was their denial of God's signs and their heedlessness toward them.

They differ on what the pronoun in "heedless of them" refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it to refer to the vengeance, meaning they had not been mindful of the punishment before it struck. Al-Zajjaj, Abu Hayyan, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur instead take it to refer to the signs, meaning they did not reflect on them or take warning from them. Al-Razi explains that heedlessness here means turning away from the signs and paying them no regard, while al-Alusi notes that one who denies a thing cannot truly be unaware of it, so the word is used figuratively for a lack of concern.

Regarding the broken pledge, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi understand the "rijz" as the punishment mentioned earlier, such as the flood and the locusts; al-Baghawi reports from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it was the plague. Ibn 'Atiyya considers it more sound that the term refers to the previously mentioned punishments. The "appointed term" is read by some as the moment of their drowning, and by others as the time set for each of them.

The verse closes the story of Pharaoh and his people. As al-Jaza'iri and Ibn 'Ashur point out, it carries a warning to those who persisted in denial.

This verse says that God gave the people who had been oppressed, the children of Israel whom Pharaoh and his people enslaved and whose sons they slew, the eastern and western reaches of the blessed land. Most commentators understand this as Syria, as al-Hasan and Qatada state explicitly, while az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also include Egypt. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baghawi explain that its blessing lay in water, trees, fruit and plenty. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir take the fulfilled word of God to be the promise of victory and settlement mentioned in Surah al-Qasas. Nearly all link its fulfilment to the Israelites' patience, and az-Zamakhshari draws the lesson that whoever meets trial with patience is granted relief by God. The destruction of what Pharaoh and his people built is read by the commentators as total ruin. The meaning of ya'rishun is debated: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as building, al-Hasan as vines and trellises, and Ibn 'Ashur as raised structures. Al-Tabari finds the reading with kasra more familiar and al-Yazidi calls it more eloquent, while Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read with damma.

This passage recounts how God brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and as they passed a people devoted to their idols, they asked Moses to make for them a god like theirs. Moses replied that they were an ignorant people. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i, agree that this answer was a stern rebuke, expressing Moses' astonishment at such a request after the great signs they had just witnessed. Al-Sam'ani and Ibn Kathir note that the request did not reflect doubt about God's oneness but ignorance of His greatness. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain that the desired 'god' was an image to be venerated in order to draw closer to God. Opinions differ on the identity of the idolaters: Qatada said they were from the tribe of Lakhm, others said Canaanites or Amalekites, and Ibn Jurayj said their idols were statues of cows, which he linked to the origin of the calf. In the next verse Moses says these people are doomed and that their deeds are vain. Al-Kalbi and al-Wahidi take 'mutabbar' to mean destruction and ruin, while al-Zamakhshari understands it as being shattered. Several commentators, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Alusi, cite the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi at Hunayn, when some companions asked for a lote tree on which to hang their weapons, and the Prophet ﷺ saw in this a path toward idolatry. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan hold that only some of the people said this, since the seventy chosen men were present. Ibn 'Ashur sees the request as evidence that enslavement had caused the Children of Israel to lose the monotheism of their forefathers.

This passage reports that after the Children of Israel crossed the sea and passed a people devoted to their idols, Moses told them that those who cling to these idols are doomed in what they do, and that their deeds are vain and will vanish, bringing them no benefit when God's command comes upon them. Most commentators understand the word mutabbar as ruin, destruction or loss. Al-Kalbi renders it as void, Abu al-Yasa' as misguided, and Ibn 'Abbas as loss. Al-Zajjaj notes that the root means breaking, as a broken vessel is mutabbar, while al-Dahhak says it is a Nabataean word. As for vain (batil), all agree it means something that has perished and has no worth. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress that worshipping idols is futile even when its followers intend to draw closer to God. Al-Razi explains that devotion to other than God turns the heart away from remembering Him, which defeats the very purpose of worship. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur point out that the request stemmed from ignorance and that the address is to the Children of Israel, who had just witnessed great signs. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi about Dhat Anwat, where the Prophet said that this is like the request of the Children of Israel. The verse is therefore read as a warning against imitating peoples in idolatry and against glorifying falsehood.

This verse records Moses' reply to his people when they asked him to make for them a god like the gods of those people: should he seek for them a deity other than God, who has favoured them above the peoples of their time with blessings and signs? The commentators generally read the question as a rebuke and a denunciation, meaning that worship belongs only to God, the Giver of these favours. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "the worlds" means the people of their own age, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that this is the most likely sense because the community of Muhammad is superior to them. Al-Alusi limits the preference to the signes God gave them rather than to an absolute superiority. The grammarians differ on the grammar of "ghayr" and "ilahan": Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan offer different analyses, and Abu Hayyan rejects the idea of an implied verb. Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani cite the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi about Dhat Anwat, in which the Prophet compares his companions' request with that of the Children of Israel. Most commentators, such as al-Baghawi, hold that the people's request came from ignorance of God rather than doubt about His oneness. Almost all read "mutabbar" as a reference to the ruin of what they worship, which is vain and brings no benefit.

The verse reminds the Children of Israel of God's favour in rescuing them from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted terrible torment on them, slaying their sons and sparing their women. The commentators agree that the verse is part of Moses' reminder to his people, although al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also mention the view that it addresses the Jews of the Prophet's time, reminding them of what their forebears endured. The closing phrase, 'and in that there is a great trial from your Lord', is read in two main ways. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as a test or a favour, while al-Mawardi reports three views: that Pharaoh's deeds were a great affliction, as al-Kalbi said; that it was a test, as al-Akhfash said; and that the deliverance itself was a great blessing, as Ibn Qutayba said. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi allow both readings, with the reference being either the rescue or the torment, and the word bala meaning either a favour or a trial. Ibn Atiyya considers the first interpretation, that the reference is to the torment, to be the more apparent. On recitation, Ibn Amir reads anjaka, Nafi' reads yaqtulun with a lighter form, and most read it with emphasis. The commentators on the whole focus on the lesson of gratitude rather than on legal rulings.

The commentators explain that God appointed thirty nights for Moses to meet Him on the mountain, then added ten more, so the appointed time was completed at forty nights. Most, including Mujahid, Ibn Abbas, Masruq and Ibn Jurayj, identify the thirty nights with the month of Dhu al-Qa'da and the ten with the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. Others, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Mawardi, hold that the forty nights were a single term that was later extended. They differ on the reason for the extension. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi report that Moses fasted for thirty days, then used a siwak, which altered the scent of his breath, so God ordered ten more days. Al-Mawardi sees it as a punishment or trial for his people, and Ibn Atiyya as a way of informing them of his absence. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Jurayj, relates that Moses appointed his brother Harun as his deputy, charging him to reform the people and not to follow the path of the corrupters. Most understand reform as preventing the worship of the calf or treating the people gently. Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari note that Harun was a prophet and that the charge was a reminder and emphasis. Several, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy, report that Moses asked to see God; God replied, 'You will not see Me,' then manifested Himself to the mountain, which crumbled, and Moses fell unconscious. They agree that the refusal concerns sight in this world, while the Sunni tradition, as Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi note, affirms vision in the hereafter.

The commentators explain that Moses, having come to the appointed time and been addressed by his Lord, asked to see Him. God told him that he would not see Him in this life, but that he should look at the mountain: if it remained in place when God manifested Himself to it, he would see Him. When God manifested Himself to the mountain, it was crushed to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. Upon recovering, he glorified his Lord, repented of his request, and declared himself the first to believe that God cannot be seen in this world. The scholars agree that vision is impossible in this life, since human beings lack the capacity for it, and that the mountain, being firmer than Moses, did not endure. They also agree that his repentance was not for a proven sin but for having asked without permission. The disagreement concerns the meaning of the passage. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, relying on Moses's request, hold that vision is rationally possible and will occur in the hereafter, as the Ash'arites and Sunnis maintain. Al-Zamakhshari, speaking for the Mu'tazilites, considers it impossible: he argues that Moses only wished to rebuke his people, and that the word 'lan' in 'lan tarani' denotes a perpetual negation. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi reject this reading, while al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi take 'lan' to refer only to the present life. On the readings 'dakkan' and 'dakka'', grammarians debate the sense of the word, and on 'sa'iqan' opinions split between fainting and death, fainting being preferred because the text says Moses 'recovered'.

In this verse God addresses Moses, telling him that He has chosen him above the people of his time through his mission and through speaking to him directly, and He orders him to take what he has been given firmly and to be among the grateful. The commentators agree that istifa means preference and distinction, and that 'the people' means his contemporaries, since other messengers shared his mission before and after him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the plain meaning is to accept the law, act upon it and give thanks for the mission and the speech received, while al-Zamakhshari holds that Aaron was not granted direct speech and was only his deputy and helper. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi clarify that this distinction does not exclude others from being addressed, since some reports mention Adam and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ during the Night Journey, but the combination of mission and direct speech is the basis of the preference. Al-Sam'ani, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan read the verse as a consolation to Moses after he was refused the vision of God, and Ibn Kathir connects it to the tablets given afterwards as compensation. The commentators draw no specific legal ruling here, treating the command to take firmly and to give thanks as general duties of the religion.

The commentators explain that God wrote for Moses on the tablets, that is the Torah, everything the Children of Israel needed for their religion: admonitions that restrain from sin and a detailed account of the lawful and unlawful, of commands and prohibitions. He then tells Moses to take them with firmness and to order his people to follow what is best in them, and warns that He will show the defiant the fate of the wicked. Scholars differ on the meaning of 'firmness': Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir understand it as striving and earnestness, al-Rabi' ibn Anas as obedience, Ibn Jubayr as gratitude, and 'Ali ibn 'Isa as steadfastness of resolve. As for 'what is best in them', al-Tabari takes it to mean acting on what is commanded rather than avoiding what is forbidden, while Qutrub reads it as 'their goodness, since all of it is good'. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy distinguish obligations, recommended acts and permissible acts, and give as examples pardon and patience preferred to retaliation and vindication. On 'the abode of the defiant', Mujahid and al-Hasan say Hell, Qatada the tyrannical places of Syria, 'Atiyya al-'Awfi and Ibn Jubayr the land of Pharaoh in Egypt, and al-Kalbi the ruins of 'Ad and Thamud along the road. Al-Tabari holds that the verse is a warning to whoever neglects God's command. The reading 'I will make you inherit' is noted by several authors. The commentators do not settle the material or number of the tablets, said to be of chrysolite, emerald or wood, seven, ten or two.

In this verse God declares that He will turn away from His signs those who act arrogantly on earth without right, preventing them from grasping the proofs and taking lessons from them. The commentators differ on what the signs and the turning away mean. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and Qatada understand it as preventing them from understanding the Quran or reflecting on it. Ibn Jurayj takes the signs to be the creation of the heavens and the earth, so that they do not reflect on them or learn from them. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the wording covers both meanings, since it concerns hindering their observation and reasoning. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi define arrogance as refusing faith or despising people, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see the turning away as a sealing of hearts imposed as punishment for pride. Al-Kalbi and 'Ata' al-'Awfi limit the verse to the nine signs given to Moses among the people of Egypt, whereas most scholars read it generally. The verse continues: if they see every sign they do not believe in it, if they see the path of right guidance they do not take it, and if they see the path of error they adopt it, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them. The readings differ between al-Rushd and al-Rashad. Abu 'Amr distinguishes the first as soundness in affairs and the second as rectitude in religion, while al-Kisa'i holds they are two forms with one meaning. All agree that the heedlessness meant is deliberate turning away, not mere forgetfulness. The verse ends by stating that those who denied the signs and the meeting of the Hereafter have their deeds annulled, and are repaid only for what they did.

This verse states that those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the hereafter will have their deeds made void, and that they will be repaid only for what they did. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and most commentators understand the verb habitat (made void) to mean that their deeds are nullified and will not benefit them in the hereafter, so that their recompense matches their misdeeds. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that this voiding can be judged by their own beliefs, since they regarded their deeds as sound while they were corrupt from the start. The verse follows the verses about those who are arrogant on earth and whom God turns away from His signs. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain this turning away as being prevented from understanding the Quran or reflecting on creation, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the statement is general and not limited to the people of Egypt. Al-Razi draws from the verse that retribution concerns actions, and he records the debate between the Ash'aris and Abu Hashim over the abandonment of a duty, with the Ash'aris replying that the punishment for it is itself a form of recompense. Commentators also discuss a reading question: rushd may be read with one or two vowels, and Abu 'Amr distinguished between rectitude in affairs and rectitude in religion, which grammarians treat as two forms of one root. As for the phrase meeting the hereafter, it may mean meeting the last abode or meeting what God promised there, as Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud explain.

This verse describes how the people of Moses, after he went up to meet his Lord, made a calf from their ornaments, a body that gave out a lowing sound, and worshipped it. God rebukes them: it neither speaks to them nor guides them to any path, and by taking it as a god they wronged themselves by placing worship where it does not belong. The commentators agree that the craftsman was al-Samiri, while the act is attributed to the whole people because they approved of it, as when one says that a tribe did something that only one of its members did. They also note that the ornaments were originally borrowed from the Copts. The nature of the calf is disputed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi transmit, through Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada, that it became flesh and blood after a handful of dust from the hoofprint of Gabriel's horse was cast into it, whereas others hold that it had no life and that its sound came from air passing through a hollow body, a view Al-Razi presents among the Mu'tazilites. Ibn Atiyya judges the first view weak. Al-Hasan holds that all of them worshipped the calf except Aaron, while others limit the idolatry to some of them. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy draw from the verse the principle that a god must be able to speak and to guide. The verse closes with the people's remorse and their plea for mercy.

This verse describes the remorse of the Israelites who had worshipped the calf, after Moses returned to them. Their regret was so intense and their helplessness so complete that, seeing that they had strayed, they cried out in supplication: if our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we shall surely be among the losers. The commentators agree that this remorse came after Moses returned. The phrase 'suqita fi aydihim' is generally read as an idiom for deep regret and helplessness, the image being of a remorseful person biting his hand in grief. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi keep this image, while al-Zajjaj understands it as regret falling into their hearts and souls; Ibn 'Atiyya notes that loss and failure may also be meant, and he considers the phrase obscure. Al-Tabari explains that they realised they had left the straight path and the religion of God. On the reading, most readers say 'yarhamna rabbuna' with a yā' and a raf' on 'rabbuna', whereas Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'tarhamna rabbana' in the second person. Al-Tabari prefers the first, while Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Abu al-Su'ud find the second more expressive of humility and pleading. Overall the commentators see here an acknowledgment of sin and an appeal to God for mercy.

When Moses returned to his people angry and grieved, he said: Evil is what you did as my successors after me! Did you hasten ahead of your Lord's command? He threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward him. Harun pleaded that the people had oppressed him and nearly killed him, and asked that his enemies not be given cause to gloat and that he not be counted among the wrongdoers. The commentators explain 'asaf' either as intense anger, as Abu al-Darda and Ibn Atiyya did, or as grief, as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi did; al-Wahidi noted the two meanings are close. As to why Moses threw the tablets, Ibn Abbas and most commentators say it was anger at the calf-worship, while Qatada's report that it was because of the virtues of Muhammad's community is judged weak by Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya. Many hold that the tablets broke and parts of them were lifted, though some say the verse does not state this. Regarding the seizing of the brother's head, most say Moses suspected Harun had failed to restrain them, while others saw it as a sign of affection. The address 'son of my mother' is taken by al-Hasan and others as an appeal to tenderness through the mother's bond, since the two shared a mother. Several also note the verse shows that a person who fears death for himself may stay silent when forbidding wrong, and that anger does not change Moses' legal actions.

This verse records Moses' prayer after he had recognised that his brother Aaron was not at fault. He asks God to forgive him for what he did to his brother in his anger, and to forgive Aaron for any shortcoming in opposing those who worshipped the calf or in governing the people in his absence. He then asks to be admitted into God's mercy and ends by calling God the most merciful of those who show mercy. The commentators agree that Moses included his brother in the prayer to appease him and to deny the enemies any cause to gloat. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others explain the word asif either as intense anger, following Abu al-Darda', 'Ata' and al-Zajjaj, or as grief, following Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi; al-Razi holds that the two meanings are close. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that Moses sought forgiveness for his own haste in throwing the tablets and for his treatment of his brother. Al-Tabari reports Ibn Jurayj's view that the following verse's threat applies only to those who died among the calf-worshippers, but al-Tabari himself takes it as general. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Atiyya al-Awfi understand the humiliation as the jizya, or the punishment of the Jewish tribes; Abu Qilaba and Ibn 'Uyayna extend it to every innovator and liar until the Day of Resurrection. Several commentators also report that the tablets broke and part of their content was lifted, though Ibn Kathir considers the report from Qatada unreliable.

This verse describes the fate of those who took the calf as a god among the Israelites: wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the present life will reach them, and this is how God requites those who fabricate lies against Him. The commentators agree that the verse first addresses the calf-worshippers of Moses' time, and that the wrath and humiliation refer to the command that they kill one another, as Abu al-Aliya said, a view followed by al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi. Ibn Jurayj held that it concerned those who died before Moses returned or who fled from the killing, but al-Tabari rejected this, arguing that the apparent meaning of the text and the majority of interpreters go against it, since God later accepted their repentance. Ibn Abbas, Ata and Ibn Kathir understand the humiliation as the poll tax (jizya), while Atiyya al-Awfi applies it to their descendants, namely the tribes of Qurayza and al-Nadir who were expelled or killed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the humiliation to be the abasement of exile, the state of the stranger. Many draw a general lesson: Malik ibn Anas, Abu Qilaba and Sufyan ibn Uyayna state that every innovator or fabricator of falsehood suffers humiliation. The following verse opens the door of repentance to those who commit evil deeds, then repent and believe, and the commentators debate how faith is added to repentance in that verse.

This verse states that those who committed evil deeds, whether disbelief or other sins, and then repented, returned to God and believed, will be forgiven and shown mercy by their Lord, however great or numerous their sins. Most commentators read it as a general rule that covers the worshippers of the calf as well as everyone else. It follows the mention of the anger and humiliation that struck those worshippers in this life. Most agree that repentance is an indispensable condition and that God's forgiveness is greater than any sin. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud stress this. On the meaning of 'and believed' after repentance, al-Mawardi gives three explanations: persevering in faith after repentance, believing that God accepts repentance, or repenting out of faith. Ibn 'Atiyya suggests the mention of faith may emphasise that it is necessary after repentance, or may simply reinforce the point. Ibn 'Ashur explains that faith is singled out because it is the basis of good deeds, and so that no one thinks shirk cannot be forgiven. Ibn Kathir also reports a narration from Ibn Mas'ud about a man who committed adultery and then married the woman; Ibn Mas'ud recited the verse without ordering or forbidding anything. Al-Zamakhshari notes a dispute: the Mu'tazilites hold that a grave sin is forgiven only through repentance, while the People of the Sunna hold it may be forgiven by sheer grace. Al-Razi observes that the verse covers all evil deeds, which is a source of hope for sinners.

The commentators explain that when Moses' anger subsided, he took up the Tablets he had thrown down in rage at his people for worshipping the calf. In what was copied or written in them there is guidance from error and mercy from punishment, for those who fear their Lord and dread His punishment. They differ on the meaning of the word «silence». Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi read it as a metaphor: the anger that had driven Moses to act ceased, as though it had fallen silent. Some, such as 'Ikrima, cited by al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, take it as a reversal of the phrasing, meaning that Moses silenced his anger. Mu'awiya ibn Qurra's reading «sakana» conveys the same sense. On the Tablets, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' say that the «copy» refers to what remained of them after they broke, while others report that Moses fasted forty days and was given them back in two tablets. Ibn Kathir notes that many commentators say the shattered pieces were reassembled. On the particle «li» before «their Lord», the grammarians disagree: al-Kisa'i and the Kufans consider it superfluous, al-Akhfash takes it as expressing purpose, and al-Mubarrad links it to an implied verbal noun. Ibn 'Abbas holds that those who fear are all who fear God in general, while Qatada understands them specifically as the community of Muhammad.

The commentators explain that Moses chose seventy men from his people to attend the appointed meeting with God, in order to apologise to Him for the worship of the calf and to seek repentance for those left behind. When the tremor, described either as an earthquake or a thunderbolt, struck them and they died or fainted, Moses turned to his Lord, astonished at the death of the best of his people. He said that God could have destroyed them before, and himself too, and then asked not to be punished for the deeds of the foolish among them, affirming that this was a trial from God by which He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi agree that these words were a humble plea rather than an accusation against God. On the cause of the tremor, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Juraij attribute it to the seventy's failure to separate from or forbid the worship of the calf, while al-Sudi and Ibn Ishaq link it to their request to see God. A report from Ali about a charge against Aaron is judged weak by Ibn Kathir. Scholars also differ on who the "foolish" are: the calf-worshippers, or those who asked to see God. Most read "fitna" as a test, whereas al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as punishment. Finally, the plea for forgiveness and mercy is taken as a request that God cover the sin, lift the punishment and show mercy, for He is the best of forgivers.

The commentators explain that after the trembling struck the people, Moses prayed to his Lord, asking good for himself and his people in this world and the next, and saying they had turned back in repentance. God answers that His punishment reaches whom He wills, that His mercy encompasses all things, and that He will write this particular mercy for those who are mindful of Him, pay zakat and believe in His signs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi agree that the word hudna means that they repented and turned back, and that the good of this world includes health and help in obedience, while the good of the Hereafter is Paradise and forgiveness. The divine will in punishment is taken by some to apply to those who deserve it, while al-Zamakhshari, in the Mu'tazili manner, ties it to those whose punishment wisdom requires. On the scope of the mercy, Ibn 'Abbas and others read it as general in wording but specific in meaning, meaning the community of Muhammad; al-Hasan and Qatada take it as general in this world, for the righteous and the wicked alike, and reserved for the God-fearing in the Hereafter; Ibn Zayd identifies it with repentance. On the meaning of piety, Ibn 'Abbas says it is avoiding association with God, while Qatada includes all disobedience, and Ibn 'Atiyya holds the term to be general. Many report that this mercy passed to the community of Muhammad after Iblis and the Jews and Christians had coveted it, and that the description of the unlettered prophet appears in the Torah and the Gospel. The commentators conclude that these are the successful.

This verse states that the special mercy Moses asked for his people will be written for those who follow the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. Most commentators, beginning with al-Tabari, identify this community as the followers of Muhammad, peace be upon him: Moses had asked that mercy be written for his people, and the answer reserves it for those who fear God, pay zakat and believe in His signs. They agree that the unlettered Prophet is Muhammad, who could neither read nor write; some say the title refers to his people or to Mecca, Umm al-Qura. The commentators list what the earlier scriptures say of him: he enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, makes lawful the good things and forbids the foul. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the burden (isr) means the heavy covenant or the harsh rules of the earlier law, and the shackles are the restrictions of that law. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy see in this the mark of the ease of the new law. Malik takes the good things to be what is permitted and the foul things what is forbidden, while al-Shafi'i takes them to mean what taste finds pleasant or repugnant; Ibn Kathir reports both readings without choosing. The commentators finally agree that those who believe in him, honour him, support him and follow the light sent down with him, which is the Quran, are the successful. Al-Baydawi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the Quran is called a light because it illuminates hearts.

God commands His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to declare to all people that he is the messenger of God sent to them all, not to one particular nation as the prophets before him were. The commentators describe God as possessing absolute sovereignty over the heavens and the earth, the only one worthy of worship, who gives life and causes death; therefore one must believe in Him, in His messenger the unlettered Prophet, who believes in God and His words, and follow him in the hope of being guided. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Baydawi agree that Muhammad's mission extends to humankind and the jinn, citing the well-known hadith that he was sent to all people. The meaning of 'His words' divides them: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the revealed books or verses, Mujahid and al-Suddi take it to mean Jesus son of Mary, al-Zamakhshari reads it as the word 'Be' by which Jesus was created, and al-Razi includes the miracles. Most note that the shift from the first person to the third in 'believe in God and His messenger' emphasises fairness and the greatness of the mission. In the next verse the commentators report that among the people of Moses there is a community that guides by the truth and judges justly; they differ on who they are: al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak place them beyond China, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir understand them as believers among the Children of Israel, and Ibn Kathir warns about the weak reliability of the Israelite narratives on this point. Overall, the exegetes agree that following the Prophet is the condition for true guidance, and that faith in God alone is its foundation.

This verse says that among the people of Moses there is a community that follows the truth, guides others by it and judges with justice according to it. The commentators agree that it refers to a faithful part of the People of the Book, mentioned right after the description of the deviation of many of them, so that the blame is not extended to the whole people. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take them to be repentant believers who teach and judge fairly, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider either believers at the time of Moses or those who embraced Islam in the Prophet's time. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi mainly point to converts such as Abdullah ibn Salam, and Ibn Kathir links the verse to other passages praising a portion of the People of the Book. Al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi also suggest those who held to the truth during a period of error, or a distant people beyond China. The latter account, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj and cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, is judged unsupported by Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Alusi and Abu Hayyan, who find no reliable chain for it. Ibn 'Ashur notes that guiding and judging justly require knowledge and insight, not mere chance agreement with the truth.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls God's favours to the Children of Israel during their wandering in the wilderness. He divided them into twelve tribes, called asbat, each with its own spring when, thirsty, they asked Moses for water; God told him to strike the rock with his staff, and twelve springs gushed forth. He shaded them with clouds, sent down manna and quails, and told them to eat of the good things He had provided. The verse adds that they did not wrong God but wronged themselves. The commentators agree that the asbat were the descendants of Jacob and that the division was meant to prevent disputes over water. They differ, however, on the grammar of the feminine 'twelve' with a masculine noun: al-Farra' links it to the feminine 'umam', al-Zajjaj supplies the word 'firqa', and al-Zamakhshari says that asbat stands for tribes, as in the phrase 'twelve tribes'. They also differ on the meaning of 'anbajasa' and 'infajara': Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' holds that the first is a slow seeping and the second a full gushing, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and most others treat them as synonyms. Ibn Kathir notes that the story was explained in the chapter of al-Baqara and that this passage belongs to the Meccan period. As for the manna and quails, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di describe the manna as a honey-like or gum-like substance and the quails as a bird resembling the common quail, while others simply refer back to earlier explanations.

God reminds the Children of Israel that He commanded them to dwell in the town, which most commentators identify as Jerusalem, to eat from its produce wherever they wished, to say "hittah", meaning "remove our sins from us", and to enter the gate bowing or in humility. In return He promises to forgive their sins and to increase the reward of the good-doers. The commentators agree on the central sense: they are to seek forgiveness, humble themselves before God and give thanks after being delivered from the wandering in the desert. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take the town to be Bayt al-Maqdis, while Qatada and al-Hasan point to the Levant or Jericho, a view also reported by al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur. On the word "hittah", al-Tabari explains it as a prayer asking that sins be removed, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it as a statement of faith and gratitude. The recitations differ between "naghfir" and "tughfar" and between "khatiyat" and "khataya", and Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan regard these variants as mutually compatible. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur compare the passage with its counterpart in Surat al-Baqara and conclude that the differences in wording are stylistic variation, not contradiction. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the context is Meccan. As for the disobedience, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that they changed the word to "a grain in a barley-corn" and entered crawling on their backsides, and Ibn Ashur holds that only some of them did so.

This verse tells that some of the wrongdoers among the Children of Israel changed the word they had been commanded to say. Instead of saying "hitta" (remove our sins), they said "a grain of wheat in barley" or "a grain in a hair", and instead of entering the gate prostrating, they entered crawling on their buttocks. God then sent upon them a punishment from heaven because of their wrongdoing. Some report that this punishment was a plague plague. The word "among them" indicates that not all of them committed this change. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the change concerned the words, while al-Shawkani and al-Alusi also include the act of entering improperly. Al-Sha'rawi holds that the distortion was in speech and that some also changed their conduct, a point others do not affirm. On the choice of words, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur explain that "sending" (arsalna) implies continuity and repetition, unlike "sending down" (anzalna) used in al-Baqara, and they do not see any contradiction, only variety of style. Ibn Ashur and al-Razi also note that the verse's wording differs from al-Baqara according to the purpose of each passage. In the matter of the city, Ibn Kathir and others mention Ayla, Madyan, and Jericho, with the commentators relying on transmitted reports. The commentators agree that the verse warns against altering God's command and mocking it, and that the punishment follows from wrongdoing.

This verse tells the Prophet Muhammad to ask the Jews of his time about the town by the sea whose people broke the Sabbath by fishing. The fish came to them in great numbers on the surface of the water on Saturdays and did not appear on other days. The commentators explain that this was a trial from God because of their wickedness. The question is meant to rebuke the Jews and to show that such knowledge could only come by revelation, which confirms the Prophet's truthfulness.

Most exegetes identify the town as Ayla, a coastal place between Madyan and Mount Sinai, as reported by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and others. Other views name Madyan, Tiberias, or Maqna between Madyan and 'Aynuna. Al-Tabari says no authentic report settles the matter, so any of these places could be meant, and he does not choose among them.

The commentators also differ on the word shurra'an, meaning visible and rising on the water, according to Ibn 'Abbas; coming in succession, according to al-Dahhak; or lifting their heads at the doors like white rams, according to al-Hasan. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report the trick of digging pools to trap the fish on the Sabbath and taking them on Sunday.

Regarding the group that asked the preachers why they warned a people God would destroy, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan hold that this group was saved, while al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi consider it more apparent that only those who forbade the evil were saved and that the punishment fell on the transgressors alone.

This verse recounts a moment from the story of a coastal town whose people broke the prohibition of fishing on the Sabbath. A group of the righteous asked those who were admonishing the transgressors why they warned a people whom God would destroy or punish severely. The admonishers replied that their advice was a plea of excuse to their Lord, and that they hoped the people would become mindful of God. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, take these words to come from a third group who neither transgressed nor admonished, and they hold that the admonishing group was saved while the transgressors were punished and turned into apes. Opinions differ on the fate of that silent group. Ibn Abbas is reported to have said he did not know what became of them, while Ikrima reported that they were saved; al-Hasan held that they were saved along with the admonishers, and Ibn Zayd that only the admonishers were saved. Ibn Kathir considered Ikrima's account the more sound. Al-Tabari also cites those who held that the speakers themselves belonged to the saved group, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya read the question as a separate voice. On the linguistic side, Hafs's reading of ma'dhira in the accusative is explained in two ways by the grammarians, while the majority reading in the nominative is preferred by Sibawayh. The word bi'is has several recitations, and commentators generally understand it to mean severe or painful.

This passage of Surat al-A'raf tells of the people of the town by the sea who transgressed the sabbath. The verse states that when they neglected what they had been reminded of and did not turn back from their disobedience, God saved those who forbade evil and seized the wrongdoers with a severe punishment for their defiance of God's command. The commentators agree that the word "evil" (al-su') covers sins in general, and that the wrongdoers were those who broke the sabbath by fishing. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain "ba'is" as harsh or painful, and al-Tabari favours the reading "ba'is" with a long vowel, because the exegetes agree on its meaning. As for the third group, those who asked "why do you admonish a people whom God will destroy?", the scholars disagree. Ibn 'Abbas in one report, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan and others hold that they were saved, while Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Kalbi hold that they perished; Ibn 'Abbas himself at one point withheld judgment. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud consider salvation the more apparent view, since punishment was reserved for the wrongdoers and forbidding wrong is a collective duty. Al-Zamakhshari also counts the speakers among the saved. The commentators further report that those who persisted in rebellion were turned into apes, and they differ on the details of that transformation.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of some of the Children of Israel, the people of a town on the sea shore, who broke the prohibition on fishing on the Sabbath. When they arrogantly refused to give up what had been forbidden to them, God said: "Be apes, despised and cast out." Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi largely agree that this punishment fell on the transgressors, and that the divine command is one of creation rather than of obligation, as al-Zajjaj explains. According to Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others, the young were turned into apes and the elders into swine; Mujahid holds that it was their hearts that were transformed rather than their bodies. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and others report that they lived three days, or seven according to Muqatil, before dying, although some hold that their offspring survived.

As for the group that admonished the transgressors, asking "why do you admonish a people whom God is about to destroy?", the scholars differ on its fate. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Hasan report that it was saved, while Ibn al-Kalbi and others hold that it perished with the wrongdoers. Ibn Kathir and most exegetes consider the first view more likely, since destruction is attributed only to the wrongdoers. Ibn Ashur notes that admonition is a collective duty, and that the verse affirms the rescue of those who forbade evil. Some commentators draw from the story a prohibition on legal stratagems designed to get around divine prohibitions, as al-Shawkani reports, citing Ibn al-Qayyim.

This verse states that God made known that He would send against the Children of Israel, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict a grievous torment on them, and that your Lord is swift in punishment yet forgiving and merciful. Most commentators take the verb taʾadhdhana to mean he informed or proclaimed. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi add that it carries the force of a solemn decree, like an oath, which is why it is followed by the emphatic lam. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also report Mujahid's explanation that it means he commanded.

They differ on who carries out the punishment. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr identify the Arabs, and in another report Ibn Abbas identifies Muhammad and his community. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi prefer Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his successors, while Mujahid speaks of Jews and Christians. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the torment is the jizya, the poll tax, together with humiliation and subjugation. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi add fighting until people accept Islam or pay the tax, and Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi stress lasting humiliation and exile. Al-Mawardi reports Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab's view that the Nabateans should be the ones who collect the tax.

Al-Razi holds that the verse addresses the Jews of the Prophet's time, while al-Qurtubi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Ashur explain that the decree stands as long as they persist in disbelief, with the tax continuing after the Prophet. Ibn al-Qayyim links such afflictions to sins, and al-Biqa'i explains that forgiveness is for those who repent and believe.

This verse says that God scattered the Children of Israel across the earth in separate communities, so that they never again united under one word or one state.
