The commentators explain that among them were righteous people, those who believed and remained steadfast in their faith, and others below that level, namely the disbelievers and the wrongdoers. God tested them with blessings and with hardships, hoping that they would turn back from their unbelief and repent. The exegetes agree that the dispersion covered the whole earth. They differ, however, on who the righteous were. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand them as those who believed in the Prophet ﷺ in his time, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, while al-Tabari identifies them as those who stayed firm in their religion before the coming of Jesus. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi mention the believers of Medina or those beyond China, and Ibn 'Atiyya leaves both readings open. Ibn Kathir, continuing the passage, reports that the generation that followed inherited the Book yet took bribes and hoped for forgiveness while persisting in sin; al-Zamakhshari draws a parallel with some Muslims of his own day. Al-Qurtubi notes a linguistic debate over whether khalaf signifies a good or a bad successor. Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri conclude that the threatened punishment is tied to repentance, and that the door of return stays open to those who hold fast to the Book and keep the prayer.

This verse describes a generation that came after the Children of Israel who had been given the Torah. They read it and knew its contents, yet abandoned it in practice: they grabbed whatever worldly gain came their way, such as bribes and other unlawful profits, claimed that God would forgive them, and persisted whenever similar opportunities arose. God rebukes them for the covenant of the Book, that they should say nothing about God but the truth, though they had studied what it contains. He then declares that the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God, and calls them to reason. The commentators agree that the verse censures those who prefer this world to the next and hope for forgiveness while clinging to sin. They differ on who is meant: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Jawzi identify them as Jews, Mujahid as Christians, while al-Tabari finds the context more consistent with the Jews, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports a third view that they are from the community of Muhammad. On the phrase 'the lowly goods of this life', Ibn Kathir, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid take it to mean any worldly gain, lawful or not, whereas al-Sudi and al-Baydawi understand it as bribery in judgments. Ibn al-Qayyim warns that any scholar who prefers this world may speak falsely about God. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi emphasise the call to hold fast to the Book and note variant readings, and the prayer is singled out for its special excellence.

The commentators explain that this verse praises those who hold fast to the Book, act upon it and establish the prayer, and that God does not waste the reward of the righteous. They differ over who is meant. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, followed by Ibn Kathir, identify them as believers among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, who kept the Torah without distorting or concealing it. 'Ata' holds that they are the community of Muhammad, peace be upon him, while al-Hasan says they are the believers among the People of the Book. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the phrase may be linked to 'those who are mindful of God' or stand as an independent clause, with an implied pronoun or a repeated noun serving as the link. On recitation, most read 'yumassikun' with a doubled letter, while 'Asim, through Abu Bakr, and Abu al-Aliya read 'yumsikun'. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the doubled form, since one says 'tamassaktu bi-l-shay''. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi explain that the prayer is singled out to show its excellence as the pillar of the religion. Ibn 'Ashur observes that, placed after the earlier reproaches, the verse contrasts these believers with those who abandoned the Torah.

This passage from Surat al-A'raf describes the moment God lifted the mountain above the Children of Israel when they refused to accept the laws of the Torah. The mountain was uprooted and held above them like a canopy, and they thought it was about to fall on them. They were told to take what had been given to them with strength and to remember what is in it, so that they might be mindful of God.

The commentators agree that "nataqna" means to raise up or to uproot. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take this sense, while al-Zamakhshari notes that its root meaning is to shake or pull out, as when butter is drawn from a waterskin, and Abu 'Ubayda and others cite verses of poetry in support. The word "dhulla" means anything that gives shade, such as a canopy or a cloud. On "wa dhannu", most exegetes read it as "they were certain", but al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi understand a strong expectation, and Ibn 'Atiyya argues that certainty does not fit because Moses set a condition, so he prefers strong likelihood.

The commentators agree on the report transmitted by al-Hasan al-Basri, that each Jew fell prostrate on his left brow while watching the mountain with his right eye for fear of its fall, and that this posture persists among Jews. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan also relate that the Torah made mountains, trees and stones tremble. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur see these accounts as images or vivid signs meant to impress the mind, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat them as transmitted events.

This verse tells that God brought forth the offspring of the children of Adam from their loins and made them bear witness against themselves, asking, "Am I not your Lord?" They answered, "Yes, we bear witness," lest they say on the Day of Resurrection, "We were unaware of this," or "Our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were their descendants." The commentators differ on its meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, relying on reports traced to the Prophet, Ibn Abbas and Umar, take the event literally: God drew out Adam's descendants and took from them a covenant acknowledging His lordship, binding on every human being. Al-Tabari notes that some reports place it at Nu'man near Arafat and others in India. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi read it as a figure of speech: God set up proofs of His lordship which human minds acknowledge, as if they had testified. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as the implanting of the recognition of the one God in human nature. Al-Razi adopts the traditional reading while discussing at length how such a covenant could be forgotten, and offers replies. Ibn al-Qayyim accepts the meaning of these reports but questions some chains of transmission. Al-Sa'di considers the fitra the more sound reading, since the text itself does not prove the event. Grammarians differ over "an taqulu": the Basran school supplies "lest," the Kufans "so that ... not." Readers divide over the second and third person forms. The verse thus removes the excuses of forgetfulness and of blindly following ancestors.

This verse reports that God took a covenant from the descendants of Adam, having them acknowledge His lordship, so that on the Day of Resurrection people could not plead heedlessness or the imitation of their ancestors in associating others with God. The commentators explain that, had this covenant not been taken and no messenger come to recall it, the disbelievers would have had two arguments: that they were heedless, and that they followed misguided forefathers. The witnessing therefore cuts off both pleas. Al-Tabari holds that the two readings, with ya and with ta, are both sound and agree in meaning. Ibn Kathir sees in it evidence of the fitra, the natural disposition on which God created people. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi read it as the establishment of proofs and of reasoning faculties leading to acknowledgment of divine lordship, which amounts to a real testimony. Several scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, hold that the covenant literally occurred in the world of atoms, relying on reported traditions, whereas the Mu'tazilites reject this and al-Razi refutes it with rational arguments. Al-Qurtubi notes that the hadith related from 'Umar has a broken chain, though its meaning is upheld through other transmissions. Heedlessness is not accepted as an excuse, since the proofs and the ability to reflect were present, as al-Shawkani and al-Alusi stress. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the address concerns Arab polytheists rather than the Jews, and that monotheism is rooted in human nature.

In this verse God explains that just as He has made the signs of this sura clear, including the punishments He sent upon earlier nations for their disbelief and association of partners with Him, He likewise makes the signs clear to the people of the Prophet ﷺ so that they may take heed, desist from associating partners with God, repent and return to monotheism. The commentators connect the verse to what precedes it, namely the covenant taken from the descendants of Adam, and they differ on its meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, relying on the transmitted reports, understand that God brought forth the offspring of Adam from his back like particles and made them acknowledge His lordship, so that this acknowledgment serves as evidence against them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di see instead an image of the innate disposition, the fitra, which God placed in human nature so that reason itself bears witness to the Oneness of God. Al-Razi and Ibn Sa'di object that people do not remember any such covenant. As for the story of Balaam son of Ba'ura that follows the verse, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas identify him as a man of the Children of Israel or of the Canaanites who was given God's signs and then cast them off, others say it was Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and al-Tabari notes that the signs may mean the Greatest Name, prophethood or a divine book without settling the man's identity. The common lesson is that heedlessness and blind imitation of one's forefathers are no excuse once the proofs are clear.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to recite to his people the story of a man to whom He gave His signs, but who withdrew from them and cast them behind his back. Satan then caught up with him and led him astray, and he became one of the misguided. The commentators broadly agree that the signs are the proofs of God's oneness, that withdrawing from them means abandoning them after knowing them, and that he was not raised by them because he inclined to the earth and followed his desires. His likeness is that of a panting dog, whether it is chased or left alone. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Ibn Kathir identify him as Bal'am ibn Ba'ura (or Bal'am ibn Ba'ir), who was pressed by his people to curse Moses and was tested for it. Others, including 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Zayd ibn Aslam, name Umayya ibn Abi as-Salt al-Thaqafi, while al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan speak of hypocrites among the People of the Book, and Qatada sees a general example of one who rejects guidance once it is offered. On the meaning of the signs, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and as-Suddi say it is the Greatest Name of God, others a revealed scripture, and Mujahid prophethood, which al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir reject since prophets are protected from error. Tabari does not choose among these views and holds that the text should be taken at its apparent sense. Several commentators, Ibn al-Qayyim among them, explain the dog comparison as greed and attachment to worldly things.

This passage says that God could have raised the man who had received His signs through them, but he inclined to the earth and followed his desire, so his state is likened to a dog that pants whether it is chased or left alone. The commentators say the example applies to those who denied God's signs, and that the Prophet ﷺ is to recount these stories so that they might reflect. As to who the man was, opinions differ. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid identify him as Balaam son of Ba'ura, who knew the Greatest Name or had knowledge of the signs and, under pressure from his people, cursed Moses' army. Others, including Ibn 'Abbas in another report, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, name Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt or the monk Abu 'Amir. Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate lengthy accounts about Balaam, while Ibn Kathir and Razi stress that the verse is severe for scholars who incline to this world.

The commentators agree that inclining to the earth means attachment to the pleasures of this world. They differ on the promised elevation: for Ibn 'Abbas it is elevation through knowledge, for Mujahid being protected from disbelief, and Tabari holds it includes rank, honour and a good reputation. On the dog comparison, Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and Tabari see it as the image of one who reads the Book without acting on it, whereas Sudi reports that Balaam literally panted like a dog. Ibn Kathir considers the figurative sense more likely. Ibn 'Ashur links the comparison to the polytheists who received the Qur'an and rejected it.

The commentators explain that this verse condemns those who denied Our signs, calling their example evil and stating that they wronged only themselves. Al-Tabari and the grammarians note that « sa'a » here means « bi'sa » (how evil), and that the sentence contains an omission: the word « example » is dropped and « the people » takes its place. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the second clause in two ways: either it joins the relative clause, so that they combined denying the signs with wronging themselves, or it stands apart, meaning they wronged no one but themselves, the fronted object signalling exclusivity. All agree that wrongdoing here is disbelief, which deprives its bearer of good in this world and the next. For the preceding passage, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas identify the man who was given the signs and abandoned them as Bal'am ibn Ba'ura, Abd Allah ibn 'Amr names Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, while Mujahid and others take it as a general example of anyone who knows the truth and does not act on it. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain the comparison with the dog: it pants whether chased or left alone, so the misguided man is not moved by admonition or its absence. Al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i stress the baseness of the image, and al-Razi observes that denial strips a person of dignity.

This verse states that guidance and misguidance belong to God alone: whom God guides is truly the guided one, and whom He leaves astray is among the losers. Al-Tabari explains that the guided person is one whom God has enabled to reach the truth and to obey Him, while the misguided one is one whom God has forsaken, and that loss means ruin. Ibn Kathir follows this reading and takes from it that there is no misleader for the one God guides and no guide for the one He misleads, supporting this with Ibn Mas'ud's sermon hadith; al-Shawkani, al-Qasimi, Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri share this line. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note a grammatical point: the word "the guided" is singular, following the form of "whom", while "the losers" is plural, following its meaning. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur repeat this observation. Al-Razi sets out the Mu'tazilite readings, which tie guidance to reward in the afterlife or to divine favours, judges most of them strained, and concludes that guidance and misguidance come only from God. Al-Qurtubi and al-Sam'ani read the verse as a rebuttal of the Qadariyya. Al-Nasafi argues that if guidance were mere explanation, believer and disbeliever would be equal, so it must be a divine grant of success. Ibn 'Ashur understands guidance here as God's decree that the person be guided. The verse closes the preceding account of the man who turned away from God's signs.

This verse states that God created many jinn and humans for Hell, meaning that He created them knowing they would end there because of their disbelief. It describes them as having hearts with which they do not understand truth and guidance, eyes with which they do not see God's signs, and ears with which they do not hear the Qur'an's admonitions. They are therefore likened to cattle, and indeed judged more astray, since cattle perceive what benefits and harms them and follow their keeper, whereas these people left their God-given faculties unused. The commentators agree that the verse concerns those who persist in disbelief, and that this neglect results from their turning away from truth rather than from a fixed nature. Ibn Juzayy clarifies that the negation of hearing and sight does not mean they lack perception altogether, but that they do not benefit from it in matters of religion. On the meaning of the lam in 'for Hell', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others take it as the lam of outcome, God knowing their destiny. Al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites read the phrase as an image of their deep immersion in disbelief, while al-Razi cites it as evidence for the Sunni position on the creation of actions. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi keep the apparent sense with qualifications. Some report that these are children born of unlawful unions, a view Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan reject. Most conclude that the verse warns against heedlessness toward God's signs, and that cattle are in a better state than these people, because they were made only for what they do, whereas humans were given reason and choice.

The commentators explain that the most beautiful names belong to God alone, meaning names that express the noblest meanings, and that believers should call upon Him by them in prayer, praise and worship. Most agree that the "deviators" are the polytheists who derived the names of their idols from God's names: al-Lat from Allah, al-Uzza from al-Aziz, and Manat from al-Mannan, as reported by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, and repeated by al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir.

Many cite the hadith of Abu Hurayra that God has ninety-nine names, and whoever memorises them enters Paradise. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim note that the detailed list is of doubtful origin, and al-Nawawi and Ibn al-Qayyim hold that the hadith does not restrict the names to that number, a view Ibn Hazm disputes, judging the reports confused. On the meaning of the verb yulhidun, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas takes it as denial, Qatada as associating partners with God, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan as swerving from the truth in describing God, and al-Sa'di as twisting the names from their intended meaning.

On the reading, Hamza reads yalhadun with fatha, while the others read yulhidun, and al-Tabari holds that both forms mean the same. On whether the command to "leave them" is abrogated, Ibn Zayd considers the verse abrogated by fighting, whereas al-Tabari, al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy read it as a threat rather than an abrogation. Some commentators mention an occasion of revelation: a man who called upon Allah and al-Rahman in his prayer drew the objection of a polytheist.

This verse speaks of a community (ummah), that is, a large group or band among the creatures God has made, who are guided by the truth, call to it, and judge between people by it. The commentators read it as the counterpart of the preceding verse about those created for Hell: it describes another category, destined for Paradise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that this community is the community of Muhammad, relying on narrations from Qatada, Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabi' ibn Anas in which the Prophet links this verse with verse 159 of al-A'raf about the people of Moses, and on the hadith of Mu'awiya about a group within the community that remains upright in the truth. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Baghawi, means the emigrants, the helpers and their faithful followers. Others, such as al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan, say they are the scholars and preachers of the religion. Ibn Jurayj, al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Sa'ib mention believers among the People of the Book or all of creation, and al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi also record that the prophets are meant. The commentators do not settle the matter. Al-Razi and al-Jubba'i draw from it an argument for the authority of consensus and for the claim that no era is free of people upholding the truth, while Abu Hayyan disputes that reading. Ibn 'Ashur sees in it a praise of the Muslims set against the misguidance of the polytheists.

The commentators explain that this verse concerns those who denied God's signs, meaning His proofs, indications and the Qur'an, and did not take heed from them. The prevailing sense of istidraj is that God leads them gradually, step by step, by granting them favours and respite, so that they feel secure and think they are right, and then seizes them suddenly when they are unaware. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir give this meaning, while al-Dahhak and Sufyan al-Thawri add that each act of disobedience is met with a new blessing that makes them forget gratitude. Al-Kalbi adds that God makes their deeds appear fair to them before destroying them. The word imla' means granting a long respite, and Ibn 'Abbas explains that "My plan is firm" means that His seizing is strong. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that it is called a plan because it looks like kindness while in reality it is abandonment.

Opinions differ on who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the people of Mecca, and some specifically the mockers of Quraysh. Al-Razi considers this too narrow and holds that the wording is general and covers all who deny, unless evidence excludes some. As for the subject of "they do not know", al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi suggest it refers either to their not knowing that this is istidraj or not knowing that it leads to ruin. Al-Razi reports that al-Jubba'i took the punishment to be in this world or the next, while some predestinarians read it as leading them into further disbelief, an interpretation he rejects since the verb is in the future tense.

In the wider context, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi relate this verse to the community that guides by the truth, set against those who reject it. The verses that follow call for reflection on the Prophet, accused of madness, and on the dominion of the heavens and the earth, with the occasion of revelation recounted by Qatada concerning Mount Safa.

This verse states that God grants respite to those who deny His signs, prolonging their lives so that they increase in their transgressions, and that His stratagem is firm and powerful. The commentators explain istidraj as a gradual leading, step by step, in which blessings are given while the people do not realise they are being led to their ruin. Al-Tabari links imla' to a long period of delay and explains that matin means strong and firm. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir agree that kayd means scheming or punishment, and that the respite increases rebellion and therefore the torment. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that it is called kayd because its outward appearance is kindness while its reality is abandonment. Ibn 'Abbas interprets the kayd as a severe plot. Some report that the verse was revealed about the mockers of Quraysh whom God destroyed in one night, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya extend it to all who deny the signs. Al-Razi sets out a theological debate: Sunni scholars see in the verse proof that God directs the servant towards disbelief, whereas al-Jubba'i replies that istidraj leads to punishment. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that Ibn 'Amir's reading with an open hamza gives the sense of 'because'. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi stress the figurative force of the expression.

This verse rebukes the disbelievers for not reflecting on the state of the Prophet ﷺ, so that they would see there is no madness in him as they claim. He is only a clear warner who cautions them against God's punishment if they persist in disbelief. The commentators agree that the question "Have they not reflected?" is a rebuke, and that the denial "there is no madness in their companion" answers the accusation of insanity made against him.

The occasion of revelation, reported from Qatada and cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and others, is that the Prophet climbed Safa one night and called the clans of Quraysh one by one, warning them of God's punishment. One of them then said that their companion was mad, for he had cried out all night until morning.

Al-Razi explains that the ignorant accused him of madness for two reasons: his conduct differed from theirs, as he turned away from worldly things, and he experienced a state resembling a faint when revelation descended. He argues that his wisdom, eloquence and character exclude any madness. Ibn Sa'di notes that their long companionship with him should have shown them his integrity. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the word "clear" addresses those who did not benefit from the warning, which removes any excuse they might have.

The commentators connect this passage to what precedes it, namely istidraj and the respite granted. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that istidraj means leading the disbelievers step by step towards their ruin through successive favours that deceive them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat the word "plot" as a figure of speech, since the outward appearance is a kindness while the reality is abandonment. The verse then invites reflection on the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and on the approach of death; Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read this as an invitation to infer the Creator from creation.

This verse calls people to reflect on the realm of the heavens and the earth, that is, God's vast dominion, and on everything He has created, so that they may find in it proof of His oneness and perfect power. The commentators add that people should also consider that their own term may be near, and hasten to believe before death overtakes them in disbelief. Most take the pronoun in 'after it' to refer to the Quran, so the sense is: what speech will they believe in after rejecting the Quran? Others refer it to the Prophet ﷺ or to the term of life. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the question as a rebuke and a warning, since after such clear evidence no further message remains to be awaited. Al-Zamakhshari links the question to the phrase 'perhaps their term has drawn near', as if to ask why they do not hasten to believe in the Quran before it is too late. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan take the verse as evidence that reflection and reasoning are obligatory. Ibn Kathir explains istidraj as successive blessings that lead their recipients deeper into disobedience. Ibn Abbas links the nearness of the term to Badr or Uhud. All agree that whom God leads astray has no guide and remains in his transgression, though they differ on whether 'ya'mahun' means being lost or hesitating.

This verse states that whoever Allah leads astray has no guide, and that Allah leaves them in their rebellion, wandering in confusion. Al-Tabari explains that their turning away is caused by Allah's misguidance: had He guided them, they would have reflected and seen their right path. He adds that Allah leaves them in their persistence so that they deserve the punishment He has decreed. The commentators agree that the word ya'mahun means to wander, be bewildered or hesitate. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya draw from this that guidance and misguidance belong to Allah, while al-Zamakhshari notes that the singular "man" and the plural "yadharuhum" show that the rule covers everyone. The readings differ on "wa yadharuhum": some read it with a yā and a damma, others with a nūn, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a yā and a jazm, matching the position of the conditional answer. Ibn 'Ashur observes that this judgment is general, and that people do not know who is thus destined to error, a matter known to Allah alone. Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri explain that Allah leads deniers step by step toward ruin, granting them blessings and respite, and that His scheme is firm. Al-Shawkani reports that this respite consists of favours that distract them from gratitude. These commentaries connect this verse to the preceding one, which calls for reflection on creation and the approach of death.

The disbelievers ask the Prophet ﷺ when the Hour will come, and God instructs him to answer that knowledge of it rests with his Lord alone, who alone will reveal it at its appointed time. Its knowledge has been hidden from the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, so that neither a nearby angel nor a sent prophet knows its time, and it will come suddenly, while people are heedless. The commentators agree that this concealment is a divine wisdom: since people do not know when it will happen, they remain vigilant, which encourages obedience and restrains sin. They differ on the meaning of 'thaqulat' (it weighed heavy): al-Tabari, al-Hasan and Ibn Jarir take it to mean that its arrival is heavy upon the heavens and the earth because of its terror; Qatada takes it that the knowledge of its time weighs heavily on the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth; as-Suddi understands that it remained hidden; Ibn Juraij holds that it weighs on the heavens and earth because of the upheavals it brings. On 'ka'annaka hafiyyun 'anha' (as if you were insistent in asking about it), Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak take it to mean: as if you already knew it, having pressed hard with questions. Others, including Ibn 'Abbas in another report and Qatada, read it as: as if you were close to them by kinship and favoured them with this knowledge; Ibn Kathir considers the first reading more convincing. Most commentators conclude that most people fail to realise that this knowledge belongs to God alone, and assume that human beings can attain it.

God instructs His Prophet to declare that he possesses for himself neither benefit nor harm except what God wills, that had he known the unseen he would have multiplied good and no evil would have touched him, and that he is only a warner and a bringer of good news to a believing people. The commentators agree that the verse displays servanthood and disavows any claim to knowledge of the unseen, and that it answers the polytheists' questions about the Hour. The meaning of multiplying good, however, is disputed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jurayj, followed by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, take it as righteous deeds: had he known his term, he would have increased his acts of devotion. Ibn Abbas, and the commentators who follow him, understand wealth and storing up plenty for lean years, with al-Farra' cited on the same point. Al-Mawardi lists several opinions, and Ibn Atiyya widens the sense to everything. Al-Razi prefers answering questions and matters of religion. As for harm, al-Hasan takes it as the madness the Quraysh attributed to the Prophet, while most read poverty, injury or denial. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see a lesson in humility. On the phrase for a believing people, many attach it to both warning and good tidings, since only believers benefit from them, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy attach it to good tidings alone, with the object of the warning left implied as the disbelievers. Most conclude that the verse defines the limits of the Prophet's mission: he warns and announces, and knows the unseen only what God teaches him.

This verse recalls that God created you from a single soul, Adam, and made from it his spouse Eve, so that he might find rest and affection with her. When he came to her, she conceived a light burden which she carried without distress, and when it grew heavy, the two of them called upon God to grant them a righteous child so that they would be among the grateful. The commentators agree that the passage affirms God's oneness and refutes associationism. As for the single soul, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it to mean Adam, while al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi stress that all humanity descends from one father. The nature of the association attributed to the couple is also debated. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir explain it as naming the child Abd al-Harith at the urging of Iblis, which they treat as associationism in the name rather than in worship, while al-Wahidi and others note that some relate it to people of other faiths. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi attribute the passage to the Quraysh, descendants of Qusayy, whereas Ibn Juzayy finds that view unconvincing. Al-Hasan and Ibn Atiyya hold that the association concerns the descendants of Adam in general. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi observe that the reports about Iblis largely come from earlier scriptural sources and cannot be accepted without reservation. The verse closes by declaring God exalted above what the associators ascribe to Him.

The commentators explain that this verse describes a couple who, after Allah granted them a healthy child as they had asked, made partners in what He had given them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the verse concerns Adam and Eve, relying on a hadith narrated by Samura ibn Jundub and reports from Ibn Abbas that they named their son Abd al-Harith at the urging of Satan. For them the association was only in the name and in obedience, not in worship, since Adam was a prophet protected from shirk. Al-Mawardi, al-Samani, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi largely agree, and al-Samani compares it to people naming children Abd al-Dayf or Abd Yaghuth without harming monotheism. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatada, by contrast, hold that the verse refers to the descendants of Adam, such as polytheists or Jews and Christians, with the pronouns referring to the human species rather than to the two parents. Ibn Kathir considers this the best interpretation, while al-Razi rejects the Abd al-Harith account on rational grounds and reads the verse as describing the polytheists of Mecca or all of Adam's children. Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur also read the passage as a rebuke of idol worship, since idols create nothing, cannot help, and cannot guide. Some commentators link the verse to Qusayy ibn Kilab and his offspring, a reading Ibn Atiyya finds unconvincing. All agree on the conclusion that Allah is exalted above what they associate with Him.

In this verse God rebukes those who associate with Him what creates nothing, when these idols are themselves created. The commentators explain that the phrase 'and they are created' refers to the idols, which are spoken of as if they had reason because their worshippers regarded them as divine. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take it that the idols are carved and made, and so created, which makes them inferior to those who fashion them. The following verses, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi explain, stress that these idols cannot help their worshippers or defend themselves, that they do not hear a call to guidance, and that calling on them or remaining silent makes no difference. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the nominal sentence 'and you are silent' expresses the constant habit of these people, who called on God alone in times of distress. Opinions differ on the subject of the verse. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi relate, following Ibn Zayd, that it concerns Adam and Eve, who named their child Abd Shams or Abd al-Harith on Iblis's advice. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur hold that it addresses the Arab polytheists and their idols. Ibn Atiyya considers the reading that ties the verse to Adam to be strained, and Ibn Kathir finds it less likely. Al-Razi prefers the reading about the idolaters, judging it more coherent with the sequence of the verses. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the plural pronouns are used according to the worshippers' belief, a point on which the commentators broadly agree.

This verse states that the idols worshipped by the polytheists cannot help their worshippers nor defend themselves, because they are lifeless, created objects. Al-Tabari explains that a worshipper turns to his god to gain a benefit or ward off harm, yet these deities bring neither benefit nor harm to anyone. Al-Baghawi, quoting al-Hasan, adds that they cannot repel someone who wants to break them. Ibn Kathir recounts how Mu'adh ibn 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh found his idol defiled, washed it, and left a sword beside it, until he realised the futility of his worship.

The commentators agree that an inability to defend oneself makes the inability to help others even more evident. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note that the worshippers, not the idols, were the ones who protected them. Abu al-Su'ud explains that the word "victory" is used to match the earlier wording, and that the idols are not called creatures here because they are not fit to be helped. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the emphasis on victory reflects the Arabs' culture of raids and vengeance, in which triumph was highly valued.

Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi discuss the grammar: although the idols are objects, they are referred to with the pronoun used for rational beings, because the polytheists believed they had intelligence. Ibn 'Ashur also notes that the present tense signals repeated occurrence. Commentators differ on the context: al-Tabari, al-Suyuti and others read the verse as addressing the polytheists of Mecca, while al-Tha'alibi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that some scholars linked the preceding verses to Adam and Eve and their naming of a child. The majority view holds that the verse is an argument against polytheism through reason, showing that worship presupposes the power to benefit and to avert harm, which these idols lack.

This verse states that the idols worshipped by the polytheists cannot follow one who calls them to guidance and cannot respond to those who invoke them. They are lifeless and without hearing or reason, so calling them or remaining silent makes no difference. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain that the address is to the polytheists, and that the idols do not answer as God answers those who call upon Him. Ibn Kathir adds that they do not even hear the call. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy note two possible readings: the pronoun may refer to the idols, or to the unbelievers, in which case the Prophet and the believers are being addressed. Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari observe that the nominal clause "and you are silent" is used to show the lasting nature of that silence, since the polytheists turned to their idols only in times of hardship. Al-Razi and al-Sha'rawi develop the same point, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur also stress the rhetorical reason of verse endings. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the idols are addressed as rational beings according to the belief of their worshippers. On recitation, Nafi' reads "yattabi'ukum" with a lighter form, while the others use the doubled form, with little difference in meaning. The commentators agree that the verse exposes the futility of worshipping what cannot hear or guide.

This verse says that the beings the polytheists call upon besides God are servants like themselves, owned and created by Him, and so they do not deserve worship. The commentators agree that the purpose is to challenge and rebuke the idolaters: if these idols were gods, they should answer those who call upon them. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi explain that 'servants' means they are possessed and created by God. Al-Zamakhshari reads the phrase ironically: at best the idols are living, reasoning beings, and then they are no better than their worshippers. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note that the idols are lifeless objects lacking perception, and that the address to them in the language of rational beings follows the beliefs of their worshippers. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir stress that the idols cannot create, help or answer, whereas humans have hearing, sight and strength. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi list the missing limbs of the idols: no feet to walk, no hands to grasp, no eyes to see, no ears to hear. Al-Sam'ani notes that 'servants' can mean subjected and made to submit, and reports that Muqatil took the phrase to refer to angels, a view he calls weaker. Ibn al-Qayyim takes the verse as proof that idols are mere forms empty of any divine attribute. Several commentators also discuss a variant reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, which grammarians explain differently. Overall, the commentators present the verse as a demonstration of the helplessness of whatever is worshipped besides God.

This verse, in the context of the preceding verses, shows that the idols worshipped by the polytheists are created beings owned by God like themselves, and that they cannot walk, grasp, see or hear, so they do not deserve worship. The commentators explain that a human being is superior to these idols, since he has feet to walk with, hands to strike with, eyes to see with and ears to hear with; how then can the superior worship what is inferior to him? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, as well as the Tafsir al-Jalalayn, share this basic reading, which is a rebuke and an argument against the helplessness of the idols. Al-Razi offers two ways of developing this proof: first, the superiority of the human over the idol; second, establishing that the idols cannot bring benefit or harm. All agree on the meaning of the command 'Call your associates, then plot against me and give me no respite': it is a challenge and an demonstration of incapacity, meaning that the adversaries cannot harm the Prophet ﷺ, who fears nothing because of God's protection. Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi report several readings, including Ibn Jubayr's reading with a light 'in' and 'ibadan', which al-Nahhas considers not to be recited, as well as the reading 'yabtushun' with a u vowel. Ibn 'Ashur and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the order in which the organs are mentioned follows a progression tied to the purpose of giving help. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di stress the weakness of the idols as lifeless objects and God's protection of the righteous. Disagreement concerns mainly linguistic details, readings and rhetorical explanations rather than the general meaning.

The commentators explain that this verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to tell the idolaters that his protector and helper is God, who sent down the Book, and that He supports the righteous among His servants and does not forsake them. It belongs to the challenge issued to the polytheists: call upon your partners and plot against me without delay. All agree that wilaya here means support and protection, and the verses before it establish the powerlessness of the idols, which have limbs but neither walk, strike, see nor hear, being created beings like their worshippers and unworthy of worship. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold that the wali is God, and that the sending down of the Book is the sign of this guardianship, with al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi adding that it is His custom to help the righteous. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan set out the readings of the word (waliyyiya); al-Qurtubi reports from Abu 'Amr al-Dani a reading (waliyya Allah) in the annexed form, which would refer to Gabriel according to those who accept it. Al-Akhfash and al-Nahhas attribute it to al-Jahdari, which Abu Hatim considered weak, while the majority holds that the meaning is God, as the surrounding verses confirm. Al-Sam'ani also mentions this reading. As for the righteous, Ibn 'Abbas describes them as those who associate nothing with God, while Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di describe them as those whose intentions, words and deeds are sound. Al-Razi and al-Shawkani stress that the idols can neither harm nor answer a call to guidance.

This verse says that those whom the idolaters invoke besides God cannot help them, nor can they help themselves. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi read it as a conclusion to the preceding argument: since the idols have no feet, hands, eyes or ears, they are shown to be powerless, whereas God is the protector of His righteous servants. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir explain that the verse answers the polytheists and belittles their gods, with Ibn Kathir stressing that these idols are lifeless creations. Al-Razi gives two readings: either the description applies to the idols, or it describes the polytheists themselves, who, because of their obstinacy, gain nothing from their sight or hearing. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan accept both readings as possible. Ibn Sa'di also notes that some say the verse refers to the disbelievers, though most commentators take the idols as the subject. Al-Qurtubi adds that the repetition of the phrase serves to emphasise that what they worship neither benefits nor harms. No legal ruling is drawn from this passage.

This verse states that the idols worshipped by the polytheists do not respond to anyone who calls them to guidance. They are lifeless objects that neither hear nor see, though they appear to look at the one who addresses them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that the Prophet ﷺ is the addressee and that the attributed gaze means the idols face their interlocutor without perceiving anything. Al-Kisa'i, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand this looking as mere facing, as one says that a house looks at another house. Al-Wahidi notes that the idols had eyes made of precious stones, which gave the impression that they were seeing.

Commentators agree that the passage aims to belittle the idols and show their helplessness. Al-Tabari notes that the singular pronoun after the plural shift comes from the address to the Prophet, and Ibn 'Atiyya observes that these attributes confirm that these supposed deities cannot even defend themselves.

However, opinions differ on who the pronoun refers to. Al-Sudi, Mujahid and Qatada, as well as Ibn Kathir in one of his reports, hold that it refers to the polytheists themselves, who look with their eyes but do not see the truth with their hearts. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the first reading, which fits the context better. Al-Razi notes that this reading separates looking from seeing and answers that seeing here means supposing. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur regard the phrase as an eloquent comparison, while al-Hasan reports a reading in which the address is to the believers, and al-Alusi finds this explanation acceptable.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet to accept what people offer easily in their conduct, not to demand of them what is burdensome, to enjoin what is right, and to turn away from the ignorant without answering their folly in kind. The commentators regard it as a summary of noble character, and Ja'far al-Sadiq is quoted saying that the Quran contains no verse more comprehensive in this respect. On the meaning of 'al-'afw', there are three views. Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan and 'Urwa take it to mean what is easy in people's manners, without probing or strain. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak take it to mean the surplus of wealth, before zakat was prescribed, which they hold was then abrogated. Ibn Zayd takes it as leniency toward the polytheists before the command to fight. Al-Tabari prefers the first view and rejects abrogation. On 'al-'urf', most explain it as what is known to be good, and a report attributed to Gabriel, whose chain Ibn Kathir weakens, explains it as pardoning those who wronged you, giving to those who withheld, and keeping ties with those who cut them. Regarding turning away from the ignorant, Ibn Zayd and 'Ata' consider it abrogated by the verse of the sword, while Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi consider it still in force, al-Qurtubi relying on the episode of al-Hurr ibn Qays with 'Umar. Al-Razi observes that turning away does not preclude fighting when commanded.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ that if an incitement from Satan reaches him, a prick or whisper that moves him to anger or to repay the ignorant in an improper way, he should seek refuge in God. The commentators explain that nazgh originally means a goad or a stirring up of discord, and that it is applied to Satan's whispering and urging toward sins. They agree that istiʿadha means seeking refuge and protection in God, and that God hears the plea and knows the state of the one who makes it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the verse came after the command to take pardon, enjoin what is good and turn away from the ignorant, when the Prophet ﷺ asked how to deal with anger. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read nazgh as a figurative expression for the onset of anger, comparing it to Abu Bakr's words about a devil that seizes him. Al-Razi, who draws on the argument about the infallibility of the prophets, holds that the address is a general instruction for all believers, and that seeking refuge works only when its meaning is present in the heart. He adds that the God-fearing, when a touch of Satan reaches them, remember and see clearly, whereas the brethren of the devils are carried on in error without cease. The readings ṭāʾif and ṭayf are noted, and the commentators treat their meanings as close, such as a passing thought or whisper.

This verse describes the conduct of the God-fearing: when a passing whisper or impulse from Satan touches them, they remember God's command, His prohibition, His reward and His punishment, and at once they regain their clear sight and turn back from sin. The readers differed over the word ṭā'if versus ṭayf. Al-Farra' and some grammarians treated them as meaning the same, something that visits a person like a dream, while al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' distinguished ṭayf as the passing whisper or lapse, and ṭā'if as what circles around a person. On its meaning, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr took it to be anger, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali ibn Abi Talha took it as a stirring or touch of Satan, and al-Kalbi as a sin. Al-Tabari concluded that these views are close in meaning, since anger and lapse both come from Satan's prompting, and he preferred a general reading. The remembrance is explained by Sa'id ibn Jubayr as restraining anger, by Mujahid as abandoning a sinful intention by remembering God, and by al-Zajjaj as reflection on God's proofs. Ibn Kathir reports that the believers repent quickly after a slip. The verse is contrasted with the fate of those who follow the devils, whom the devils keep pushing deeper into error without let-up. Commentators differ on whether the pronoun for their brothers refers to the devils or to the disbelievers.

This verse describes those who are the brothers of the devils, the disbelievers and sinners: the devils extend them in error, urge them on and make it grow, and they neither stop nor hold back. The commentators contrast their fate with that of the God-conscious: when a touch from Satan reaches the latter, they remember God's command and prohibition, see clearly and stop. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the pronoun in 'their brothers' to refer to the devils, who never relax their enticement, and they present this as a lasting nature. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi prefer to take the brothers as the disbelievers themselves, since 'brothers' is set against 'those who feared God'. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the pronoun may refer to the devils, the unbelievers being their followers. On the reading, Nafi' reads 'yumiddunahum' with the causative form, while the others read 'yamuddunahum'. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi keep the majority reading, because the verb used for evil is usually 'madda'. On 'la yuqsirun', some understand 'do not stop', others 'do not diminish'. Ibn 'Abbas says that humans do not refrain from their bad deeds and the devils do not cease to urge them on. The commentators do not settle these questions, and each reading has its own coherence.

This verse reports that when revelation was delayed or the Prophet did not bring the sign the disbelievers demanded, they said to him: why did you not invent it yourself? The commentators agree on the answer he is commanded to give: he follows only what is revealed to him by his Lord, and he does not invent or propose signs on his own initiative. The verse commands believers to listen attentively when the Qur'an is recited and to remain silent, so that they may understand its meaning, take heed of its admonitions, and hope for God's mercy. The commentators agree that the listening and silence are owed to Qur'anic recitation as a mark of honour and reflection. They differ, however, on the setting. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and al-Nakha'i hold that it concerns the prayer, meaning that one should not talk or recite aloud behind the imam; al-Tabari adopts this view, citing the authentic report, "When the imam recites, be silent." Mujahid, 'Ata' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr apply it to the Friday sermon, a view rejected by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, who note that the sura is Meccan while the sermon was instituted in Medina, and that little Qur'an is recited in sermons. Ibn Sa'di and others take a broader reading covering both prayer and sermon, while al-Razi argues that the address may originally have been to the disbelievers during the early preaching. Ibn Juzayy and al-Zamakhshari regard the general meaning as the strongest, since the wording is universal. Al-Alusi reports the Hanafi and Shafi'i positions on reciting behind the imam, and most scholars consider silence outside prayer to be recommended.

This verse commands the Prophet, and through him every believer, to remember his Lord within himself with humility and awe, in a voice that is neither loud nor silent, at the beginning and end of the day, and not to be among the heedless. Most commentators hold that the address is to the Prophet but applies to the whole community, and that the remembrance covers recitation, supplication, glorification and other forms of dhikr. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Mujahid, read it as an exhortation to remember God often, and they reject the view of Ibn Zayd and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd that it means listening silently to the Qur'an during its recitation. Ibn Zayd himself takes it as the worshipper reciting quietly after the imam, while Ibn Abbas takes it as reciting in the prayer in a low voice. On the meaning of the terms, all agree that tadarru' is humility and khifa is fear of God. Linguists differ over al-aasal, the plural of asil or of asl, which denotes the late afternoon until sunset. Mujahid and Qatada specify that al-ghuduw is the dawn prayer and al-aasal the afternoon prayer. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that inner remembrance and reflection accompany the remembrance of the tongue, and that fear must be joined with hope. The verse then mentions the angels who do not disdain to worship their Lord, who glorify Him and prostrate before Him, so that believers may follow their example. Most commentators consider this the first prostration verse of the Qur'an.

This verse describes the angels who are near your Lord: they do not disdain His worship, they glorify Him, and they prostrate before Him alone. The commentators read it as an encouragement to believers to imitate them in devotion and in remembrance of God. Nearly all explain "near your Lord" as nearness of rank and favour rather than of place. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan stress this, while al-Razi calls it nearness of honour and compares it to a vizier's closeness to a king. On the glorification, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir understand it both as declaring God free of every flaw and as the words "Glory be to God", and Ibn Kathir treats it as inner purity joined to outward remembrance. On prostration, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean prayer, others take it to mean submission and humility. Al-Razi notes that placing the object first signals exclusivity: they prostrate to no one but God. The commentators agree that this is the first prostration of recitation in the Quran and that it is recommended for the reader and listener. They differ on whether it is obligatory: Abu Hanifa holds it to be obligatory, while Malik and al-Shafi'i do not. Some reports cited by al-Wahidi and al-Mawardi link the verse to the Meccans who refused to prostrate, showing them that the angels, higher than they are, still prostrate before God.
